title: rplatypus
text:
A detector that knows three classes, followed by a classifier that knows eighty: find the objects, cut them out, hand the pieces to something else. predict() returns boxes in each image’s own pixels precisely so they can be used on the photograph they came from, and this is what uses them.



detection_crops(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "test",
  score_threshold = NULL,
  context = 0,
  size = NULL,
  fit = "letterbox",
  ...
)







object


A platypus_fit() from a detection specification.




model


Which model, if the fit holds several.




split


Which split’s images to read.




score_threshold


Crop at this confidence instead of the specification’s operating_point.




context


Expand every box by this fraction of its own width and height, per side.




size


c(height, width) every crop is brought to, or NULL to keep each as cut. Crops of one image differ in size otherwise, which is why this returns a list either way.




fit


“letterbox” to preserve the aspect by padding, “stretch” to fill the frame.




…


Unused.






Cut from the image at its native size, not from the square the network sees. Cropping the letterboxed frame would cut a shrunken object and then scale it back up: on a 1024-wide photograph fed to a 416 model, every crop would be two fifths of the size the data allows.
Four more decisions, each of which taken the other way changes what a downstream model sees without changing anything you would notice:


Rounded outward, so the crop contains the whole box. Rounding to nearest loses up to a pixel per side, which on a 26-pixel platelet is a twelfth of the object.


context grows with the box, not by a number of pixels, so one value suits a platelet and a white cell. Zero by default: a detector’s box is tight by construction, and a classifier trained on whole objects does worse on something cut exactly at the edge - but expanding silently would put things nobody asked for into every crop.


size letterboxes rather than stretches. Resizing a tall box to a square changes the aspect of every non-square object, and a classifier then sees a shape that does not occur in nature. fit = “stretch” is there for models trained that way, and has to be asked for.


Read at operating_point, not at the specification’s score_threshold. That one sits near zero so that average precision integrates the whole ranking - hundreds of boxes an image, almost all of them the tail it exists to measure over. Cropping those would hand a classifier mostly noise.


dropped is the number of boxes that clipped to nothing. A model may place a box off the frame and predict() reports what it said, so at a low threshold some arrive with no extent at all; those are dropped and counted rather than the arrays quietly coming back shorter than the detections.



A list with one entry per image, each a list of key, crops (a list of height x width x channels arrays), boxes, scores, labels, names and dropped.




library("rplatypus")

found <- detection_crops(fit, size = c(224, 224))
length(found[[1]]$crops)
plot_masks(found[[1]]$crops[[1]])        # look at one

# Everything above the operating point, as one flat list ready for another model.
pieces <- unlist(lapply(found, `[[`, "crops"), recursive = FALSE)

title: rplatypus
text:
The data block for task = “classification”. What this constructor is for is as much the fields it has not got as the two it adds: colormap, labels, regions, classes_from, channels_from and target_spacing all describe a mask or a grid, and a label is neither.



classification_data(
  train,
  validation = NULL,
  classes,
  test = NULL,
  split = NULL,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  strict_labels = TRUE,
  window = NULL,
  subdirs = NULL,
  column_sep = ";",
  shuffle = TRUE
)







train


Path to the training data: a directory of class directories in “nested_dirs” mode, or a CSV in “config_file” mode.




validation


Path to the validation data, or FALSE to train without one.




classes


The class names, in class order. Position is the class index the model learns, which is why it is written rather than read off the directory listing: taken from the filesystem the order would be alphabetical - reproducible, and unrelated to anything - so a model trained where index 1 meant “benign” and used where it means “malignant” reports plausible probabilities and nothing downstream can tell.
In “nested_dirs” mode these are the directory names. At least two, where detection_data() allows one: a detector with one class answers where are the cells, which is a question, and a classifier with one class answers is this a cell with the only answer it has.
There is no background entry. An image is one of these, and a picture of nothing in particular is a class somebody has to name.




test


Path to a held-out set, scored but never trained on.




split


A split() block, to cut a validation and test set out of the training data. For this task the cut is stratified by the engine, so every class reaches every side - a random 70/15/15 of 100 images at a 3% prevalence leaves some part with none of the rare class 91% of the time, and a per-class metric cannot average over a class its pass never held.




mode


“nested_dirs” or “config_file”.




strict_labels


Refuse an image whose label is not in classes. FALSE skips it instead, which is how to train on two of a dataset’s three classes without moving any files. It matters more here than it does for a box: a skipped object leaves the rest of its image in the training set, while a skipped image leaves nothing, so the same setting quietly changes how much data there is.




window


How values in real units reach the model, for DICOM and NIfTI - see segmentation_data(), which documents the named windows. Ignored for ordinary pictures.




subdirs


Refused, and named rather than dropped because every sibling data constructor has it. For segmentation and detection a sample is a directory with the image in one subdirectory and what labels it in the other; a classification sample is one image whose label is the directory it sits in, so there is no second subdirectory.




column_sep


For config_file, what separates several paths in one cell.




shuffle


Shuffle the training data between epochs.






Where the labelling is written follows from mode rather than being said twice. In “nested_dirs” mode the directories under train are the classes, with the images inside them - the layout nearly every image dataset ships in. In “config_file” mode the CSV’s label column holds the class name.



A data specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



classifier(), class_balance(), available_metrics()




library("rplatypus")

classification_data("train/", "valid/", classes = c("benign", "malignant"))

title: rplatypus
text:
What to report beside the loss for task = “classification”. These are a different family from metrics rather than more of it: there is no overlap to measure, no background class to leave out, and no smooth - a label is right or it is not.



metric_accuracy()

metric_balanced_accuracy()

metric_f1()

metric_auc()




They are also scored differently, and that is measured rather than stylistic. An overlap metric is a formula on counts, so averaging a batch’s scores is the score; three of these four are not means over images at all. On 4000 images at a prevalence of 3%, against a model whose own probabilities are the truth, pooling the whole pass against averaging batches of 8 moves balanced accuracy by 0.0035, macro F1 by 0.0734, and the AUC by up to 0.0371 in a direction that does not settle with a bigger batch - because at that prevalence 398 of 500 batches hold no positive at all, so a per-class recall is an average over whichever batches happened to contain the rare class. The engine therefore accumulates these over the pass and computes them once at the end.
metric_auc() is the engine’s default and the other three are offered rather than recommended. At a 3% prevalence a calibrated model never crosses the threshold, so everything read off the hard prediction sees the same all-negative answer: accuracy spans 0.0100 across models of genuinely different quality and is not even monotone - a model with no signal scores above two that have one - while the AUC spans 0.4631. Balanced accuracy and F1 do not rescue it; they move by 0.0000 and -0.0005 between a real signal and a collapse. Being threshold-free is the property that separates them.
So metric_accuracy() is here because it is the number people ask for, and its page says what it costs.



A metric specification.



classifier(), metrics for masks, class_balance() for the prevalence these measurements are all about




library("rplatypus")

metric_auc()

$name
[1] "auc"

# The number people ask for, beside the one that can tell a signal from a collapse.
classifier("cnn", input_shape = c(128, 128),
           metrics = list(metric_auc(), metric_accuracy()))

$metrics
$metrics[[1]]
$metrics[[1]]$name

$metrics[[2]]

title: rplatypus
text:
Masks come two ways, and this reads both. colormap is for masks stored as pictures, one colour per class. labels is for masks stored as label maps - a vector of the voxel values, in class order - which is how volume formats store them.



read_masks(paths, colormap = NULL, labels = NULL, size = NULL, tolerance = 0)







paths


Image files.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class. Give this or labels.




labels


The voxel value of each class, in class order: c(0, 1) for a binary segmentation. For NIfTI and other label maps. Give this or colormap.




size


c(height, width) to read at, or NULL to keep each image’s own size - which only works if they all agree.




tolerance


Passed to colours_to_classes(). Ignored for label maps, which are compared to within half a unit - a label map that has been resampled or merely passed through a float will not satisfy an exact comparison, and a label that fails to match becomes background.






An array of class indices, counted from 1.




library("rplatypus")

# Masks stored as pictures: the colormap says which colour is which class.
truth <- read_masks(list.files("masks/", full.names = TRUE),
                    colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 255, 255)))

# Masks stored as label maps, which is how volumes do it. Exactly one of the two.
truth <- read_masks("case_01/seg.nii.gz", labels = c(0, 1))

# `tolerance` is for masks that have been through a lossy resize, where a colour
# that should be (255, 0, 0) arrives as (254, 1, 0) and matches nothing.
truth <- read_masks(paths, colormap = voc_colormap, tolerance = 2)

title: rplatypus
text:
One function per fit rather than one per task, because the question - what does this model say about this split - is the same one. What comes back is not: a mask for segmentation, a table of boxes for detection, a label map of objects for instances, and a row per image for classification. The arguments that describe a grid are refused where there is no grid, by name, rather than accepted and ignored.



## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
predict(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "test",
  type = c("class", "probability", "channels"),
  space = c("model", "source"),
  cases = NULL,
  each = NULL,
  decode = NULL,
  ...
)







object


A platypus_fit().




model


Which model, by the name given in the specification. Defaults to the first one trained.




split


Which data to predict on.




type


“class” gives the class index per pixel, which is the mask to look at; “probability” keeps the per-class channel. “channels” is for an instance model only and means the model’s own output before any decoding: the class channels are probabilities and a flow field’s components are raw, which is why they are not called probabilities here - a softmax across a flow component and a class returns a number that means nothing. Read them with flow_to_colours().
On an instance fit, “class” is a label map of objects, numbered from 1, and “probability” is refused by name for the reason above.
With regions - overlapping classes - “class” is refused rather than computed. The channels are independent binary questions and do not compete, so the most likely one is not an answer: a pixel may be in three classes and naming one of them drops the rest with nothing in the result to say so. Ask for “probability” and write it with save_class_masks().
On a classification fit the two readings are a table and a matrix rather than two arrays: “class” gives one row per image with the answer and how sure the model was, and “probability” gives one row per image and one column per class. “channels” is refused - a classifier has no channels, only one number per class, and those numbers are the probabilities.




space


“model” or “source”; see above. Note that the two return different shapes of thing, an array and a list, because they are different things. Refused on a detection, instance or classification fit, each for its own reason - boxes are in the source image’s coordinates already, an object identity cannot survive resampling, and a label is not on a grid at all.




cases


Case names to predict, as evaluate_cases() reports them. With this the result is a named list of just those, in the order asked for. A name that is not in the split is an error rather than a missing entry. Both this and each exist so that a split of full-resolution masks never has to be in memory at once, so both are refused on a classification fit, where the whole answer is one row per image.




each


A function called as each(case, mask) once per image, instead of the predictions being returned together. Whatever it returns is collected under the case’s name; return NULL from it and nothing accumulates. This is the form that does not need the split to fit in memory.




decode


Which decoding turns the predicted channels into objects, by the name used in the model’s decode list. Unset takes the model’s first, which is the engine’s own default rather than one restated here. Instance models only; for anything else it is refused, because a semantic or detection fit decodes nothing.




…


Unused.






With space = “model”: for “class”, an integer array of image x height x width, classes numbered from 1 to match the colormap; for “probability”, the same with a trailing class axis. Tiled models return images at their original size, reassembled.
With space = “source”: a list of such arrays, one per scan, each on that scan’s grid, named by case. The name and the mask come out of one step of the engine’s own stream, so they cannot be misaligned - which matters because the usual next move is to join them to something else per case, and a list paired by position is one dropped batch away from naming the wrong picture.
On an instance fit: a list of integer label maps named by case, objects numbered from 1 and 0 for background, one entry per image. A list rather than an array for the reason the detection one is a list, and named rather than ordered because a list paired against case names by position is one dropped batch away from naming the wrong picture. Draw them with overlay_instances() and measure them with instance_sizes().
On a classification fit: for “class”, a data frame of one row per image with key (the name the split calls it, which is what joins this to anything else), label (what it was labelled, or NA on a split that carries no labelling), predicted and probability - the probability of the class that was chosen, not of the right one. For “probability”, a numeric matrix of images by classes, with the keys as row names and the class names as columns, in the order classes was written.



space = “model” returns everything on the grid the model worked at, stacked into one array. That is what training saw, and it is the only form that can be a single array, because a stack needs one shape.
space = “source” maps each prediction back onto the grid of the scan it was computed from - undoing the resampling and the crop - and therefore returns a list, one mask per scan. This is what you want for anything that has to meet the original data: laying a mask over the scan in a viewer, writing it beside the scan with save_volumes(), or measuring it in millilitres of the scan’s own voxels. Scans differ in size, so the list is not a limitation being worked around - resizing them to a common shape is exactly how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
Two things are lost mapping back, and neither can be recovered. Interpolation softens a boundary, so the mask returns slightly smoother than the model drew it. And where reading cropped anatomy away, the mask comes back padded with background - which means not examined, not nothing there. Give the model an input_shape that covers the anatomy if that distinction matters.



The default returns everything together, which for a tiled run is the whole split at full resolution: 200 fundus photographs at 2048 x 2048 is about 6.7 GB before anything is drawn, and the engine’s own predict was killed by exactly that. Two arguments avoid it.
cases names the ones wanted. each hands them over one at a time and keeps only what the function gives back. They compose: cases says which, each says what to do with them.
The saving is in memory and not in time. The engine’s stream is sequential, so asking for two cases out of two hundred still runs the model over two hundred - it simply never holds more than one answer at once.




library("rplatypus")

masks <- predict(fit, "unet")                     # an array, on the model's grid
masks <- predict(fit, "unet", space = "source")   # a list, on each scan's own grid

# The two worst cases, without holding the other 198.
cases <- evaluate_cases(fit, split = "validation")
worst <- cases$case[order(cases$dice)][1:2]
two <- predict(fit, split = "validation", cases = worst)

# Or walk the split, keeping one number per image and none of the masks.
coverage <- predict(fit, split = "validation", each = function(case, mask) mean(mask > 1))

# `space = "source"` returns a list and not an array, which is the API being
# honest: scans differ in size, a stacked array needs one shape, and resizing
# them to match is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
crumbs: Predict masks, boxes, objects or labels

title: rplatypus
text:
The package is named after the animal, and this prints something true about it. It has nothing to do with segmentation.



platypus_fact(number = NULL)







number


Which fact, from 1 to the number there are. NULL, the default, picks one at random.






A fact is also printed once when the package is attached, in an interactive session only. To stop that, set options(rplatypus.facts = FALSE) in ~/.Rprofile, or the environment variable PLATYPUS_FACTS to 0 or false in ~/.Renviron.
Each fact carries the source it was read from, because several of the best-known claims about platypuses are wrong and four of these exist to say which. The numbering is stable across versions: facts are added to the end and never reordered, so a number can be quoted.
Picking one at random does not disturb the random number stream, which is the only part of this worth any care: library() must not change what set.seed(1) then produces, and suppressPackageStartupMessages() hides the message without preventing the side effect, so avoiding it is the only fix that works.



An object of class platypus_fact, which prints as the fact and its source.




library("rplatypus")

platypus_fact(1)

Platypus fact nr 1: There are five living species of egg-laying mammal:
the platypus, the short-beaked echidna, and three long-beaked echidnas.
One of those is named after David Attenborough.
-- Flannery & Groves (1998), Mammalia 62:367-396; Mammal Diversity
   Database

platypus_fact()

Platypus fact nr 6: That venom will not kill a person, and it is not a
sting to shrug off either: the pain is severe, lasts for days or
longer, and responds poorly to ordinary painkillers - morphine
included.
-- Australian Platypus Conservancy, platypus.asn.au

title: rplatypus
text:
The model block for task = “classification”, and the one model constructor in this package that is not named after an architecture. u_net(), linknet(), res_u_net() and u_net_plus_plus() choose between four decoders that read the same features; a classifier has nothing after the pooling but a dense layer, so the contracting path is the architecture and encoder is the whole answer. The engine has no architecture field here for that reason, and the name follows its own build_classifier.



classifier(
  name,
  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,
  blocks = NULL,
  filters = NULL,
  block_width = NULL,
  pooling = NULL,
  head_dropout = NULL,
  dropout = NULL,
  batch_normalization = NULL,
  separable_conv = NULL,
  spatial_dropout = NULL,
  activation = NULL,
  initialiser = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  metrics = NULL,
  optimizer = NULL,
  callbacks = NULL,
  augmentation = NULL,
  epochs = NULL,
  batch_size = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  fit = NULL,
  encoder = NULL,
  pretrained = NULL,
  freeze_encoder = NULL,
  encoder_learning_rate = NULL
)







name


A name for the model, used in the score table and in file names.




input_shape


The size every image is read at, c(height, width). Unlike a segmentation model nothing has to divide by 2^blocks - there is no decoder to line up with - but every side must still be at least 2^blocks, or the deepest level has nothing left to pool.




channels


Input channels: 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale.




blocks


How many times the resolution is halved before the features are pooled, so how much context the answer is made from. Ignored, and refused, when encoder names a backbone - the backbone’s own depth is then the only one there is.




filters


Filters in the first block, doubled at every level, so this and blocks set how wide the pooled feature vector is: filters * 2^blocks. Ignored, and refused, with encoder.




block_width


Convolutions per block, at every level. Raising it adds depth without adding levels, which is the lever to reach for when the objects are small enough that halving the resolution again would lose them - a crop of one cell is exactly that case. Ignored, and refused, with encoder.




pooling


How the feature map becomes one vector per image. “avg” averages evidence over the whole frame, which is what every classification head since the networks that replaced the flattened dense layer does; “max” takes the strongest response anywhere, which is the one to reach for when the thing being looked for is small and somewhere in the picture rather than the picture itself.




head_dropout


Drop this fraction of the pooled vector before the dense layer. Separate from dropout, which sits between convolutions and reaches nothing at all when the contracting path is a pretrained backbone with its own regularisation - this is then the only one left.




dropout, batch_normalization, separable_conv, spatial_dropout


Regularisation and shape of the contracting path, as in u_net().




activation, initialiser


The non-linearity between convolutions, and how the weights start.




loss


The objective. Fewer are admissible here than anywhere else in this package, and the two that are - loss_cce() and loss_focal() - are the ones that score each answer on its own rather than scoring an overlap. available_losses(“classification”) lists them and the engine’s refusal names them.




metrics


What to report beside the loss. metric_auc() is the engine’s default and that is a measurement rather than a preference: at a 3% prevalence a calibrated model never crosses the threshold, so accuracy, balanced accuracy and F1 all report a real signal and a collapse as the same number. See metric_auc().




optimizer, callbacks, augmentation, epochs, batch_size, weights, fit


As in u_net(). A callback watching val_<metric> is refused when nothing in metrics will produce it, and there is no foreground to watch - a classification epoch has no background class and reports no such share.




encoder


A pretrained backbone instead of our own contracting path, by name - see encoders for the table and what it is actually good for. With this, blocks, filters and block_width are refused.




pretrained, freeze_encoder, encoder_learning_rate


How the backbone arrives and how it is trained, as in u_net().






n_class is not an argument, for the reason it is not one on u_net() either: the number of classes comes from classes in classification_data(), and a model that also declared it could only ever disagree with its own data.



A model specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



classification_data(), metric_auc()




library("rplatypus")

classifier("cnn", input_shape = c(128, 128), blocks = 3, filters = 16)

$name
[1] "cnn"

$input_shape
[1] 128 128

$blocks
[1] 3

$filters
[1] 16

attr(,"task")
[1] "classification"

# A pretrained backbone instead of ours, with its early levels held still
classifier("resnet", input_shape = c(224, 224), encoder = "resnet34",
           pretrained = TRUE, freeze_encoder = 2)

$name
[1] "resnet"

$input_shape
[1] 224 224

$encoder
[1] "resnet34"

$pretrained
[1] TRUE

$freeze_encoder
[1] 2

attr(,"task")
[1] "classification"
crumbs: A contracting path, pooled, with one dense layer on top

title: rplatypus
text:
The convention optical flow has used for twenty years, and a convention rather than a palette decision - which is why it is not in drawing_style(). Nothing about it is a choice this project gets to make differently from everyone else’s figures, and a reader who has seen one flow visualisation can read this one.



flow_to_colours(flow)







flow


A two-channel vector field: 2 x height x width, channel 1 the row component and channel 2 the column component, which is the layout the engine’s targets use.






What it is for: debugging a separation_flows() model. A field that is right everywhere except reversed looks obviously reversed here and identical in any loss. predict() with type = “channels” is where the field comes from.
A zero vector is black, which is also what the background is, and that is honest - the background has no direction.



A height x width x 3 array of integers, 0-255.



separation_flows() for the model that predicts one.




library("rplatypus")

field <- array(0, dim = c(2, 2, 3))
field[1, 1, 1] <- 1   # pointing down
field[2, 1, 2] <- 1   # pointing right
shown <- flow_to_colours(field)
# Two directions, two hues; and no vector, no colour.
!identical(shown[1, 1, ], shown[1, 2, ]) && all(shown[2, 3, ] == 0L)

[1] TRUE
crumbs: A vector field as a picture: hue is the direction, value is the length

title: rplatypus
text:
One detector, as an entry in platypus_spec()’s models.



yolo3(
  name,
  input_shape = c(416, 416),
  channels = NULL,
  anchors = NULL,
  anchors_per_grid = NULL,
  ignore_threshold = NULL,
  score_threshold = NULL,
  nms_threshold = NULL,
  operating_point = NULL,
  min_visibility = NULL,
  box_loss = NULL,
  optimizer = NULL,
  callbacks = NULL,
  augmentation = NULL,
  epochs = NULL,
  batch_size = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  fit = NULL
)







name


Unique within a spec; names the outputs.




input_shape


c(height, width), each a multiple of 32. The three grids are the input divided by 32, 16 and 8, so a side that does not divide gives a coarsest grid that does not tile the image. Bigger is not obviously better: on BCCD, 608 bought 0.014 of mAP@0.5 for twice the training time, and the grid does not quantise a box’s centre - the strides are fixed and the offset is a continuous output, so a larger input buys more cells rather than finer ones.




channels


Channels the model takes.




anchors


Box shapes to predict offsets from, as fractions of the input size: a list of three groups, coarsest grid first, each group a list of c(width, height) pairs. COCO publishes its nine in pixels at a 416 input, so those need dividing by 416. NULL fits them to your data.




anchors_per_grid


How many anchors to fit per grid when anchors is unset. It also sets the head’s width, which is anchors_per_grid * (n_class + 5).




ignore_threshold


A cell that is not responsible for an object but whose box overlaps one this much is left unsupervised rather than trained towards "no object". Without it, a nearly-correct guess beside the responsible cell is punished, which is the one thing a detector should not learn.




score_threshold


Discard a predicted box below this confidence. Low on purpose: average precision is computed over the whole ranking, so a cut here is a ceiling on recall that no threshold chosen later can lift.




nms_threshold


Two boxes of the same class overlapping this much are one object and the lower-scoring one is dropped. Per class, so a platelet on a red cell survives.




operating_point


The confidence at which precision and recall are reported. Separate from score_threshold because they answer different questions: that one decides what is computed at all, this one decides where on the curve to stand.




min_visibility


How much of a box must survive an augmentation that removes part of the frame, as a fraction of its original area. A convention rather than a measurement; what is defensible is the direction. A box keeping two pixels of a cell teaches the model that a two-pixel fragment is a whole cell, which produces false positives everywhere, while dropping a heavily truncated object only fails to teach it about that object. Irrelevant unless a transform can lose part of the frame, which flips and rotations never do.




box_loss


How the box coordinates are scored: “offsets”, YOLOv3’s own, or “giou”. Unset uses the engine’s default, which is “offsets” - what the published bccd-yolo3 weights were trained with.
“giou” is not the better objective, and that is measured. Blood cells, three seeds each, 150 epochs, on the dataset’s own test split:



box_loss


mAP@0.5


mAP@[.50:.95]


matched IoU




giou


0.8666 ±0.0147


0.5078 ±0.0083


0.7929 ±0.0069




offsets


0.8583 ±0.0167


0.5172 ±0.0195


0.8038 ±0.0001



Average precision separates them in neither direction - both gaps are smaller than the seed spread. The overlap of the boxes it matched does separate them, and “giou” is worse by 0.011, which is 2.7 standard errors of the difference. It is also sixty times less repeatable on exactly that quantity.
The reason is visible in detection_anchors(): GIoU exists because plain IoU is a flat zero for boxes that do not touch, so it has no gradient where a detector is most wrong - and anchors fitted to blood cells already cover them at a mean IoU of 0.877, so a prediction never starts disjoint and the advantage never arrives. On data whose fitted anchors cover poorly it should be a different story, which is untested and so not claimed.
Choose it to read the loss, not to raise the score. The offsets term cannot reach zero - cross-entropy against a soft target bottoms out at that target’s entropy - so a converged run and a stalled one print the same number, near 5.9. Under “giou” the coordinate term in training_history() reads about 0.05 on training against 0.47 on validation: a localisation gap you can see, because zero means the boxes are right.




optimizer, callbacks, augmentation, epochs, batch_size


As for u_net(). There is no loss and no metrics: YOLOv3’s objective is part of its architecture, and mean average precision is not one option among several. A field that accepts a value and ignores it is worse than no field.




weights


A registry name such as “bccd-yolo3”, an hf://owner/repo/file@commit reference, or a path to a local file. The anchors come with it.




fit


Set FALSE to load weights and skip training, which is how you get boxes on an image without a GPU and an afternoon.






Anchors. Unset, they are fitted to your training boxes with k-means under an IoU distance, which is what you want: COCO’s nine anchors borrowed for blood cells cover their boxes at a mean overlap of 0.65 against 0.88 for anchors fitted to them. Fitted anchors are recorded with the run and in the sidecar when weights are exported, because a detector cannot be reloaded without them - the same weights read with other anchors decode every box scaled by a fixed factor, with plausible boxes, plausible scores, wrong places, and nothing in the output to say so.
For the same reason, naming weights and anchors together is an error: loading takes the anchors recorded beside the file, which would leave the ones here describing nothing.



One model specification.



detection_data(), plot_boxes(), available_weights()




library("rplatypus")

yolo3("cells", input_shape = c(416, 416))

$name
[1] "cells"

$architecture
[1] "yolo3"

$input_shape
[1] 416 416

attr(,"class")
[1] "platypus_detection_model" "list"                    
attr(,"task")
[1] "object_detection"

yolo3("cells", input_shape = c(416, 416), weights = "bccd-yolo3", fit = FALSE)

$name
[1] "cells"

$architecture
[1] "yolo3"

$input_shape
[1] 416 416

$weights
[1] "bccd-yolo3"

$fit
[1] FALSE

attr(,"class")
[1] "platypus_detection_model" "list"                    
attr(,"task")
[1] "object_detection"

text:
Every value plot_masks(), plot_boxes(), overlay_mask() and overlay_agreement() use when you do not give them one: which colours mean found, missed and invented, one colour per class for plot_anchors(), how much of the image an overlay lets through, how a box is labelled, and which boxes are worth drawing at all.



drawing_style()




They belong to the engine - pyplatypus.style - and are mirrored here so that drawing needs no Python. A test holds the two together, so the same call draws the same picture from either package.
Reach for this when you want to match a figure rather than restate it: passing colours = drawing_style()$box_colours to something else keeps one source, and typing the hex codes starts a second.



A named list: agreement_colours, box_colours, class_colours, overlay_alpha, box_label_format and box_min_score.



plot_masks(), plot_boxes(), overlay_agreement()




library("rplatypus")

drawing_style()$agreement_colours[["missed"]]

[1] "#E63C3C"

# The same list the engine returns, which is what keeps the two drawings the same.
str(drawing_style())

List of 6
 $ agreement_colours: Named chr [1:3] "#3CDC5A" "#E63C3C" "#F0C83C"
  ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:3] "hit" "missed" "false_alarm"
 $ box_colours      : Named chr [1:2] "#d95f02" "#1b9e77"
  ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:2] "prediction" "truth"
 $ overlay_alpha    : num 0.55
 $ box_label_format : chr "%s %.2f"
 $ class_colours    : chr [1:8] "#1b9e77" "#d95f02" "#7570b3" "#e7298a" ...
 $ box_min_score    : num 0.5

title: rplatypus
text:
Detection only. On a segmentation fit this refuses by name and points at evaluate_cases(). The name carries no detection_ prefix on purpose: this is an S3 generic, so a future task gains a method under the same name rather than a second spelling of one idea.



evaluate_images(object, ...)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
evaluate_images(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "validation",
  score_threshold = NULL,
  ...
)







object


A platypus_fit() on a detection specification.




…


Unused.




model


Which model, by the name in the specification. Defaults to the first.




split


Which data to score on.




score_threshold


The confidence at which the counts are read. Unset, the specification’s operating_point is used, which is what it is for: "how many were missed" is undefined over the whole ranking, where every box the model dimly considered counts as a prediction.






evaluate() gives one row per model and evaluate_classes() one row per class. This gives one row per image, which is the question asked next: not how well on average, but which pictures it fails on. A mean over a split says 0.86; it does not say the misses are four frames where the stain is dark, and that difference is usually something about the data rather than the model.
Sort by missed for the frames it cannot see, and by mean_matched_iou for the ones where it finds everything and places it badly. Those are different problems - the first is usually the data, the second usually the anchors.
There is no average precision here, deliberately. Average precision is the area under a precision-recall curve, so it is a property of a ranking over a whole dataset; computed on one image with three boxes it moves on a single box’s rank and means nothing. What is meaningful for one picture is counting and overlap, which is what the columns carry.
mean_matched_iou is NA rather than 0 when nothing matched. An image where the model found nothing and one where it found badly-placed boxes are different failures, and a zero would merge them.



A data frame of class platypus_images, one row per image: key, n_truth, n_predicted, matched, missed, spurious and mean_matched_iou.



evaluate_classes() for one row per class, evaluate_cases() for the segmentation counterpart.




library("rplatypus")

images <- evaluate_images(fit)
head(images[order(-images$missed), ])          # the frames it cannot see
head(images[order(images$mean_matched_iou), ]) # the ones it places badly

title: rplatypus
text:
One per model, and it decides the head’s width and which losses are admissible - both derived by the engine rather than stated here, so there is no channel count to get wrong. Pass the result as a model’s separation; see u_net().



separation_rim(width = NULL)

separation_flows(mode = NULL, loss = NULL, weight = NULL)







width


For rim, how many pixels wide the rim is, in the model’s input resolution. Unset uses the engine’s default, which is 2 and stands on an argument rather than on a measurement: the published sweep peaked at 3 pixels of source resolution, which on a 520-pixel case read at 256 is about 1.5 pixels of model input, and a sweep in model pixels has not been run.




mode


For flows, “diffusion” or “centroid”. Unset uses the engine’s default of “diffusion”, which stands on a measurement: decoded against the truth it reaches 0.9924 where “centroid” reaches 0.9478, because a straight line to a centroid leaves a crescent-shaped object.




loss


For flows, the objective for the vector channels, which has to be one defined over numbers rather than over classes. Unset uses the engine’s default.




weight


For flows, how much of the total objective the vector half provides.






separation_rim() trains three classes - background, object interior, object rim - and the rim is what separates two touching objects. separation_flows() trains a vector field pointing at each object’s own sink, so every foreground pixel carries a value and none of them is spent on being a boundary.
What this is worth was measured and it is not flattering. On the Data Science Bowl’s held-out cases the flow route is worth +0.0680 of instance average precision over decode_connected_components(), which ignores the signal entirely, and the rim route +0.0640 - while substituting a perfect mask is worth +0.2398. So the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6, and a run that beats the published weights’ 0.4888 without reaching 0.7655 has improved its mask and said nothing about separation.
There is no hv. Its markers lose to a one-pixel erosion on perfect inputs, 0.9382 against 0.9807, so naming it would promise a mechanism that was measured as absent.



A separation block, to be passed as a model’s separation.



decodings, instance_data()




library("rplatypus")

separation_rim(width = 2)

$name
[1] "rim"

$width
[1] 2

separation_flows(mode = "diffusion")

$name
[1] "flows"

$mode
[1] "diffusion"

For flows, “diffusion” or “centroid”. Unset uses the engine’s default of “diffusion”, which stands on a measurement: decoded against the truth it reaches 0.9924 where “centroid” reaches 0.9478, because a straight line to a centroid leaves a crescent-shaped object.




loss


For flows, the objective for the vector channels, which has to be one defined over numbers rather than over classes. Unset uses the engine’s default.

For flows, how much of the total objective the vector half provides.






separation_rim() trains three classes - background, object interior, object rim - and the rim is what separates two touching objects. separation_flows() trains a vector field pointing at each object’s own sink, so every foreground pixel carries a value and none of them is spent on being a boundary.
What this is worth was measured and it is not flattering. There is no hv. Its markers lose to a one-pixel erosion on perfect inputs, 0.9382 against 0.9807, so naming it would promise a mechanism that was measured as absent.



A separation block, to be passed as a model’s separation.

separation_rim(width = 2)

$name

$width
[1] 2

$name
[1] "flows"

$mode

title: rplatypus
text:
One row per directory, saying whether it is a usable series and what is wrong with it if it is not. Problems are reported as a column rather than raised, because a hundred cases out of an archive will contain a few with a missing slice, two series in one folder, or duplicated files - and stopping at the first turns an afternoon’s work into a week’s.



series_report(paths)







paths


Directories, each holding the slices of one series.






Reads no pixels. Every check runs on the DICOM headers, so this is usable on a hundred gigabytes of data and is the first thing worth running on a new dataset.



A data frame with one row per directory: path, ok, slices, sorted_by, spacing_1/2/3, series_uid and problem.



A missing slice, which does not make a volume shorter - it puts everything past the gap in the wrong place, and no metric would show it. Two series in one folder, which is the normal state of an archive export: a scout, a reconstruction and a phase sitting together, which stacked would interleave two anatomies. Duplicated slices, from a copy or from several echoes mixed together. Slices of different size, angle or spacing.
It also reports how the slices were ordered. “position” means the geometry decided, which is what you want. “instance_number” means the files carry no positions and the order came from a number that is only required to be unique - worth knowing before trusting the result.



volume_info() for NIfTI files, split_dataset() for dividing the cases up.




library("rplatypus")

cases <- list.dirs("dicom_export", recursive = FALSE)
report <- series_report(cases)

report[!report$ok, c("path", "problem")]     # the ones to deal with first
table(report$sorted_by)

title: rplatypus
text:
evaluate() gives one row per model: one number for a whole set. This gives one row per case - each image, or each patient when group_by is set - because one number hides the distribution, and the distribution is usually the finding. A model averaging Dice 0.86 that scores 0.1 on three patients has a failure mode, and the mean is where it hides.



evaluate_cases(object, ...)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
evaluate_cases(
  object,
  model = NULL,
  split = "validation",
  group_by = NULL,
  at = NULL,
  ...
)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_cases'
summary(object, ...)







object


A platypus_cases from evaluate_cases().




…


Unused.




model


Which model, by the name in the specification. Defaults to the first.




split


Which data to score on.




group_by


A pattern picking a group out of each case’s name, as in split_dataset(). With it, the rows are patients rather than slices: a patient’s slices are pooled into one score, the way a volume would be.




at


Which grid to score on, as in evaluate(). Unset is the model’s own load_shape; “source” reads each truth as stored and scores the prediction there, which is the only form in which rows from two models - or from two runs with different target_spacing - mean the same thing.






summary() on the result gives the distribution: mean, standard deviation, median, range, and which case scored worst.
Tiled models are scored on the whole image, not on tiles. Overlaps are accumulated across a case’s tiles and the metric applied once, which is that image’s score exactly; averaging the tiles’ scores would be a different number, and unkind to any case whose object happens to straddle a boundary.



A data frame with one row per case, of class platypus_cases.



split_dataset() for keeping a patient out of two sets in the first place.




library("rplatypus")

cases <- evaluate_cases(fit)
summary(cases)
head(cases[order(cases$dice), ])          # the ones worth looking at

evaluate_cases(fit, group_by = "^(patient\\\\d+)_")

# On the grid the files are on, which is what makes two models comparable.
evaluate_cases(fit, at = "source")

title: rplatypus
text:
What gets reported. Unlike the losses these are computed on the hard prediction - the mask you will actually be handed - because a metric taken on probabilities reads higher than the model deserves.



metric_iou(smooth = 1, include_background = TRUE)

metric_dice(smooth = 1, include_background = TRUE)

metric_tversky(alpha = 0.5, smooth = 1, include_background = TRUE)

metric_cldice(iterations = 5, smooth = 1, include_background = FALSE)

metric_surface_dice(tau, smooth = 1, include_background = FALSE)







smooth


Smoothing. Zero is allowed and is the honest choice for a reported number: with smoothing, a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.




include_background


Average over the background class as well. In medical images the background is usually most of the picture, so leaving it in can turn a model that found nothing into one that looks respectable. Papers report foreground only. It defaults to TRUE for the three overlap metrics and FALSE for metric_cldice() and metric_surface_dice(), where the background class does not merely flatter a model but measures something that is not the question - its skeleton and its boundary are both artefacts of the frame rather than of what was found. The paragraphs above give both measurements.




alpha


For Tversky, the weight on false negatives.




iterations


For clDice, how many times the skeleton is peeled. It has to reach the half-width of the thickest structure, or its core is never reduced to a centreline and the score is refused rather than reported - an empty skeleton otherwise reads as a perfect 1.




tau


For metric_surface_dice(), the tolerance a boundary is allowed to be wrong by, and it is required because no default would be honest. A tolerance belongs to the structure and the dataset rather than to a package: conventionally it is the inter-observer variability for that structure - the distance two people drawing the same boundary differ by - and published values exist per organ and per challenge. Take one from the protocol you are comparing against. In millimetres where target_spacing puts every case on a common grid, and in voxels where it does not, which is the same pair of answers the signed distance map in loss_boundary() gives and for the same reason: a 0.5 mm and a 2.5 mm acquisition are not comparable in voxels at all.






Three of these ask the same question and two ask different ones. metric_iou(), metric_dice() and metric_tversky() all ask how much of the mask coincides and differ in how they weigh the ways of being wrong. metric_cldice() asks whether the structure coincides, and metric_surface_dice() asks how far wrong the boundary is - which is the question a contour somebody has to approve is actually judged by, and the one nothing here reported until the pin moved to 0.8.0a26.
For something thin and connected clDice is the question worth asking, and it and Dice disagree in a way worth knowing. Measured on a nine-pixel vessel: one drawn two pixels thin scores Dice 0.875, and the same vessel severed in the middle scores 0.947 - Dice prefers the severed one. clDice gives them 1.000 and 0.943.
Its limit, also measured: at one pixel wide a displacement of one pixel leaves no overlap at all, and every overlap-based metric reads 0, this one included.
metric_surface_dice() is the other kind of disagreement. loss_boundary()’s own page reports a model at Dice 0.9525 whose volumes run 5% small and 17% wrong per case, and no overlap column says that: a displaced boundary and a correct one of the same area score alike. This is normalised surface Dice (Nikolov et al., 2018), symmetric on purpose - the truth’s surface near the prediction is the boundary’s recall, the prediction’s surface near the truth is its precision - and it is the one metric here that reads the voxel spacing, so tau is in millimetres when target_spacing has put the data on a common grid and in voxels when it has not. It is also what loss_boundary() optimises, so until now that loss was being judged by the metric it exists to improve on.
Like clDice it is a property of a whole mask rather than of a batch of counts, so on a tiled run (splits) it is reported per case by evaluate_cases() and is absent from the epoch history - a per-batch average of per-tile boundaries would be a number about nothing. A callback asking to watch val_surface_dice on such a run is refused when the configuration is read, the way one watching val_cldice is - so the choice to tile and the choice of what to stop on are settled together, before anything is trained.
include_background defaults to FALSE for those two and TRUE for the three overlap metrics, and each has its own measured reason. The background’s skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1 for clDice whatever the model did - averaging it in moved 0.7865 to 0.8933 on a three-pixel vessel. The background’s boundary is the foreground’s boundary plus the edge of the picture, and that edge agrees between any two masks whatever happened in them: measured on four random pairs at tau = 2, the background scored 0.6110 to 0.7030 against the foreground’s 0.5583 to 0.6266 - higher every time. That is agreement on the field of view rather than on the object.
Metrics for one label per image are a different family and have their own page. metric_accuracy(), metric_balanced_accuracy(), metric_f1() and metric_auc() score a classifier, where there is no overlap to measure and no background class to leave out - see classification_metrics. None of the names on this page appears there and none of theirs appears here, which is the honest shape: a Dice over one label would be the label itself.



A metric specification.




library("rplatypus")

metric_dice(include_background = FALSE)

$name
[1] "dice"

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

# Vessels, airways, neurons, cracks: thin and connected, where Dice asks the wrong thing.
metric_cldice()

$name
[1] "cldice"

$iterations
[1] 5

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

# How far wrong the boundary is, rather than how much of the area coincides. 1.5 mm
# because that is this structure's inter-observer variability, not because of anything
# here.
metric_surface_dice(tau = 1.5)

$name
[1] "surface_dice"

$tau
[1] 1.5

$smooth
[1] 1

$include_background
[1] FALSE

title: rplatypus
text:
What a sonographer writes down. A fetal head circumference is the perimeter of the ellipse fitted to the skull, and no overlap score stands in for it: two masks with the same Dice can be eight times apart in millimetres, depending on whether they are wrong in a ring all the way round or wrong in a ragged edge.



ellipse_measure(mask, spacing = NULL, class = 2L)







mask


A mask of class indices, as predict() returns - one image, not a stack.




spacing


Pixel size in millimetres, length 2, in the array’s own order: rows first, then columns. Unset measures in pixels. Measure on the grid the spacing belongs to: a prediction resized to the model’s input shape has pixels of a size nobody recorded, so this wants predict(space = “source”).




class


Which class is the structure, numbered from 1 as the colormap and labels are. Defaults to 2, the foreground of a binary segmentation. It is an argument rather than an assumption because this package writes 1 for background where the engine’s own masks write 0, so treating anything above zero as foreground would measure the whole image.






The fit is not iterative. For a uniform filled ellipse the covariance of the member pixels has eigenvalues a^2 / 4 and b^2 / 4, so the axes come out of a 2 x 2 eigendecomposition, and the circumference is Ramanujan’s second approximation - right to about 1e-7 relative at the eccentricities a fetal skull has, where pi * (a + b), which is what one reaches for instead, is wrong by 1.5% at an axis ratio of 0.7.
The largest connected piece is taken and its holes filled before anything is measured. A prediction is not an ellipse: it can arrive in two pieces or with a hole in the middle, and the second moments of either belong to neither - a hole pushes the variance outwards and a stray island drags the centre.



A one-row data frame with major, minor and circumference - the two semi-axes and the perimeter, in millimetres when spacing was given and in pixels otherwise. All three are 0 for fewer than three pixels of that class, because a region that small has no second moment; that is an ordinary outcome for a model that found nothing, not an error.



mask_volume() for the same argument in three dimensions, and instance_sizes() for it per object.




library("rplatypus")

# A filled ellipse of 60 x 40 pixels, on half-millimetre pixels: semi-axes of 30 mm and
# 20 mm, whose perimeter is 158.8 mm.
rows <- matrix(rep(seq_len(201), 301), nrow = 201)
columns <- matrix(rep(seq_len(301), each = 201), nrow = 201)
mask <- ifelse(((columns - 150) / 60)^2 + ((rows - 100) / 40)^2 <= 1, 2L, 1L)
# Wrapped because this one does cross to the engine - unlike [mask_volume()], which is a
# count times a product and stays in R so that a reader needs no Python to run its page.
ellipse_measure(mask, spacing = c(0.5, 0.5))

title: rplatypus
text:
u_net() and the other model constructors take an encoder, which replaces the built-in contracting path with a backbone architecture, and a separate pretrained flag that loads that backbone’s ImageNet weights. This page is the measurement behind them, because the honest summary is narrower than the idea.




u_net("polyps", input_shape = c(256, 256),
      encoder = "resnet34",      # the architecture
      pretrained = TRUE,         # and its ImageNet weights
      freeze_encoder = 5)        # held still while the decoder settles


Two flags rather than one, so naming an architecture never reaches the network on a machine that has none - a hospital network often has none.



Measured on three datasets, one per modality, three seeds each, every configuration compared at its best validation Dice with the best weights restored. Training sets of 40 to 100 images on purpose, because that is the regime transfer learning is for.



configuration


DS Bowl, microscopy


SIIM-ACR, chest X-ray


Kvasir-SEG, endoscopy




built-in encoder, 1.9M parameters


0.8460


0.0531


0.5830




encoder = “resnet34”, 9.0M


0.7891


0.1073


0.5670




the same, pretrained, freeze_encoder = 5


0.8333


0.1203


0.5932




the same, encoder_learning_rate = lr/10


0.8326


0.1011


0.5329



Four things come out of it, and each repeats on all three:


Use freeze_encoder, not encoder_learning_rate alone


Freezing was the better of the two everywhere. On Kvasir a tenth of the rate is the worst row in the table - below the built-in encoder and below the same backbone trained from nothing. Giving one rate to the whole network is worse still: a randomly initialised decoder’s gradients undo the transferred weights before the decoder has learned anything worth having.


Do not expect a better score


The best pretrained configuration beats the built-in encoder on one dataset of three, by 0.0102, against a seed-to-seed spread of 0.0170 - inside the noise. And endoscopy is the fairest test available within medical imaging: camera photographs of tissue, three channels, natural lighting. With the backbone frozen for a whole run on DS Bowl the score is 0.6068 against 0.8460, so the features genuinely do not transfer to these images.


Expect to reach the same score sooner


On Kvasir the built-in encoder needed 150, 110 and 83 epochs across its three seeds; pretrained and frozen needed 64, 82 and 83. That halving is the one benefit that showed up consistently, and on a dataset that takes a day to train it is the difference that matters.


A bigger encoder earns its place where the target is thin


On SIIM-ACR, where a pneumothorax covers a median 0.59% of the frame, every backbone variant roughly doubles the built-in encoder’s score - and the built-in encoder’s spread between seeds there (0.0586) is larger than its own mean, with two of three seeds never learning at all. This is a reason to be able to swap the encoder that has nothing to do with ImageNet.


Measure on your own images before trusting any of this: the regime where transfer helps is narrow, and three public datasets are three public datasets. The engine ships examples/compare_pretrained_encoders.py, which is this measurement parameterised.



Any convolutional family timm names, as timm names it: “resnet18”, “resnet34”, “resnet50”, “resnext50_32x4d”, “efficientnet_b0” through “b3”, “mobilenetv3_large_100”, “densenet121”, “regnety_040”, “vgg16”, “inception_v3” and others. blocks then says how many of the backbone’s stages to use.
Two kinds are refused rather than approximated:


A 3D input_shape. ImageNet is images, so there is nothing to transfer to a volume. Refused while the specification is read, before anything is downloaded.


The patch-based families (“convnext_”, ”swin_”). Their features begin at a quarter of the input, so the half-resolution level a U-shaped decoder recovers fine detail from does not exist. Inventing it would put a made-up level exactly where the detail comes from.


The finest level is always platypus’s own: every ImageNet stem halves the input, so no backbone has a full-resolution feature, and the decoder’s output head sits on one. That stage is trained from scratch, which is why freeze_encoder and encoder_learning_rate leave it alone - it is the one part with everything to learn.



Nothing to do. The environment this package builds always includes the backbones, which cost 10 MB against PyTorch’s own several hundred - not a trade worth making anyone opt into. On a GTX 10-series card or older see platypus_use_torch().



models for the arguments, platypus_spec() for the specification.

title: rplatypus
text:
u_net() and the other model constructors take an encoder, which replaces the built-in contracting path with a backbone architecture, and a separate pretrained flag that loads that backbone’s ImageNet weights. This page is the measurement behind them, because the honest summary is narrower than the idea.




u_net("polyps", input_shape = c(256, 256),
      encoder = "resnet34",      # the architecture
      pretrained = TRUE,         # and its ImageNet weights
      freeze_encoder = 5)        # held still while the decoder settles


Two flags rather than one, so naming an architecture never reaches the network on a machine that has none - a hospital network often has none.



Measured on three datasets, one per modality, three seeds each, every configuration compared at its best validation Dice with the best weights restored. Training sets of 40 to 100 images on purpose, because that is the regime transfer learning is for.



configuration


DS Bowl, microscopy


SIIM-ACR, chest X-ray

Use freeze_encoder, not encoder_learning_rate alone


Freezing was the better of the two everywhere. On Kvasir a tenth of the rate is the worst row in the table - below the built-in encoder and below the same backbone trained from nothing. Giving one rate to the whole network is worse still: a randomly initialised decoder’s gradients undo the transferred weights before the decoder has learned anything worth having.


Do not expect a better score


The best pretrained configuration beats the built-in encoder on one dataset of three, by 0.0102, against a seed-to-seed spread of 0.0170 - inside the noise. And endoscopy is the fairest test available within medical imaging: camera photographs of tissue, three channels, natural lighting. With the backbone frozen for a whole run on DS Bowl the score is 0.6068 against 0.8460, so the features genuinely do not transfer to these images.
