The README says what changed since 0.1.1, written by diffing the two NAMESPACE files rather than from memory: of 0.1.1’s 37 exports, 30 are gone, and three of the seven survivors are worse than gone because they are still callable and mean something else.




The day the package stopped being a bridge and became a surface. Five engine releases, each followed here.

A worked vignette on the Data Science Bowl, precomputed so that reading it needs no GPU, and a README.
Continuous integration: five R CMD check jobs - Ubuntu on R devel, release and oldrel-1, plus macOS and Windows on release - and an engine job that installs the built package and runs the suite against the engine resolved from PyPI. That last one is the job that matters: pkgload::load_all() exposes a package’s internals, library() does not, and local work had been using the most permissive of the three ways a test can reach them.
Plotting and masks: plot_masks(), plot_boxes(), overlay_mask(), overlay_agreement(), read_masks(), unite_masks(), mask_coverage().
DICOM, properly: modality LUT, a fixed window, MONOCHROME1 inverted. Plus series_report() for a folder of slices, whose decision is that a problem is a column, not an exception - a hundred cases contain a few bad ones, and stopping at the first turns an afternoon into a week.
Splitting by patient (split_dataset(), split_path()) and evaluate_cases().
Volumes. input_shape = c(64, 64, 32) had been building a 3D U-Net since the first release; what was missing was reading NIfTI, where orientation is the whole problem, and labels as a second way to describe a mask, because volumes label with integers. save_volumes() writes NIfTI carrying the affine of the scan the mask was predicted from - without it a mask cannot be laid over its scan by any viewer, and the file looks perfectly normal while being wrong. mask_volume() reports millilitres, because a voxel count is meaningless outside one scanner.
target_spacing: resample to a common voxel size. What makes it necessary is not slice thickness but field of view - forty slices of 1 mm is 40 mm of patient and forty of 2.5 mm is 100 mm, which is the ordinary state of clinical data.
channels_from: one channel per file, stating the order and never inferring it. A model trained with FLAIR in channel one and used where channel one is T1 answers plausibly, with the right shape and range, and nothing downstream can tell.
Augmentation in 3D, and available_transforms(rank = 3) to say what is usable - 97 of albumentations’ transforms accept a volume and the rest raise from inside the library.
A second vignette, on volumes, which generates its own data. It ends on a model at Dice 0.88 whose volumes are 12-23% too large, which is the argument for reporting volume beside overlap: Dice is dominated by an object’s interior and forgiving about its boundary.
segmentation_data(window = ) replaced dicom_window, since NIfTI needs the same thing. The old name is still accepted; giving both is an error.




The package exists.

The bridge. py_require() plus uv, resolving an isolated ephemeral environment at library(rplatypus) - deliberately not the shared-Python arrangement that broke this package’s Keras stack in 2020. platypus_status() says what it found rather than leaving a failed import to be guessed at, and PLATYPUS_ENGINE_PATH points the bridge at a source tree during development.
platypus_spec(), built either from arguments or from a YAML file and producing the same thing. One pipeline, two constructors.
platypus_fit(), evaluate(), predict(), training_history(), and the engine’s complaints translated into R conditions rather than passed through as Python tracebacks.





The last release of the TensorFlow package, kept here for the record rather than as an ancestor of the entries above. It built Keras models through the R keras package: yolo3() and darknet53() with load_darknet_weights() for the original Darknet weights, a plain u_net(), segmentation_generator(), loss_dice(), the COCO and VOC colormaps, and readers for LabelMe JSON and Pascal VOC XML.
It is still installable and still pinned:
remotes::install_github("maju116/rplatypus@0.1.1")
Its source is on the master branch and the issues filed against it stay open. What has aged is its dependencies rather than its code - the pinned TensorFlow no longer installs on a current Python, which is the reason for a rewrite rather than a consequence of one.

title: Change Log
text:
The pin moves to 0.8.0a49, and this is the first release this package could not take by moving the pin alone. platypus_spec() sends a YAML file or a bare data list straight to the engine’s validator, so a pin at 0.8.0a49 with no constructors would have accepted task: classification from a file and refused it from classification_data() - one configuration with two answers, which is the divergence recorded for regions in 0.8.0a28. So the pin and the surface arrive together, and a test holds the two paths to the same specification.
classification_data() and classifier() are the two new constructors. classification_data() is as much the fields it has not got as the two it adds: colormap, labels, regions, classes_from, channels_from and target_spacing all describe a mask or a grid, and a label is neither. classifier() is the one model constructor in this package not named after an architecture - a classifier has nothing after the pooling but a dense layer, so the contracting path is the architecture and encoder is the whole answer.
Four metrics of their own, and the default is measured rather than chosen. metric_auc(), metric_accuracy(), metric_balanced_accuracy() and metric_f1() share no name with the mask metrics. auc is the engine’s default because at a 3% prevalence a calibrated model never crosses the threshold: everything read off the hard prediction sees the same all-negative answer, so accuracy spans 0.0100 across models whose AUC spans 0.4631 and is not even monotone in their quality. class_balance() is the function that makes that prevalence visible before a run rather than after it, and it prints the engine’s own remark instead of a copy of its threshold.
predict() answers per image and is joinable. type = "class" gives a row per image with key, label, predicted and probability; type = "probability" gives a matrix of images by classes with the keys as row names. Named rather than ordered, which is the lesson predict(space = "source") cost on the semantic side: a prediction handed back as a bare sequence has to be paired with whatever else the caller holds by position.
What is refused, by name, is as much of this as what is returned. space and the cases/each pair describe a grid and a split of masks too large to hold at once, and neither means anything for one label per image. evaluate(at = ) is refused for the same reason. evaluate_cases() is refused for a different one: a case here is one image whose score is 0 or 1, so a split’s worst case is 0 for any model that gets a single image wrong - a number that carries nothing while reading like one that does.
Two defects found by doing this rather than by any test. The shim dropped the check_masks option for a detection specification by comparing the task against "detection", where the value is "object_detection" - so the branch never fired, the option reached an engine that has no such argument, and the TypeError was reported as this engine predates check_masks about an engine that is current. And predict()’s decode guard sat below the task branches, so a detection fit - the one branch that returns before reaching it - accepted decode and silently ignored it. Both are fixed here, because classification is the second task in the first position and would have inherited both.
?metrics also gains the prose it never had: it was A list of metrics, see [metrics]. against seven hundred characters in the engine, and the sentence it was missing is a mechanism - a callback watching val_<metric> is refused when nothing in the list will produce it.



The pin moves to 0.8.0a46, and what it brings is a measurement the engine could not make per object. ellipse_measure() fits an ellipse to a whole mask, which is what a fetal head circumference needs and not what a field of nuclei needs. The engine now has instance_shapes(): one row per object out of one label map, beside the rows instance_sizes() already gives, with the semi-axes largest first and - for an image - eccentricity, which is the number shape analysis reports.
instance_shapes() is on this side too, and it forwards - the way ellipse_measure() does and unlike instance_sizes(), which stays R’s own arithmetic. That split is not a style choice: a count times a product needs no Python and a reader can verify it by eye, while an eigendecomposition per object cannot be reimplemented here without becoming a second implementation. The visible consequence is that this page’s example is wrapped in \dontrun{} and instance_sizes()’s is not, because R CMD check runs examples and CRAN has no interpreter.
It is per object in one pass, which is the whole reason it exists rather than being a line in the documentation: calling ellipse_measure() on labels == k once per object rescans the whole array every time, and on a 512 by 512 map of 1939 objects that is 1989 ms against 143.
One thing to know before calling it through the bridge, because it is the trap and not a detail. eccentricity is unitless and it is not spacing-free: it describes whichever space it was computed in, so on anisotropic voxels the grid and the millimetres disagree completely, in both directions.
a circle of 80 px at spacing (2, 1)       grid 0.0000    mm 0.8660
an 80 by 40 px ellipse at spacing (1, 2)  grid 0.8667    mm 0.0685
The second row is physically almost a circle and the grid calls it strongly elongated. The engine says which space a row is in through the key names - major_px and minor_px without a spacing, major_mm and minor_mm with one - so pass your voxel size and read the _mm keys unless you mean the grid. platypus_device() is unaffected and so is everything else: this release adds a function and changes none.
A volume gets three axes and no eccentricity, because an ellipsoid has no single one.



A file is now read as a picture only if its contents are PNG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP or GIF. Nothing about how you name your files changes, and that is the point: the engine’s reader identified a file by its contents and was handed nothing but a path, so a file carrying any other format - under any extension - went to whichever decoder its bytes asked for. One of those decoders hands the file to Ghostscript. A dataset of ordinary medical images is unaffected; a path holding something else is refused by name now, with a message saying that the extension was not what decided.
segmentation_data(), instance_data() and detection_data() all reach that reader, and so does anything that asks for a shape without reading pixels. Volumes, DICOM and DICOM series never went through it and are untouched.
This package now needs Python 3.11 or newer, and SystemRequirements says so. Python 3.10 reached end of life on 2026-10-01. For almost everybody this changes nothing: the package declares what it needs through reticulate and uv provisions the interpreter, so it simply provisions a newer one.
The exception is worth knowing before it happens. If you point RETICULATE_PYTHON at an interpreter of your own - the route this package warns about when the pyplatypus it finds there is not the pinned one, naming both versions - and that interpreter is 3.10, the engine can no longer be installed into it, and what you will see is a resolution failure from uv rather than anything this package wrote. The fix is a 3.11 interpreter, or letting py_require() choose one. platypus_device() is what reports the environment you ended up with.
Why the engine moved: its pillow floor was >= 10.0 while the decoder fixes it needs arrived in pillow 13, and pillow 13 requires Python 3.11 - so the floor could not be raised without dropping 3.10. Measured rather than assumed, nothing in the dependency tree moves forward with it: thirteen locked entries differ and every one is the removal of an old-Python branch.
A Python 3.10 user of the engine directly is served 0.8.0a43 by any installer rather than an error, which is the migration path and asks nothing of them. This package pins 0.8.0a44.



The numbers plot(fit) draws for a detection run change, and nothing you wrote changes with them. The engine averaged each epoch over batches, and for a detector that is not an average over examples: every component of the YOLO loss is divided inside the loss - three of them by a grid’s object count and the fourth by the cells it supervises. A frame holding thirty blood cells therefore counted the same as a frame holding two.
An epoch is now pooled by what the loss divided by. maju116/rplatypus[#218](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/218).
What this means for a run you already have:

fit$history’s loss columns are on a new definition for detection. On BCCD the reported val_loss moves by up to 0.33 over 150 epochs, and not as a constant offset - it changes sign over the course of a run. Comparing a recorded detection loss against a new run compares two definitions.
No score changes. evaluate() and evaluate_cases() on a detector report average precision through their own path, which this does not touch, and the published bccd-yolo3 weights are unchanged with them.
Semantic and instance runs are untouched. Their epoch was repaired in 0.8.0a40 and the arithmetic there was a different one.

It was measured before it was changed, on 150 instrumented epochs of the engine’s own BCCD example: both poolings pick the same epoch, and that is reported as too close to call rather than as no effect - the gap between them varies across the best epochs by 1.05 times the margin separating the winner from the runner-up. The change is made because weighting a per-object quantity by batches is wrong, not because an epoch visibly moved.



available_weights() lists hc18-unet. A U-Net for the fetal skull in 2D ultrasound, trained on HC18 and published for measuring head circumference in millimetres rather than for an overlap score. Nothing in this package changed but the pin: the registry lives in the engine, so a new published name arrives in R through it.
available_weights()[["hc18-unet"]]
median absolute error     2.44 mm   against the sonographer's measurement, 199 images
mean                      3.84 mm   quoted beside the median because they disagree
worst                    48.07 mm
against the truth mask    3.41 mm   the model's own contribution, not the drawing
Dice                       0.9494   and the description says not to choose on it
Read that last line rather than the Dice. On this run the Dice and the millimetres order the same cases differently - Spearman 0.153 - and 85 of the 144 cases scoring 0.95 or better are still wrong by more than 2 mm. A ragged boundary barely moves an integral over a region and a mask that is systematically fat or thin moves it linearly, which are the two errors Dice is respectively most and least able to see, and they are the wrong way round for anybody measuring a length. These are the first published weights in this family where the score a reader reaches for first is the wrong one.
They are CC BY 4.0 rather than MIT, because HC18 is - the second set in the registry that is not MIT, after fives-unet, and attribution travels with them. The sidecar carries the citation and weights_licence.
Measuring with them from R is ellipse_measure(), which arrived in 0.8.0a39:
ellipse_measure(mask, spacing = c(px, px))
Predict on the source grid and measure there. The pixel size is a property of the file, so a prediction resized to the model’s input shape has pixels of a size nobody recorded.



evaluate()’s figure no longer depends on batch_size. The engine divided an epoch’s totals by the number of batches, so the examples of a short last batch counted more than the others and a split’s reported score moved with a training setting. Measured on 199 validation cases: 2.3e-04 at batch_size 4 and 3.5e-03 at 32, and the size of the gap is not even predictable from the setting, because it depends on which cases land in the short batch.
It is a repair rather than a change of definition, which is why the numbers move at the fourth decimal rather than being restated: the per-batch value was already the mean over the examples in that batch, so a mean of means was reaching for the mean over examples and mis-weighting one batch of it.
The larger half is for tiled runs. evaluate() now pools a case’s tiles by adding their overlap counts before scoring, the way summarise_cases() already did - so the table’s figure is the mean over images rather than the mean over tiles. On the retinal-vessel runs that is worth +0.033 to +0.049 of Dice, and it is why the table in vignette("retinal-vessels") needed no editing: every number in it was computed from the per-case route already, and this brings the one-row table into agreement with it.
The figure is now exactly the mean of evaluate_cases()’s own rows, which is what anybody comparing the two expected and did not get.
Nothing here needs editing in a script. One consequence worth knowing: best_model() ranks on this table, so where two models sat within the shift of each other the winner can change - on the eleven-loss comparison the winner is unchanged and its margin grows from +0.0006 to +0.0033.
And a defect this did not fix, filed rather than folded in: the detection trainer divides by batches too, but every component of the YOLO loss is normalised by the number of objects in the batch, so averaging over batches weights a frame of thirty cells like a frame of two platelets. That is a different repair and it has its own issue, [#218](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/218). No published detection number comes through it - the AP table is scored per image.
[#196](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/196).



[ellipse_measure()] is new: the ellipse a segmented structure implies, as major, minor and circumference. It is what a sonographer writes down, and no overlap score stands in for it - two masks with the same Dice can be eight times apart in millimetres depending on whether they are wrong in a ring all the way round or wrong in a ragged edge.
class is an argument rather than an assumption, and it is the whole reason this is not a straight forward: the engine reads a foreground as anything above zero, which is right for its own argmax masks and silently wrong for this package’s, where which.max writes 1 for background. Read that way the measured ellipse becomes the whole frame - 459.8 mm against 158.8 on the example in ?ellipse_measure - so mask == class happens here, before anything crosses.
And a decision worth more than the function: [mask_volume()] and [instance_sizes()] stay in R. The engine’s 0.8.0a39 gained both, so forwarding them was the obvious move; it was written, measured and reverted.
It is faster - 0.035 s against 0.341 s on a 512 x 512 x 300 label map, because sum(mask == class) builds a logical vector of 78 million elements first - and what settled it was not speed. The engine’s first call downloads about 5 GB, so a user holding a mask and a spacing would pay a torch install for a count times a product. R CMD check also runs examples and CRAN has no Python, so forwarding would have put mask_volume()’s page into \dontrun{}, on arithmetic a reader can verify by eye.
So the rule drawn, and both halves of this entry are on opposite sides of it: a measurement that is arithmetic stays here; a measurement that needs a library crosses. The ellipse wants connected components, hole filling and an eigendecomposition - reimplementing those would be a second implementation rather than a second copy of two lines.
tests/testthat/test-measure-pair.R holds both: R’s answers against the engine’s own on the same arrays, with a positive control, and a check that the functions with runnable examples do not reach the bridge - asked of their bodies, because calling them on a machine that has the engine proves nothing, which is exactly how the reverted version passed its gates.
One new condition kind travels with the pin: platypus_measure_error, for a spacing that does not fit the array it was given. ?platypus_conditions lists it, and nothing here noticed it was needed - test-conditions.R failed the moment the engine defined the kind, and named it.
maju116/pyplatypus[#270](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/270).



The PyTorch build can be chosen once. options(rplatypus.torch = "pascal") in ~/.Rprofile, or PLATYPUS_TORCH=pascal in ~/.Renviron for runs that never load one - Rscript, a scheduler, CI. Both are read when the package loads, which is the last moment anything can change what the environment will be.
Until now the only way was to call [platypus_use_torch()] at the start of every session, because py_require() is session state. On a card older than Turing, forgetting it costs about ten times the training time without costing an error - the run completes, the numbers are right, and the card sits idle. That is the kind of bill that goes unnoticed.
The option wins over the variable, so a session can override what a machine was configured with; "default" turns the setting off for one session without editing the file it came from; and a value neither recognises is reported at load and ignored, because a bad line in a startup file should not make the package unloadable.
An engine that is not the pinned one now says so. The pin is what keeps an R release from breaking when the engine moves underneath it, and on one route it was never in force: a RETICULATE_PYTHON pointing at somebody’s own environment brings whatever pyplatypus is in it, and nothing compared the two. The failure arrived as a validator refusing a configuration field by name, which tells a reader nothing about their interpreter.
A warning rather than a refusal, naming both versions: the only way to reach this state is to have gone out of one’s way, and refusing would also break somebody deliberately testing an engine they built. PLATYPUS_ENGINE_PATH is exempt - that route asks for a source tree with no version at all.
maju116/rplatypus[#211](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/211), [#214](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/214). No engine release: both are about what an R session settles before Python starts.



platypus_device() behaves as it did, and the answer now comes from the engine rather than from this package. The report used to be computed in inst/python/platypus_shim.py - a file of Python shipped by this package - so a Python user could not reach any of it, which is backwards: the engine owns the decisions and this package reads them.
What stays here is the advice. The line telling you to call platypus_use_torch("pascal") is about R’s session model and would mean nothing to somebody who installed the engine with pip; their version of that sentence belongs with the engine.
An accelerator that is not CUDA is now named. Until the engine’s 0.8.0a38 it asked about CUDA alone, so an Apple Silicon Mac - every Mac sold since 2020 - reported cpu while a working mps backend sat in the same installation. platypus_device() prints the backend only when it is not CUDA, because every published set of weights was trained on a CUDA card and a score from another backend is not directly comparable with the registry’s: the unremarkable case is not worth a line, and that one is.
maju116/pyplatypus[#265](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/265) and [#266](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/266).



callback_ema() keeps an exponential moving average of the weights, updated after every optimiser step. That is what makes its decay mean what the literature means: 0.999 is 0.999 per step, so over 60 epochs of 200 batches it is 12,000 updates and a half-life of about 700 steps. A per-epoch version would have been the same name with values that do not transfer, which is why the engine gained a fourth callback hook rather than an approximation.
It is [callback_swa()]’s sibling and a run takes one of them: both replace the model when training ends, so the engine refuses the pair rather than applying them in whichever order the list happened to have. swa folds the tail uniformly from a declared start; ema weights recent steps more and needs no start at all.
Unlike swa it needs no pass over the training data afterwards. A uniform average of weights carries batch-normalisation statistics belonging to no epoch and has to have them recomputed; an exponential average of the buffers alongside the weights carries its own.
maju116/rplatypus[#203](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/203), engine half maju116/pyplatypus[#264](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/264).



training_history() carries val_<metric>_worst: the lowest any single case scored, for the metrics whose counts pool into one score. monitor = "val_dice_worst" works, and so does a when condition on it.
This package has told every reader to look at that number since it had a summary() method - a model averaging 0.86 that scores 0.11 on some patient has a failure mode, and the mean is where it hides - and then every callback it offered watched a mean. Stopping, checkpointing and cutting the learning rate can all act on the distribution now.
Validation only. The training data is shuffled between epochs, so a case has no identity in that pass; "train_dice_worst" is refused rather than quietly reported as something else.
It costs 5.6% of an epoch, measured on the engine’s side: the counts are computed in the validation pass that already happened rather than in a second one.
maju116/rplatypus[#205](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/205), engine half maju116/pyplatypus[#263](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/263).



Every epoch now reports foreground for both passes - the share of the prediction that is not background. Nothing is compared against the truth, so it is not a measure of quality: it answers whether the model is still producing a segmentation at all.
It arrives whether or not you ask for it, and that is the point. A model that collapses to predicting background everywhere is invisible in the numbers it already produced - with include_background = TRUE the Dice is a mean over class channels and the background channel is nearly perfect, so a collapsed model reports around 0.5 while its loss falls. A collapse you have to opt into noticing is one you will not notice.
callback_terminate_on_collapse() ends the run once that share has stayed at or below floor for patience epochs. A floor rather than a test for zero, because 0.01% foreground against a target that is 14% foreground has collapsed in every sense that matters; and a patience, because an early epoch legitimately predicts almost nothing. It can watch train_foreground instead, which answers a different question.
evaluate() carries the column, callback_model_checkpoint()’s when can take a condition on it, and any callback’s monitor can watch it.
maju116/rplatypus[#206](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/206), engine half maju116/pyplatypus[#262](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/262).



Three things that answer one question, which is why they arrive together rather than as three unrelated arguments.
callback_early_stopping() takes a warm-up: start as a fraction of the run or start_epoch as an epoch, one of the two and never both. patience could not express it, because it is in force for the whole run - a model needing fifteen epochs before its validation curve means anything forced patience > 15 permanently, paying that slack at the end where the point was to cut quickly. It delays the stopping and nothing else: an epoch inside the warm-up can still be the best one, and restore_best still returns to it.
callback_swa() takes start_epoch as the exclusive alternative to its fraction - the same concept, so the same two words.
callback_model_checkpoint() takes when, a named list of thresholds that must all hold before anything is written: list(val_dice = 0.9, val_loss = 0.2). The direction is derived, not configured - anything ending in loss has to be below its threshold and everything else above it, the rule monitor already uses - so there is no argument to get backwards. The names are checked against what the model reports when the specification is built. It is an extra gate beside save_best_only, not a replacement, and a run whose conditions never hold writes nothing and says so when it ends.
callback_stop_after(hours = ) is a wall-clock budget. An epoch cap cannot express it: how long an epoch takes is a property of the data and the shape. It is checked at the end of an epoch, so the real limit is the budget plus one epoch, and the run’s stop reason names the clock - a run that ran out of time does not read as one that converged.
maju116/rplatypus[#199](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/199), [#201](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/201) and [#207](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/207); engine half maju116/pyplatypus[#261](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/261).



callback_linear_annealing() is callback_cosine_annealing() with a straight line. callback_step_decay() multiplies the rate by factor at fixed points, which is how published recipes are written - divide by ten at epochs 30 and 60.
callback_step_decay() takes every or milestones, never both and never neither, and says so from R before the call reaches the engine. Two arguments rather than one that accepts either, because 30 and c(30) are different schedules and one argument holding either would be read as whichever was typed.
And a pairing this package has implied for as long as it has had a cosine does not work. A schedule recomputes the rate from the optimiser’s initial value at the end of every epoch, so it erases whatever callback_reduce_lr_on_plateau() cut. Measured on six epochs of a loss that never improves, the rate with both configured follows the cosine exactly - 0.0976, 0.0905, 0.0794 from 0.1 - where the plateau alone reaches 1e-6. The engine refuses the pair now, by name, and so two schedules at once are refused as well.
A schedule beside callback_swa() is still fine, and no longer a matter of luck: the engine fixes the order so swa’s constant tail rate wins whatever position the callbacks were written in.
maju116/rplatypus[#200](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/200), engine half maju116/pyplatypus[#260](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/260).



evaluate() and evaluate_cases() take at. Unset is what they have always done - each model scored on the grid it reads at. at = "source" puts every prediction back onto the grid of the file it came from and scores it against the truth as stored, so rows from models of different shapes answer one question and load_shape reads source.
This is the answer to a warning this package has printed since the engine’s 0.8.0a30 and to a paragraph in vignette("retinal-vessels") that said there was no option for it. There was not: the measurement behind that section rescored its arms with a script that lived outside both packages. Measured there, scoring each model on its own grid reported a resized model at +0.0187 where the honest figure was +0.0033 - 5.7 times - and the bias runs the other way on clDice, because upsampling smooths a prediction.
The grid is the files’ own and you cannot name another. A grid you name resamples the truth, so the thing both models are judged against would itself be an interpolation somebody chose. Only predictions move.
What it costs is what predict(space = "source") already documents: interpolation softens a boundary, and where reading cropped anatomy away the mask comes back padded with background - not examined rather than nothing there. For a comparison that is correct rather than unfair, but a 0 arriving that way is a result and not a fault. The loss is not reported on that grid, because a loss belongs to the objective a model trained with on the grid it trained on.
A detection fit refuses at by name rather than ignoring it: boxes are in the source image’s coordinates already, so there is no grid to choose. The refusal is R’s own and needs no engine, which is how its test runs on a machine with no Python.
maju116/rplatypus[#187](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/187), engine half maju116/pyplatypus[#259](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/259). The pooling question that came out of building it is maju116/rplatypus[#196](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/196).



0.2.1 answered the review on its own branch, from the commit the submitted tarball was built from, because sending main would have replied to two documentation comments with ten new exported functions. The same two fixes belong here as well, or 0.3.0 collects the same review.
Description writes 'PyTorch' and 'Python' in single quotes, as the policy asks of software names in Title and Description. R stays unquoted: the cookbook the review links does not address it, and its own Title Case example is Web Application Framework for R.
colormaps.Rd gained the \value tag it never had. It documents four exported objects rather than functions, so it carried \format alone; the tag is written in the roxygen source and states structure and meaning, not just class.
Worth keeping because it is a property of the review rather than of this release, and the first version of this paragraph understated it. R CMD check --as-cran with the manual, on R 4.5.3, does not flag a missing \value - checking Rd contents says OK with the tag absent - and neither does tools:::checkRdContents(). That was written as a fact about this machine. It is a fact about both sides: CRAN’s own automated pretest did not flag it either. Measured on the two logs, which are byte-comparable because the only difference between the submissions is this tag and two quoted names:
rplatypus 0.2.0, the version sent back    Windows 1 NOTE, Debian 1 NOTE
rplatypus 0.2.1, with the tag             Windows 1 NOTE, Debian 1 NOTE
mentions of `value` or `colormaps`        0 in all four logs
So the two submissions are indistinguishable to every check that runs, and the difference between them is exactly what the reviewer asked for. A clean pretest says nothing about whether the review will pass - a human read the .Rd files. The instrument that does ask the question is a check of our own: a page with \usage must have \value.



The pin does not move and the engine needs no release: this is the first thing in the package that has nothing to do with segmentation. The family is named after the animal, and platypus_fact() says something true about it. One fact is also printed when the package is attached in an interactive session; options(rplatypus.facts = FALSE), or PLATYPUS_FACTS=0 in ~/.Renviron, stops that.
Three things about it are deliberate, and each one is here because of what it prevents.
Choosing a fact does not touch the random number stream. sample() advances .Random.seed, so a fact picked at attach time changes what the user’s own set.seed(1) then produces - measured, runif(1) goes from 0.2655087 to 0.3721239 - and in a package offering seeded splits and deterministic = TRUE that is the worst available place for it. suppressPackageStartupMessages() is not a defence: the arguments are evaluated before the condition is signalled, so suppressing the message keeps the side effect and removes the evidence. The seed is saved and put back instead, and the test for it carries the naive implementation as its positive control.
Interactive sessions only, so a fact never lands in an R CMD check log, a CI run, a knitr render or anybody’s reverse-dependency check. And .onAttach rather than .onLoad, which is where this package’s other startup work lives: .onLoad also runs for rplatypus::fun(), which would print a platypus fact into the middle of a script that never called library().
Every fact carries the source it was read from, and the numbering is stable. Four of the twenty-five exist to correct a popular claim rather than to state one - the platypus does have a stomach, it does not grind food with gravel, “platypi” is not a plural and there is no accepted word for a baby platypus - which is the only form this could take in a package whose argument is that numbers should be measured rather than felt. A test holds every entry to having a source. The numbers are published the moment somebody quotes one, so facts are appended and never reordered, and a ledger of each fact’s opening in tests/testthat/test-facts.R fails if one moves.

metric_surface_dice(tau = ), normalised surface Dice (Nikolov et al., 2018). The three overlap metrics ask how much of the mask coincides and metric_cldice() asks whether the structure does; none of them asks how far wrong the boundary is, which is the question a contour somebody has to approve is actually judged by. ?loss_boundary reports a model at Dice 0.9525 whose volumes run 5% small and 17% wrong per case, and no overlap column says that - a displaced boundary and a correct one of the same area score alike. It is also what loss_boundary() optimises, so until now that loss was being judged by the metric it exists to improve on.
tau is required, because no default would be honest: a tolerance belongs to the structure and the dataset, and conventionally it is the inter-observer variability for what is being drawn. It is in millimetres where target_spacing puts the cases on a common grid and in voxels where it does not, which makes this the one metric here that reads the voxel spacing. Like clDice it is a property of a whole mask, so on a tiled run it is reported per case by evaluate_cases() and is absent from the epoch history.
include_background is FALSE, and for a measured reason rather than the usual one: a background boundary is the foreground’s plus the edge of the picture, and that edge agrees between any two masks whatever happened inside them. On four random pairs at tau = 2 the background scored 0.6110 to 0.7030 against the foreground’s 0.5583 to 0.6266 - higher every time, which is agreement on the field of view.

The wrap is worth a word because it is the one case this figure answers its own question wrongly. Its subject is where does one object end; every other colour repeat is deliberate, and a wrap is the one that repeats between neighbours - provably, since a slot is only past the end of the palette once every colour before it was taken by a neighbour, so the fold lands on a colour a neighbour already holds.
The two messages are compared word for word, in the engine job. That is a stronger pair than the palette or the pixels: a reader who meets this warning in R and then in Python has to be told the same thing, and the pin is what makes comparing prose safe - one exact engine, so a rewording on either side fails here instead of drifting. The engine refuses to conflate the two and so does this - the value is type = "channels", which says what it gives.

overlay_instances() draws an instance label map over its image, with one colour per object chosen so that no two touching objects share one. The rule is adjacency rather than identity: a colour repeats across the picture and never between neighbours, because nobody reads object 214 by its colour and everybody needs to see where one object ends.
That is an exact graph colouring - Welsh-Powell, greedy in order of descending degree - and it is affordable rather than clever. Measured in the engine over all 670 Data Science Bowl cases, 524 of which hold touching objects: the hardest needs three of the eight slots in class_colours, while the cheap alternative of colouring by object number modulo the palette paints 550 of 5436 adjacent pairs in one colour, 10.12% - one touching pair in ten drawn as a single object, in a figure whose whole subject is whether two objects are two.
Eight-connected, so two objects meeting at a corner get different colours. A label-maker goes the other way and joins only along edges, because there the risk is merging two objects into one; here the risk is drawing two as one, which is the opposite direction.
overlay_instance_agreement() is found, missed and invented objects. overlay_agreement() answers the same three-way question about pixels, and on an instance result that is the wrong unit: a merged pair and a split object are both nearly perfect pixelwise and both wrong, which is what an average precision will not tell anybody. Matched whole object against whole object at one IoU threshold, strictly greater, and below 0.5 is refused for the reason the metric refuses it.





The matching needs no greedy pass, and that is provable rather than convenient. The engine matches greedily on descending IoU; this package matches every pair above the threshold, which is equivalent above 0.5: if two disjoint true objects both exceeded 0.5 against one prediction, each intersection would exceed half of it - the union is at least the prediction - and two disjoint intersections cannot together exceed it. So the matching is one to one whatever order it is taken in, which is also why the metric refuses a lower threshold.
Written as the equivalent rather than as a copy because argsort is not stable: two pairs at the same IoU leave the engine in an order neither package controls, and a pixel-for-pixel test would then fail for something that is not a divergence.

Found by asking what a BraTS user would actually run, which is §4’s a feature is not shipped until something has used it the way a user reaches it applied to a refusal.
Detected from the array rather than from the specification, which is the same test the engine applies in onehot_to_colours - so both halves refuse the same arrays, and a caller holding only a prediction can answer the question. A softmax prediction never trips it, since its channels sum to one and at most one can reach half; that control is a test rather than a sentence, because without it every ordinary run would start refusing.
save_class_volumes() is the same thing for volumes, and it is the case regions was built for. BraTS names three overlapping regions and stores them as volumes, so a writer that only handled pictures would have left the motivating dataset with a refusal and no route to disk. One NIfTI per class, each carrying the geometry of the scan it was predicted from - which is the whole reason this is not save_class_masks() with another extension.
It needs no engine release: it goes through the same volume writer save_volumes() uses, so the affine, the integer labels and the grid check are those rather than a second copy. What is a second copy is the rule turning a class name into a filename, because the volume path never reaches the engine’s class_filename - so a test holds R’s rule to the engine’s over the names that are actually awkward, rather than a comment claiming they agree.
predict(type = "class") refused rather than computed when the classes overlap, and "class" is the default, so this is the first call an R user makes on such a fit. There is no one class per pixel to return: the channels are independent binary questions, they do not compete, and an argmax across them names one of the classes a pixel is in. The refusal says to ask for type = "probability" and names what writes it.
Read off the specification the fit carries, which is a lever this package owns - the shape cannot answer it, because sigmoid channels and a softmax’s channels are the same array.
A single of value would have crossed over as a number rather than a list. reticulate turns a length-1 integer vector into a Python scalar, and the schema wants an array, so of = 4 had to be built with as.list(). Measured both ways before the code was written, and the engine refuses the scalar - so this would have been a refusal nobody could read rather than a silent wrong answer, on the most ordinary region there is.
Still in [#152](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/152), deliberately not here, and written as a paragraph rather than a heading because R CMD check reads every ### in this file as a version and says so: save_masks() refusing an overlapping prediction and the per-class writer that replaces it, inspect_masks() naming regions rather than numbering them, and the guide section. Each is independently worth having, which is why none waits for the others.

title: Change Log
text:
A different package from 0.1.1 under the same name, and the section below says how different.


This was in the README until 2026-10-07 - seventy lines between ## Installing and the first example, about a version the reader does not have, before the one they do. It is here because this file is where R keeps what changed between versions, and because the renames table below was a second copy of one the README already carried; the fuller of the two survived.
Code written against the 2020 release will not run on this one. That version built Keras models through the R keras package and handed them back to you; this one describes a whole run as a specification and computes it in PyTorch. Of the 37 functions and objects the old version exported, 30 are gone — including all of yolo3(), darknet53(), load_darknet_weights(), get_boxes(), non_max_suppression(), plot_boxes(), segmentation_generator() and the annotation readers.
Seven names survive, and three of them are the ones to watch, because they are still exported, still callable, and mean something different:








name
0.1.1
now




u_net()
u_net(net_h, net_w, grayscale, ...) → a Keras model
u_net(name, input_shape, ...) → one model in a specification


plot_masks()
plot_masks(images_paths, masks, labels, colormap)
plot_masks(images, prediction, truth, ...)


loss_dice()
no arguments, returns a Keras loss
loss_dice(smooth = 1), returns a loss to name in a specification



The other four — binary_colormap, voc_colormap, binary_labels, voc_labels — are the same data as before.
Object detection is back, and the names are different. The old package handed you a Keras YOLOv3; this one describes a detector in a specification like everything else. So those five names are gone rather than moved, and what replaces them is:







0.1.1
now




yolo3(), darknet53()
yolo3() as one entry in platypus_spec() - same name, a specification rather than a model


load_darknet_weights()
weights = "bccd-yolo3", or a path, or hf://owner/repo/file@commit


get_boxes(), non_max_suppression()
done inside predict(), which returns boxes already suppressed and in each image’s own pixels


plot_boxes()
plot_boxes() - same name, takes what predict() returns



The annotation readers are gone as functions and are now what detection_data() reads for you: Pascal VOC XML or LabelMe JSON, named rather than guessed.
The old release is still there and still installable, pinned:
remotes::install_github("maju116/rplatypus@0.1.1")
Its source is on the master branch, and the issues filed against it stay open. What has aged is its dependencies rather than its code: the pinned TensorFlow no longer installs on a current Python, which is the reason for a rewrite rather than a consequence of one.






library(platypus) is library(rplatypus). The name collided with Platypus, archived from CRAN on 2026-02-02 - unrelated work in immunology - and the two differed only in case, which the policy treats as a conflict and which archiving does not release. cran-comments.md had promised to resubmit under another name rather than ask for an exception, so this is that name rather than a new idea: one name per language, beside the pyplatypus engine on PyPI, and a name that says what the package is - the R surface over a Python engine.
rplatypus is in neither CRAN’s current index nor its archive, checked against both with a positive control so that the absence means something.
The functions did not change. platypus_spec(), platypus_fit(), platypus_status(), platypus_device() and platypus_use_torch() keep their names, and so do the S3 classes platypus_fit, platypus_spec, platypus_split and the rest, the platypus_* condition classes, the PLATYPUS_* environment variables and the headers print() writes. The rule is that the package’s identity - what library() and CRAN see - is rplatypus, and the brand is still platypus. §3A already said the S3 class keeps the prefix even where its constructor loses it; this is the same line drawn one level up, and it means no released surface moved.
The repository was renamed too, to maju116/rplatypus. Stars, forks, watchers and every issue came with it - read back from the API rather than assumed - and github.com/maju116/platypus redirects, so links in other people’s issue comments keep working. The site moved with the repository and is now at maju116.github.io/rplatypus; the former address has no redirect, because a project page is served under the repository’s own name and the only way to hold the old one would be to occupy the name the redirect needs.
The dated entries below name maju116/platypus where they were written that way. They are the record of what it was called at the time and they still resolve, so they are left alone rather than rewritten.





This file has a gap and it is named rather than backfilled. The entry below is dated 2026-10-08 and the pin moved twice between then and here - to 0.8.0a12 for fives-unet ([#151](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/151)) and to 0.8.0a20 for the instance task ([#155](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/155)) - so the dates above this heading are not a complete record of what the pin did. Writing those entries now would be writing them from the commit log rather than from the work, which is a different thing from having written them; the heading says what this change is and the omission stays visible.



Engine pinned to 0.8.0a22, for two things R forwards rather than implements.
A regression loss is refused as any segmentation model’s own loss, not only an instance model’s. ?losses claimed the narrower rule and was measured when it was written, so it was true rather than wrong - the engine’s refusal lived on the instance class alone, and a semantic model accepted loss_mse() and trained with it, reporting a validation loss of 0.0014 for a mask that was half missing where loss_cce() reaches a Dice of 1.0000. The default where = "foreground" is what made that look like a success: it averages the objective only inside the labelled objects and leaves the background unconstrained. pyplatypus[#223](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/223).
So available_losses() is ten rows now rather than thirteen, and available_losses("instance_segmentation") is thirteen - the three regression losses are reachable where they have a target, which is separation_flows(loss = ). Nothing R sends changes: a configuration refused after this pin move was refused by the engine before it.
evaluate() on an instance fit carries foreground_dice. It is the mask column to read across models - the binary overlap of anything the model called an object against anything that is one, the same arithmetic whatever the separation is. The dice beside it is a mean over the class channels the head has, three for separation_rim() against two for separation_flows(), so it is read down one model’s rows and never across two: on the Data Science Bowl’s validation cases it showed two masks 0.09 apart that are 0.0062 apart, and in the other direction. pyplatypus[#222](https://github.com/maju116/rplatypus/issues/222).





?losses’ task parameter listed two tasks and there have been three since the engine’s 0.8.0a20.








metric_cldice(), for structures where Dice asks the wrong question. It scores each mask against the other’s skeleton, so it measures whether a vessel is connected rather than whether its pixels coincide. Vessels, airways, neurons, cracks, catheters.
The two disagree in a way worth knowing, measured on a nine-pixel vessel: one drawn two pixels thin scores Dice 0.875, and the same vessel severed in the middle scores 0.947 - Dice prefers the severed one. clDice gives them 1.000 and 0.943. Its limit is measured too: at one pixel wide, a one-pixel displacement leaves no overlap at all and every overlap-based metric reads 0, this one included.
include_background defaults to FALSE here and TRUE for the other three. The background’s skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1 whatever the model did.





Engine pinned to 0.8.0a2.








drawing_style(), the five decisions every figure in this package makes when you do not give it one: which colours mean found, missed and invented, how much of the image an overlay lets through, how a box is labelled, and which boxes are worth drawing. Reach for it when you want to match a figure rather than restate it - colours = drawing_style()$box_colours keeps one source where typing the hex codes starts a second.





The drawing decisions now come from the engine. They were written out in ten places across R/plot.R and R/masks.R, and pyplatypus.style held the same five values - which is two copies that happened to agree, not one source. They agreed because five differences between the two packages’ figures had been found by laying them side by side and fixing them by hand.
Nothing changes in any picture: the values are identical, and a test compares every one of them against the engine’s, so a change on that side now fails this package’s CI instead of being noticed by eye.
Drawing still needs no Python. That is why the values are mirrored in R/style.R rather than fetched: plot_masks(), plot_boxes() and overlay_agreement() return without touching the bridge, and a default colour that called the engine would mean a five-gigabyte download to draw a mask.








Eight functions were renamed. The engine and this package had grown two words for the same thing in eight places, and a reader moving between the halves paid for every one. One name per concept now, and where the two disagreed the engine’s name won, because it is the layer that cannot be renamed later without changing the configuration format and the schema. The exception is available_transforms(), where this package already had a family of available_* names and the engine followed instead.








was
is
why




platypus_split()
split_dataset()
the engine’s name. The S3 class is still platypus_split - that is the object’s identity, and every class here is prefixed


split_files()
split_path()
it reads one split’s path; it does not split files. split_samples() in the engine is a different function, and the two names invited pairing them


mask_report()
inspect_masks()
the engine’s name, and the method it calls


mask_classes()
colours_to_classes()
the engine’s name, and it says which way the conversion goes


mask_colours()
classes_to_colours()
likewise. Note the engine’s onehot_to_colours() is not this function - it takes probabilities and argmaxes them, this takes class indices


save_weights()
export_weights()
the engine’s name; “export” says a sidecar is written beside the file


available_augmentations()
available_transforms()
the engine’s name, and albumentations’ own word for them


augment()
augmentation_step()
augment is a generic in broom and means something else there. augmentation alone would have shadowed the augmentation = argument it builds a list for



No aliases: two names for one thing is what this removes. The S3 class returned by split_dataset() is still platypus_split - that is the object’s identity, and every class in the package is prefixed.
evaluate(), evaluate_cases(), evaluate_classes() and evaluate_images() keep their names and so does platypus_fit(). The prefix on that one is not an inconsistency: fit is a generic in the tidymodels packages, so a bare fit would have been theirs to own, while evaluate is a generic here and dispatches on the fit’s class whichever package was attached last.
PYPLATYPUS_VERSION is pyplatypus_version. It was the only ALL-CAPS name in the package, so keeping it would have meant a lint exception for a style used exactly once.





callback_swa(): average the weights over the last part of the run. What it is worth is not in the score column - Dice and per-case error do not move - it is in the spread. Measured over three seeds, the volume bias went from +4.5% / +12.2% / -11.6% to -0.1% / +4.2% / +2.1%, 5.7 times tighter. The help page says so in those words, because somebody reading “weight averaging” will look at Dice, find nothing, and conclude wrongly. Refused beside callback_cosine_annealing(): a cosine has decayed to its floor by the time averaging begins, so the average is the last epoch.
segmentation_data(validation = FALSE): say a run has no validation set. The third answer to the question a path and a split already answered, and it had to be a stated value rather than an absence, because “I have no validation set” and “I forgot” look identical and only one of them is a decision. It went in the same argument rather than a new one, so nothing can contradict it.





The Python shim shipped inside this package is now formatted and linted by ruff in CI, beside lintr. It had never been.






The site is Quarto, not pkgdown, generated from tools/reference-groups.yml into a sidebar nested in eight groups, and themed from a _brand.yml that is byte-identical to pyplatypus’s - so the two sites look alike by construction rather than by anybody remembering to copy a colour.
Every old address still works. 105 redirect stubs cover all 99 addresses the pkgdown site published, the eight renames among them.







segmentation_data(split = ) and detection_data(split = ): divide one training folder into splits without writing any files. The argument is a list of fractions (two numbers, or three to cut a test set too) and group_by, which is a required key that may be NULL. The mistake it prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient on both sides make validation measure memory rather than generalisation, and nothing in the output says so. An omitted key would be that choice made silently; NULL is the same choice made on purpose. For detection this is the only way to divide one folder, because split_dataset() writes a masks column.
detection_crops(): cut the detected objects out of the images they were found in, at a fixed size, for handing to a classifier. Crops come from the source image through the same reader the dataset uses, are rounded outward so the whole box survives, and letterbox rather than stretch.
yolo3(box_loss = "giou"). Measured on BCCD over three seeds, 150 epochs, it is worse on the metric it targets - matched overlap 0.7929 against 0.8038, established at 2.7 standard errors - and its spread is sixty times wider. It ships because its coordinate term reads zero when the boxes are right, where the default term cannot reach zero however right they are. ?yolo3 leads with that table, because the name invites choosing it and the measured answer is the other way.
loss_boundary(): a region loss plus the signed distance to the truth’s boundary. region and alpha default to NULL here and are left out of the request, so the engine’s own defaults apply - alpha = 0.9, which it pins with a test, because at 0.5 the surface term owns half the objective while the prediction is still random and the volume bias spread goes to +/-28%. What the loss trades is accuracy per case for being unbiased over a series: measured over three seeds, the systematic volume bias went from -5.18% to -0.06% and the per-case absolute error from 16.90% to 22.17%.





Every help page has an \examples section but one - 47 of 48 at the time, encoders being a concept page with no \usage - and a test parses every example in every .Rd, including inside \dontrun{}, and fails if it names a function that does not exist. What was at risk was never the functionality; it is the example text drifting from the API.
lintr runs over the package in CI and gates on its findings. Of 906 findings at lintr’s defaults, 890 were the 80-character line limit this package does not use; at 100 characters and lint_package(), 25 - two of which were defects rather than style.






evaluate_images(): one row per image for a detector - n_truth, n_predicted, matched, missed, spurious, mean_matched_iou. Order by missed for the frames it cannot see, by mean_matched_iou for the ones where it finds everything and places it badly. No average precision per image: AP is the area under a ranking’s curve and on one picture it moves on a single box.
platypus_spec(task = ) can be stated, and is checked rather than trusted - it can confirm or refuse, never override. Unset, it is still derived from the constructors. Required in YAML and optional here is not an inconsistency: task is needed exactly where the type is not already stated, and segmentation_data() with u_net() can only mean one thing.





Object detection, from R. detection_data(), yolo3(), detection_anchors(), plot_boxes(), and predict() returning a list of boxes in each image’s own pixels - not an array, because images differ in size, so does the number of boxes, and a box in a letterboxed frame cannot be drawn on the photograph it came from.
plot_anchors(): the fitted anchors against the boxes they were fitted to. It is in the vignette twice, on the split they were fitted on and the one they were not.
A README figure for detection, drawn by the published bccd-yolo3 with no training, and tools/readme_figures.R that reproduces it.
Corrected: the claim that COCO’s anchors cover BCCD’s boxes at 0.67 where fitted ones reach 0.92. Re-measured on the 2,805 real training boxes, the honest pair is 0.65 against 0.88. The direction survives and is large; both numbers were wrong in opposite directions and the gap was right by coincidence.





u_net(encoder = "resnet34", pretrained = TRUE), with freeze_encoder and encoder_learning_rate. pretrained is a separate explicit flag so that naming a backbone never downloads anything nobody asked for. Measured on three datasets, pretraining never clearly beats the built-in encoder; what it buys is epochs, and what a swappable encoder buys is capacity where the target is thin. The help page carries the table.
inspect_masks() and platypus_fit(check_masks = FALSE): a declared class appearing in no mask has a target channel that is zero everywhere, so the model is never shown what it is being asked to find, and platypus_fit() now refuses on it. A threshold on the unmatched fraction cannot do this job - on a 0.6% lesion a wholly wrong colormap is quieter than JPEG artefacts in healthy data.
Every help page renders its markdown. DESCRIPTION had no Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) although every page had been written in markdown since the rewrite began, so not one cross-reference was a link: 0 to 42 links, 0 to 266 inline code spans, 36 of 40 pages changed. Nothing in the sources was wrong; nothing was converting them.





predict(space = "source"): map a prediction back out of the model’s grid onto the grid of the scan it came from, undoing the resampling and the crop. Returns a list, and the type change is the API being honest - scans differ in size, and quietly resizing them to match is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
Named weights. weights = "dsbowl-unet" from the registry, hf://owner/repo/file@commit, or a local path, plus export_weights() for your own. A registry name carries a commit and the hf:// form requires one, because weights that change under a stable name are the worst kind of irreproducibility.
The Data Science Bowl vignette now opens with a mask in four lines - published weights, fit = FALSE, plot_masks() - before any mention of training. First contact should not need a GPU and an afternoon.
Fixed, and found by writing that vignette: weights = "dsbowl-unet" could not work from R at all. The bridge asked for pyplatypus with no extras, so huggingface_hub was never in the environment reticulate builds. Nothing in either test suite could have caught it - the engine’s tests install the extra deliberately and the R tests ran where it was already present.
The README says what changed since 0.1.1, written by diffing the two NAMESPACE files rather than from memory: of 0.1.1’s 37 exports, 30 are gone, and three of the seven survivors are worse than gone because they are still callable and mean something else.




The day the package stopped being a bridge and became a surface. Five engine releases, each followed here.

A worked vignette on the Data Science Bowl, precomputed so that reading it needs no GPU, and a README.
Continuous integration: five R CMD check jobs - Ubuntu on R devel, release and oldrel-1, plus macOS and Windows on release - and an engine job that installs the built package and runs the suite against the engine resolved from PyPI. That last one is the job that matters: pkgload::load_all() exposes a package’s internals, library() does not, and local work had been using the most permissive of the three ways a test can reach them.
Plotting and masks: plot_masks(), plot_boxes(), overlay_mask(), overlay_agreement(), read_masks(), unite_masks(), mask_coverage().
DICOM, properly: modality LUT, a fixed window, MONOCHROME1 inverted. Plus series_report() for a folder of slices, whose decision is that a problem is a column, not an exception - a hundred cases contain a few bad ones, and stopping at the first turns an afternoon into a week.
Splitting by patient (split_dataset(), split_path()) and evaluate_cases().
Volumes. input_shape = c(64, 64, 32) had been building a 3D U-Net since the first release; what was missing was reading NIfTI, where orientation is the whole problem, and labels as a second way to describe a mask, because volumes label with integers. save_volumes() writes NIfTI carrying the affine of the scan the mask was predicted from - without it a mask cannot be laid over its scan by any viewer, and the file looks perfectly normal while being wrong. mask_volume() reports millilitres, because a voxel count is meaningless outside one scanner.
target_spacing: resample to a common voxel size. What makes it necessary is not slice thickness but field of view - forty slices of 1 mm is 40 mm of patient and forty of 2.5 mm is 100 mm, which is the ordinary state of clinical data.
channels_from: one channel per file, stating the order and never inferring it. A model trained with FLAIR in channel one and used where channel one is T1 answers plausibly, with the right shape and range, and nothing downstream can tell.
Augmentation in 3D, and available_transforms(rank = 3) to say what is usable - 97 of albumentations’ transforms accept a volume and the rest raise from inside the library.
A second vignette, on volumes, which generates its own data. It ends on a model at Dice 0.88 whose volumes are 12-23% too large, which is the argument for reporting volume beside overlap: Dice is dominated by an object’s interior and forgiving about its boundary.
segmentation_data(window = ) replaced dicom_window, since NIfTI needs the same thing. The old name is still accepted; giving both is an error.




The package exists.

The bridge. py_require() plus uv, resolving an isolated ephemeral environment at library(rplatypus) - deliberately not the shared-Python arrangement that broke this package’s Keras stack in 2020. platypus_status() says what it found rather than leaving a failed import to be guessed at, and PLATYPUS_ENGINE_PATH points the bridge at a source tree during development.
platypus_spec(), built either from arguments or from a YAML file and producing the same thing. One pipeline, two constructors.
platypus_fit(), evaluate(), predict(), training_history(), and the engine’s complaints translated into R conditions rather than passed through as Python tracebacks.

title: Change Log
text:
The last release of the TensorFlow package, kept here for the record rather than as an ancestor of the entries above. It built Keras models through the R keras package: yolo3() and darknet53() with load_darknet_weights() for the original Darknet weights, a plain u_net(), segmentation_generator(), loss_dice(), the COCO and VOC colormaps, and readers for LabelMe JSON and Pascal VOC XML.
It is still installable and still pinned:
remotes::install_github("maju116/rplatypus@0.1.1")
Its source is on the master branch and the issues filed against it stay open. What has aged is its dependencies rather than its code - the pinned TensorFlow no longer installs on a current Python, which is the reason for a rewrite rather than a consequence of one.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
vignette("data-science-bowl") finds the nuclei in these pictures and stops there. Its own closing warning is the reason this document exists: the mask it produces says nucleus or not nucleus for every pixel, so two nuclei touching each other come back as one region, and a count taken from it would be wrong.
This is the same dataset, read a different way. Nothing new was collected: the 2018 Data Science Bowl ships one mask per nucleus, and the semantic vignette unites them. Here they keep their identity, which turns the question from where are the nuclei into how many are there, and which pixels belong to which one.
Every number and every picture below was produced by running the code shown.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: Before any of that: objects in four lines
text:
Before any of that: objects in four lines
Weights for this are published, so the difference is visible before anything is trained. The borrowed model predicts three channels - background, the interior of a nucleus and a rim around it - and decode says how those channels become objects:
borrowed <- platypus_spec(
  data = instance_data(validation_dir, validation_dir),
  models = list(u_net("objects", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      separation = separation_rim(width = 2),
                      decode = list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components()),
                      weights = "dsbowl-instances", fit = FALSE))
)
loaded <- platypus_fit(borrowed, verbose = FALSE)
objects <- predict(loaded, split = "validation", decode = "nearest_seed")
length(objects)
#> [1] 134
An instance prediction comes back as a list of integer label maps named by case, not as one array: objects numbered from 1, with 0 for background.
Now the same loaded file, decoded the other way. connected_components ignores the rim channel entirely - it labels connected foreground, which is what a semantic mask gives you:
merged <- predict(loaded, split = "validation", decode = "connected_components")

counts <- data.frame(
  case = substr(names(objects), 1, 8),
  separated = vapply(objects, max, integer(1)),
  as_one_region = vapply(merged[names(objects)], max, integer(1))
)
head(counts[order(counts$as_one_region - counts$separated), ], 5)
