worst <- names(objects)[order(counts$as_one_region - counts$separated)][1]
shot <- read_images(
  list.files(file.path(validation_dir, worst, "images"), full.names = TRUE)[1],
  size = c(256, 256)
)
picture <- shot[1, , , ]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
plot(as.raster(overlay_instances(picture, objects[[worst]]) / 255), main = "nearest_seed")
plot(as.raster(overlay_instances(picture, merged[[worst]]) / 255),
     main = "connected_components")



plot of chunk instances-decoded-two-ways


One file of weights, one forward pass, two answers to how many nuclei are in this picture. Neither colour map is decoration: adjacent objects are guaranteed different colours, so a colour shared across a boundary is two nuclei the decoding ran together.
No score is reported here, on purpose. These weights were trained on stage1_train and this directory is stage1_validation, which is the split they were measured on - the numbers that mean something travel with them:
listing <- available_weights()
cat(strwrap(listing$description[listing$name == "dsbowl-instances"], 88), sep = "\n")
#> U-Net, 256x256, nuclei in light microscopy, trained to separate touching objects:
#> interior, rim and background. BBBC038v1 (the 2018 Data Science Bowl, CC0), the same 134
#> held-out images as `dsbowl-unet`. **One file, three scores** - instance average
#> precision 0.5445 by nearest_seed, 0.5390 by watershed and 0.4822 by
#> connected_components - so a number from these weights means nothing without the
#> decoding it came from. Foreground Dice 0.9118. The separation signal is worth +0.0623
#> here while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398: the mask is the limit on this data, not the
#> signal.
That description is the thing to read before quoting anything. One file, three scores: the decoding is part of the number, and 0.0623 separates the best from the worst.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: The semantic sibling, side by side
text:
The semantic sibling, side by side
dsbowl-unet is the published model from the other vignette: same data, same held-out images, one foreground class. It is the comparison this whole document is about, so it is worth seeing rather than describing:
semantic <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(validation_dir, validation_dir, colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("mask", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      weights = "dsbowl-unet", fit = FALSE))
)
masks <- predict(platypus_fit(semantic, verbose = FALSE), split = "validation")
dim(masks)
#> [1] 134 256 256
where <- match(worst, list.dirs(validation_dir, recursive = FALSE, full.names = FALSE))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
plot(as.raster(overlay_mask(picture, masks[where, , ], binary_colormap) / 255),
     main = "dsbowl-unet: where the nuclei are")
plot(as.raster(overlay_instances(picture, objects[[worst]]) / 255),
     main = "dsbowl-instances: which is which")



plot of chunk instances-mask-beside-objects


The left-hand picture is not worse. It answers a different question, and if the answer you need is what fraction of this slide is nuclei it is the one to use. The right-hand one is what you need to count them, or to measure one of them.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
The data
The directory layout is the one the semantic vignette uses, because it is the same directory:
stage1_train/
  00ae65c1c.../
    images/00ae65c1c....png
    masks/8a0ac8e3c....png      # one file per nucleus, 70 of them in this case
    masks/9a1e2f4b7....png
    ...
length(samples)
#> [1] 536
length(list.files(file.path(samples[1], "masks")))
#> [1] 27
instance_data() reads those per-object files as identities rather than uniting them, which is the only difference from segmentation_data() at this level:
data <- instance_data(train_dir, validation_dir)

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: The specification, with the borrowed model beside a new one
text:
The specification, with the borrowed model beside a new one
Two models in one specification: the published file, loaded and not trained, and the same recipe trained here from scratch. evaluate() returns a row per model and decoding, so one table holds the comparison the rest of this document rests on.
decodings <- list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_watershed(), decode_connected_components())

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = data,
  seed = 0,
  models = list(
    u_net("published", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
          separation = separation_rim(width = 2), decode = decodings,
          weights = "dsbowl-instances", fit = FALSE),
    u_net("mine", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
          separation = separation_rim(width = 2), decode = decodings,
          loss = loss_cce_dice(),
          metrics = list(metric_dice(), metric_iou()),
          optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.001),
          augmentation = list(
            augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
            augmentation_step("VerticalFlip", p = 0.5),
            augmentation_step("RandomRotate90", p = 0.5)
          ),
          epochs = 40, batch_size = 32)
  )
)
spec
#> platypus specification
#>   data        : /home/maju116/Desktop/PROJECTS/Personal Projects/PLATYPUS FAMILY/pyplatypus/examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_train 
#>   classes     : 0 
#>   models      : 2 
#>     published      u_net            256x256, cce, 10 epochs
#>     mine           u_net            256x256, cce_dice, 40 epochs
separation is one block per model and decode is a list, and the asymmetry is not cosmetic: the separation sets what the network predicts, so changing it means another training run, while a second decoding is another pass over the same predictions. Measured on these 134 images, a second decoding costs 1.41 seconds.
Forty epochs rather than the published file’s hundred and twenty, deliberately: the point of the table below is what a short run gets you against a converged one, and a reader reproducing this does not need two hours to see the difference.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
Train
fit <- platypus_fit(spec, num_workers = 4)
fit
#> platypus fit
#>   models   : published, mine 
#>   device   : NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 (torch 2.7.1+cu126) 
#>   epochs   : mine=40 
#>   next     : evaluate(fit), predict(fit, "published")
num_workers = 4 is worth copying. Measured on this model and this batch size, the same epoch takes 17.5 seconds against 49.6 with the default of none: the GPU spends most of a run waiting for PNGs to be decoded, and nothing about the model changes.
plot(fit)



plot of chunk instances-history

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
Compare
scores <- evaluate(fit)
scores[, c("model", "decode", "foreground_dice", "average_precision",
           "predicted_objects", "truth_objects")]
#>       model               decode foreground_dice average_precision
#> 1 published         nearest_seed       0.9117900         0.5444811
#> 2 published            watershed       0.9117900         0.5390481
#> 3 published connected_components       0.9117900         0.4821945
#> 4      mine         nearest_seed       0.9014591         0.4939518
#> 5      mine            watershed       0.9014591         0.4923366
#> 6      mine connected_components       0.9014591         0.4608787
#>   predicted_objects truth_objects
#> 1              5378          5999
#> 2              5378          5999
#> 3              4914          5999
#> 4              5074          5999
#> 5              5074          5999
#> 6              4902          5999
Three things in that table, in the order they matter.
Within either model, the mask is identical across its three rows. There is one forward pass; the rows differ only in how its channels were turned into objects. So the spread between a model’s own rows is the decoding’s contribution and nothing else.
connected_components is the row the others are read against. It throws the rim channel away, so it is what the separation signal is worth being compared to - not a weaker model, the same model asked a question that ignores half its output.
The forty-epoch run is 0.0103 behind on the mask and 0.0505 behind on average precision - the two numbers written by the run above rather than by hand, so re-knitting this document cannot leave them stale.
Two runs of one configuration on this data differ by about 0.009 of average precision - measured, and the recorded spread every claim here is read against. The mask gap above is one of those, so on foreground Dice the short run is barely distinguishable from the published one, while the score gap is 5.6 of them. The extra eighty epochs bought a sharper rim rather than a better mask, and foreground_dice cannot see a sharper rim: the rim is a third class whose quality only becomes visible once the channels are decoded into objects, which is the same reason the class dice column exists beside it.
That is a finding about time inside one recipe, and the next section is a finding about recipes. They do not contradict each other, and reading one as the other is the mistake this document is arranged to prevent.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: What this does not settle, measured rather than guessed
text:
What this does not settle, measured rather than guessed
The instance milestone closed on numbers that say the interesting part is somewhere else:







route
instance AP on these 134 images




the published semantic weights through connected components
0.4888


a perfect semantic mask through connected components
0.7655


the published separation weights, nearest_seed
0.5445


a perfect mask through the same separation route
0.9846



So connected components caps any model here at 0.7655 - a flawless mask still scores that - and the separation signal is worth about +0.06 on top of the mask it is computed from, where fixing the mask is worth +0.24. Three trained signals were compared and they agree; a bigger network was measured and moved the score by less than the run-to-run spread.
Read that as a closed direction rather than as a run to tune: on this data the headroom is in the mask, and a document that ended on a score would be claiming the opposite of what was measured.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: Which objects, not how many pixels
text:
Which objects, not how many pixels
A score cannot tell you whether you found the wrong nuclei or drew the right ones badly. overlay_instance_agreement() matches predicted objects to true ones the way the metric does and colours the three outcomes, so the failure is visible by kind.
The truth has to be assembled from the per-object files, which is four lines and worth seeing - read_images(nearest = TRUE) matters, because interpolating a label map invents numbers belonging to no object:
truth_map <- function(case, size = c(256, 256)) {
  files <- list.files(file.path(case, "masks"), full.names = TRUE)
  stack <- read_images(files, size = size, channels = 1, nearest = TRUE)
  labels <- array(0L, dim = size)
  for (i in seq_along(files)) labels[stack[i, , , 1] > 0.5] <- i
  labels
}

actual <- truth_map(file.path(validation_dir, worst))
c(objects_in_the_files = length(list.files(file.path(validation_dir, worst, "masks"))),
  objects_that_survived_the_resize = length(setdiff(unique(as.vector(actual)), 0L)))
#>             objects_in_the_files objects_that_survived_the_resize 
#>                              257                              257
mine <- predict(fit, "mine", split = "validation", decode = "nearest_seed")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
plot(as.raster(overlay_instance_agreement(picture, objects[[worst]], actual) / 255),
     main = "published")
plot(as.raster(overlay_instance_agreement(picture, mine[[worst]], actual) / 255),
     main = "mine, 40 epochs")



plot of chunk instances-agreement


Green is a true object matched by a prediction, red one that nothing matched, yellow a prediction matching nothing. The threshold is an IoU of 0.5 and it cannot be lowered below that: under 0.5 one prediction can satisfy two true objects at once, the match stops being one to one, and the average precision refuses the same thing for the same reason.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
text:
A decoding changed without retraining
This is what decode being a list is for. No model is loaded again and nothing is trained:
again <- lapply(c("nearest_seed", "watershed", "connected_components"), function(how) {
  maps <- predict(fit, "mine", split = "validation", decode = how)
  data.frame(decode = how, objects = sum(vapply(maps, max, integer(1))))
})
do.call(rbind, again)
#>                 decode objects
#> 1         nearest_seed    5074
#> 2            watershed    5074
#> 3 connected_components    4902
Against 5,999 objects in the truth. The counts, not the scores, are where the decoding shows itself most plainly: the gap between the first row and the last is nuclei that were found and then run together with a neighbour.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: What it was for: a count and a size distribution
text:
What it was for: a count and a size distribution
instance_sizes() is the end of this road. One label map in, one row per object out:
sizes <- instance_sizes(mine[[worst]])
head(sizes, 3)
#>   object voxels
#> 1      1     72
#> 2      2     46
#> 3      3     68
summary(sizes$voxels)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    4.00   59.75   73.50   73.61   87.00  179.00
hist(sizes$voxels, breaks = 20, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "", xlab = "object size in pixels")



plot of chunk instances-sizes


per_case <- vapply(mine, max, integer(1))
c(images = length(per_case), objects = sum(per_case),
  median_per_image = median(per_case), most_in_one_image = max(per_case))
#>            images           objects  median_per_image most_in_one_image 
#>             134.0            5074.0              24.5             236.0
In pixels, because this dataset has no physical scale. instance_sizes() takes a spacing in millimetres and returns an area or a volume when you give it one - that is what a CT scan carries in its header, and vignette("volumes") ends in millilitres for exactly that reason. These are microscopy images with no calibration recorded, so a number in micrometres here would be invented. A count is still a count.

And what shape, which needs no scale at all
A size needs a scale and a shape does not, as long as the pixels are square - so on this uncalibrated dataset instance_shapes() reports something instance_sizes() cannot. eccentricity is sqrt(1 - (minor/major)^2), a ratio of two lengths, so whatever unit they are in cancels:
shapes <- instance_shapes(mine[[worst]])
head(shapes, 3)
#>   object major_px minor_px eccentricity
#> 1      1 6.489396 4.139444    0.7701373
#> 2      2 5.592754 2.662741    0.8793882
#> 3      3 5.447144 4.166351    0.6441860
summary(shapes$eccentricity)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.1547  0.6644  0.7650  0.7383  0.8347  0.9737
plot(shapes$major_px, shapes$minor_px, pch = 16, col = "#33442b66", asp = 1,
     xlab = "major semi-axis in pixels", ylab = "minor semi-axis in pixels")
abline(0, 1, col = "grey60", lty = 2)



plot of chunk instances-shapes


Every point sits below the dashed line because the major axis is the longer one by definition, and how far below is the eccentricity. A nucleus on this image is typically 0.64 times as wide as it is long.
An object under three pixels has no shape at all, and that is an answer rather than a gap: there is no second moment to take, so the row comes back as zeros instead of as an error, and a speck of a prediction does not fail a table. On this image that applies to 0 of 236 objects - at 256 by 256 a nucleus is rarely that small. Over all 134 validation images through the published weights it is 125 of 5,378, which the engine’s own article reports, and the difference is the input size rather than the model.
And “needs no scale” is a claim worth measuring rather than repeating. eccentricity is unitless and it is not spacing-free - it describes whichever space it was computed in - so the two agree here only because a pixel is as tall as it is wide. The same objects, three ways:
c(grid       = median(shapes$eccentricity),
  isotropic  = median(instance_shapes(mine[[worst]], spacing = c(0.5, 0.5))$eccentricity),
  stretched  = median(instance_shapes(mine[[worst]], spacing = c(1.0, 0.5))$eccentricity))
#>      grid isotropic stretched 
#> 0.7649915 0.7649915 0.9195459
The first two are the same number and the third is not. So reading the grid’s eccentricity as the object’s is right on this data and would be wrong on a scan whose voxels are taller than they are wide - which is most of them. The column names say which you have: major_px and minor_px without a spacing, major_mm and minor_mm with one, and the suffix on the axes is what tells you what the row is about.
A volume gets three axes - major_mm, middle_mm, minor_mm - and no eccentricity, because an ellipsoid has no single one.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: The same thing from a file
text:
The same thing from a file
spec <- platypus_spec("experiment.yaml")
fit  <- platypus_fit(spec, num_workers = 4)
The configuration guide’s Instances instead of one mask section has the YAML for this, field by field.

title: Telling touching nuclei apart
section: A note on older graphics cards
text:
A note on older graphics cards
PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta generations - a GTX 10-series card cannot run them, and no driver update changes that. Without saying anything, everything above would run on the processor instead, perhaps ten times slower.
If platypus_device() reports cpu on a machine that has a GPU, restart R and ask for the older build before anything else:
library(rplatypus)
platypus_use_torch("pascal")
platypus_device()
#> torch      : 2.7.1+cu126 
#> cuda build : 12.6 
#> device     : NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
The other vignette works on two-dimensional microscopy. This one is about volumes, which is where medical imaging mostly lives: a CT or an MRI is a stack of slices, and three things that do not exist in 2D decide whether a result means anything.
Voxels have a physical size, and it differs between scans. Slices belong to a patient, so a split that ignores who they came from measures memory rather than generalisation. And a mask has a position in space, without which it cannot be laid over the scan it describes.
The data here is synthetic, generated by the code below, so you can run every line of this without downloading anything or registering anywhere. It is deliberately crude - a ball of soft tissue in air - but it is crude in a way that leaves the three problems above fully intact.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Making something to segment
Twenty-four scans from twelve patients, two each. Each holds one spherical “lesion” in air, and the scans differ in three ways that matter, all of which are ordinary in clinical data:

slice thickness - half at 1 mm, half at 2.5 mm, so the same anatomy occupies a different number of voxels;
lesion size - 4 to 12 mm in radius, which on thick slices is the difference between an easy target and two voxels of signal;
noise - some scans are much noisier than others.

The variety is the point. A synthetic dataset where every case is equally easy would make the per-patient section below look like a formality, and it is not one.
library(RNifti)

root <- file.path(tempdir(), "scans")
dir.create(root, showWarnings = FALSE)

make_scan <- function(patient, study, slice_mm, radius_mm, noise) {
  shape <- c(48, 48, 32)
  spacing <- c(1, 1, slice_mm)

  # Millimetres from the centre of the volume, per voxel.
  grid <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x = seq_len(shape[1]), y = seq_len(shape[2]),
                                z = seq_len(shape[3])))
  centre <- (shape + 1) / 2
  offset <- sweep(grid, 2, centre) * matrix(spacing, nrow(grid), 3, byrow = TRUE)
  # Move the lesion per patient, so the model cannot learn one position and be done.
  offset[, 1] <- offset[, 1] - (patient - 6) * 1.5
  distance <- sqrt(rowSums(offset^2))

  lesion <- array(as.integer(distance <= radius_mm), dim = shape)
  # Hounsfield units: air is -1000, soft tissue about 40, plus scanner noise.
  scan <- array(ifelse(lesion == 1, 40, -1000) + rnorm(prod(shape), sd = noise), dim = shape)

  name <- sprintf("patient%02d_study%d", patient, study)
  dir.create(file.path(root, name, "images"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  dir.create(file.path(root, name, "masks"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  # The datatype goes on the write rather than on asNifti(): asking asNifti() for one returns
  # an image in RNifti's internal C representation, whose pixel dimensions cannot then be set.
  image <- asNifti(scan)
  pixdim(image) <- spacing
  writeNifti(image, file.path(root, name, "images", "ct.nii.gz"), datatype = "float")

  mask <- asNifti(lesion)
  pixdim(mask) <- spacing
  writeNifti(mask, file.path(root, name, "masks", "lesion.nii.gz"), datatype = "int16")
  name
}

design <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:12, function(patient) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(study) {
    radius_mm <- c(12, 10, 8, 6, 5, 4)[(patient - 1) %% 6 + 1]
    key <- make_scan(
      patient, study,
      slice_mm = if (patient %% 2 == 0) 1 else 2.5,
      radius_mm = radius_mm,
      noise = c(30, 40, 60, 80)[(patient - 1) %% 4 + 1]
    )
    # Keeping the truth around: the volume of a sphere is known exactly, which makes it
    # possible to ask later whether the model got the *size* right and not only the overlap.
    data.frame(key = key, radius_mm = radius_mm,
               true_ml = 4 / 3 * pi * radius_mm^3 / 1000)
  }))
}))

nrow(design)
#> [1] 24
volume_info() reads what the files say about themselves, through the same pipeline training uses:
scans <- list.files(root, pattern = "ct[.]nii[.]gz$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
info <- volume_info(scans[c(1, 3)])
info[, c("spacing_1", "spacing_2", "spacing_3", "shape_3", "voxel_ml")]
#>   spacing_1 spacing_2 spacing_3 shape_3 voxel_ml
#> 1         1         1       2.5      32   0.0025
#> 2         1         1       1.0      32   0.0010
Two scans, the same number of slices, and one covers 32 mm of patient where the other covers 80 mm. A voxel in the second is two and a half times the volume of a voxel in the first.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: Splitting by patient, not by scan
text:
Splitting by patient, not by scan
Each of these patients has two studies. Split the twenty-four scans at random and both studies of some patient land on opposite sides of the split: the model meets that patient in training and is then tested on the same anatomy.
How much that costs is a separate question, and it has now been measured rather than asserted. This paragraph used to end “Dice comes out several points too high”, which nothing had ever checked. On MSD Spleen - 41 patients, 1043 slices - a slice-level split put 29 of 29 development patients on both sides, and the model it produced overstated its own score by +0.035 against patients it had never seen. A patient-level split on the same data overstated itself by +0.039. So the inflation is real and it is not the leak: any validation set differs from any test set by a few points because patients differ, and on this data the leak added nothing on top of that.
That is one dataset, one architecture and twelve epochs, which is not evidence that the mistake is harmless where a model has room to memorise. The reason to keep patients whole is that the mechanism is certain and invisible in the result, not that the size is known.
split_dataset() takes a pattern that says which part of a name is the patient, and keeps every patient whole:
split <- split_dataset(
  root, file.path(tempdir(), "splits"),
  group_by = "^(patient\\d+)_",
  fractions = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25),
  seed = 1
)
split
#> platypus split
#>   train         12 samples in 6 groups
#>   validation     6 samples in 3 groups
#>   test           6 samples in 3 groups
#>   grouped by '^(patient\d+)_'; no group is in two sets
#>   seed 1 - the same inputs give this split again
A pattern that matches nothing is an error rather than a fallback, which is the point: a silent fallback to one-group-per-scan would reintroduce exactly the bug the argument exists to prevent.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
The specification
Three volume-specific arguments carry the weight here.
labels says the mask is a label map rather than a picture - which is how every volume format stores masks, and the reason colormap is not the only way to name classes. window maps Hounsfield units to 0-1 through a fixed window, so the same tissue is the same brightness in every scan. And target_spacing resamples everything to a common voxel size before cropping to the model’s shape.
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    split,
    labels = c(0, 1),
    window = "soft_tissue",
    target_spacing = c(1, 1, 1)
  ),
  models = list(
    u_net(
      "lesion",
      input_shape = c(32, 32, 32),
      channels = 1,
      blocks = 3,
      filters = 16,
      epochs = 12,
      batch_size = 2,
      loss = loss_dice(),
      metrics = list(metric_dice(include_background = FALSE)),
      augmentation = list(
        augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
        augmentation_step("CubicSymmetry", p = 0.5)
      )
    )
  )
)
spec
#> platypus specification
#>   data        : /tmp/Rtmp81OYn5/splits/train.csv 
#>   classes     : 0 
#>   models      : 1 
#>     lesion         u_net            32x32x32, dice, 12 epochs
input_shape has three entries, and that is the only thing that makes this a 3D run. Nothing else in the specification is different - the same losses, the same metrics, the same tiling if you want it.
Not every augmentation works on a volume. albumentations supports them unevenly, so ask rather than guess:
length(available_transforms())
#> [1] 118
head(setdiff(available_transforms(), available_transforms(rank = 3)), 4)
#> [1] "AdditiveNoise"       "BBoxSafeRandomCrop"  "ChannelDropout"     
#> [4] "ChromaticAberration"
The second call asks the same question at rank = 3 and returns fewer names. How many fewer is not printed here on purpose: it is a property of the installed ‘albumentations’ rather than of this package, and ?available_transforms says what the engine does and does not promise about it. The names are the useful part anyway.
A transform from that difference is refused by name when the run starts, rather than raising something from inside the library an hour in.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Training
fit <- platypus_fit(spec, verbose = FALSE)
fit
#> platypus fit
#>   models   : lesion 
#>   device   : NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 (torch 2.7.1+cu126) 
#>   epochs   : lesion=12 
#>   next     : evaluate(fit), predict(fit, "lesion")
plot(fit)



plot of chunk history
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: Scores per patient, not per dataset
text:
Scores per patient, not per dataset
evaluate() gives one row per model: one number for the whole validation set.
evaluate(fit)[, c("model", "loss_function", "dice", "epochs_run")]
#>    model loss_function      dice epochs_run
#> 1 lesion          dice 0.9536304         12
That number hides the distribution, and the distribution is usually the finding. With group_by, each row is a patient - their slices pooled, the way a volume would be:
cases <- evaluate_cases(fit, group_by = "^(patient\\d+)_")
cases
#> platypus scores by group (3 rows)
#>      group      dice
#>  patient06 0.9500000
#>  patient11 0.9299276
#>  patient10 0.9808831
summary(cases)
#>   metric n      mean         sd median       min       max worst_group
#> 1   dice 3 0.9536036 0.02566816   0.95 0.9299276 0.9808831   patient11
The worst_group column is the one that makes this actionable. A mean of any value with a minimum far below it is a model with a failure mode, and the mean is where it hides.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Looking at a slice
A volume cannot honestly be shown as one picture, so plot_masks() asks which plane to draw. slice = "middle" is the sensible first look:
validation <- split_path(split, "validation")
images <- read_images(validation$images, size = c(32, 32, 32), channels = 1)
truth <- read_masks(validation$masks, labels = c(0, 1), size = c(32, 32, 32))
prediction <- predict(fit, split = "validation")

plot_masks(
  images, prediction = prediction, truth = truth,
  colormap = binary_colormap, slice = "middle",
  which = 1:3, labels = validation$key[1:3]
)



plot of chunk plot
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
Millilitres, not voxels
The size of a finding is reported in millilitres. A voxel count means nothing outside the scanner that produced it - the same lesion is 4000 voxels on one machine and 12000 on another - and resampling is what makes the conversion trivial: at target_spacing = c(1, 1, 1) a voxel is exactly one cubic millimetre.
predicted_ml <- vapply(
  seq_len(dim(prediction)[1]),
  function(i) mask_volume(prediction[i, , , ], spacing = c(1, 1, 1), class = 2),
  numeric(1)
)

sizes <- merge(
  data.frame(key = validation$key, predicted_ml = round(predicted_ml, 2)),
  design[, c("key", "true_ml")], by = "key"
)
sizes$error_pct <- round(100 * (sizes$predicted_ml - sizes$true_ml) / sizes$true_ml)
sizes
#>                key predicted_ml   true_ml error_pct
#> 1 patient06_study1         0.31 0.2680826        16
#> 2 patient06_study2         0.31 0.2680826        16
#> 3 patient10_study1         0.95 0.9047787         5
#> 4 patient10_study2         0.94 0.9047787         4
#> 5 patient11_study1         0.56 0.5235988         7
#> 6 patient11_study2         0.57 0.5235988         9
These lesions are spheres, so the true volume is known exactly - which is worth doing in a synthetic example, because it asks a question Dice cannot. The overlap scores above were 0.93 to 0.98, respectable by any standard; the volumes are 4% to 16% out.
Every number in that sentence is computed rather than typed, and the first half is why: it used to read “around 0.88”, against the table directly above it. A stale number next to the measurement it contradicts is the one kind a reader can catch without leaving the page, and it survived anyway.
That is not a contradiction. Dice is dominated by the interior of an object and forgiving about its boundary, and for a small lesion the boundary is most of it. A model that draws every lesion one voxel too wide scores well and reports a volume that is wrong by between a quarter and twice over, because the error cubes: +27% on the 12 mm sphere at 1 mm slices and +95% on the 4 mm one. If the question is is there a lesion, the Dice is the relevant number. If it is has it grown since March, this table is, and the two do not follow from each other.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: Writing a mask back onto its scan
text:
Writing a mask back onto its scan
save_volumes() writes a prediction as NIfTI carrying the affine of the scan it came from. Without that affine a mask cannot be laid over its scan by any viewer or registration tool - it either lands in the wrong place or is refused, and nothing about the file looks wrong.
Carrying the affine means the mask has to be on the same grid as the scan, and after resampling it is not: these scans are 48 x 48 x 32 voxels while the model works at 32 x 32 x 32. space = "source" maps each prediction back out of the model’s grid onto the scan’s, undoing the resampling and the crop:
masks <- predict(fit, split = "validation", space = "source")
length(masks)
#> [1] 6
dim(masks[[1]])
#> [1] 48 48 32
A list rather than an array, because scans differ in size and a stack needs one shape. That is the API being explicit rather than resizing them to match, which is how a mask ends up describing anatomy it was not computed from.
Names come from the reference files unless you say otherwise, and here every scan is called ct.nii.gz inside its own directory - so the masks would all be written to one name. That is an error rather than five silently lost files, and the case keys are what to use instead:
written <- save_volumes(masks, file.path(tempdir(), "predictions"),
                        reference = validation$images, names = validation$key)
basename(written)
#> [1] "patient06_study1.nii.gz" "patient06_study2.nii.gz"
#> [3] "patient11_study1.nii.gz" "patient11_study2.nii.gz"
#> [5] "patient10_study1.nii.gz" "patient10_study2.nii.gz"
The written masks carry the scans’ geometry, which is what makes them open on top of them:
volume_info(written)[, c("spacing_1", "spacing_3", "shape_1", "shape_3")]
#>   spacing_1 spacing_3 shape_1 shape_3
#> 1         1       1.0      48      32
#> 2         1       1.0      48      32
#> 3         1       2.5      48      32
#> 4         1       2.5      48      32
#> 5         1       1.0      48      32
#> 6         1       1.0      48      32
Two things are lost on the way back and it is worth knowing which. Interpolation softens a boundary, so the mask is slightly smoother than the model drew it. And where reading cropped anatomy away, the mask returns padded with background - which means not examined, not nothing there. If that distinction matters, give the model an input_shape that covers the anatomy.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
section: DICOM, which is how the data usually arrives
text:
DICOM, which is how the data usually arrives
The scans above are NIfTI because that is what research datasets ship. Data out of a hospital arrives as a directory of DICOM files per series, and platypus reads those as volumes too - sorting them by their position in the patient rather than by filename, which is the difference between a scan and a shuffled deck.
Point the specification at directories of slices and nothing else changes. Before training, though, run the export past series_report():
report <- series_report(list.dirs("dicom_export", recursive = FALSE))
report[!report$ok, c("path", "problem")]
It reads no pixels and returns one row per directory, because an archive export of a hundred cases will contain a few with a missing slice, duplicated files, or two series sitting in one folder - and a missing slice does not shorten a volume, it moves everything past the gap.
crumbs: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores

title: Segmenting volumes: CT, spacing and per-patient scores
text:
What this leaves out
Resampling is offered, not imposed.
What it costs to impose it, and the trap in doing so, were measured on MSD Spleen - 41 abdominal CTs whose slice thickness runs 1.5 mm to 8 mm and whose voxels differ in volume by 5.9 times, which is the variation target_spacing exists for. Three arms, one input_shape of 64 cubed, every one scored against the truth as stored:



what the model reads
dice
worst case
volume error




the whole scan, squashed into the shape
0.709
0.014
87 ml


target_spacing = c(1.5, 1.5, 1.5)
0.000
0.000
231 ml


target_spacing = c(7.5, 7.5, 7.5)
0.822
0.770
29 ml



of a spleen averaging 234 ml.
The middle row is the trap and it is total. Resampling does not only change the scale: it changes what input_shape means. Without it, the shape is the whole scan squashed to fit. With it, the shape is a box of so many millimetres taken from the middle - 64 voxels at 1.5 mm is a 96 mm cube - and a spleen sits up to 165 mm off the centre of the scan and is up to 143 mm across. The organ is outside the box in every case, so the model finds nothing at all, three runs out of three.
Choose the field of view in millimetres first, then the spacing and the shape that cover it. Here that is a 480 mm box, and it is worth +0.11 of Dice over resizing and a third of the volume error - 14% of the organ against 30%.
The difference in reliability is larger than the difference in the mean: across three runs the resampled arm’s worst case stayed between 0.72 and 0.77, while the resized arm’s was 0.00, 0.58 and 0.01. It does not score a little lower; it loses a whole scan, a different one each time. Which scan is not explained by its geometry - the two volumes covering the most patient came through fine - and that is an open question rather than a tidy ending.
A coarse 7.5 mm is a poor way to see a boundary, so the arm this did not run is a finer spacing with splits, which is how a large field of view is covered without a large input. maju116/pyplatypus#201.
Several volumes per sample - one per modality, as BraTS ships - works through channels_from, where the order is stated rather than inferred. That is a design claim, so it was measured. One model was trained on MSD BrainTumour (CC BY-SA 4.0) with the four sequences named in the order dataset.json states, then read back through a specification naming the same four patterns with FLAIR and T1 swapped - the same weights, the same scans, one difference:



what channel one holds
dice




FLAIR, as trained
0.467


T1, after one swap in the list
0.110






The same weights reading one scan through two orders of four files


The case drawn is the median of the validation split rather than the best or the worst, and it scores 0.540 and 0.160 the two ways round. Nothing failed. No error and no empty mask: the model returns a region of plausible size and plausible shape in the wrong place, which is what a reader would accept from a tool they trust.
The number is the weaker half of this, in two ways. A Dice of 0.467 is not a good tumour model - 60 epochs on 120 cases, still improving at the cap - and this measurement does not need it to be, because both rows are that same model. And it is a number about one permutation of twenty-four and one training budget: the same comparison at a third of the training reported 0.023 against 0.233, which is 10% of the right arm where these two are 23%. The ratio moves with how good the model is; what does not move is that the wrong answer looks like an answer.
So take the order from the dataset’s own record and check it once, because nothing downstream will. Sorting the filenames gives flair, t1, t1gd, t2 - reproducible, and anatomically meaningless. maju116/pyplatypus#202.
Object detection, ensembling and pretrained encoders are not here at all.
platypus_device()
#> torch      : 2.7.1+cu126 
#> cuda build : 12.6 
#> device     : NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
text:
The 2018 Data Science Bowl asked for the nuclei in microscopy images: several hundred pictures, taken down different microscopes under different stains, each with its nuclei outlined. It is a good first problem because it is genuinely varied and genuinely small.
This walks through it end to end. Every number and every picture below was produced by running the code shown.
crumbs: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
section: Before any of that: a mask in four lines
text:
Before any of that: a mask in four lines
A model trained on this data is published, so the shortest way to see whether the package does anything useful is to borrow it. No training, no waiting:
validation_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "stage1_validation")

published <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(validation_dir, validation_dir, colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("nuclei", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      weights = "dsbowl-unet", fit = FALSE))
)
borrowed <- platypus_fit(published, verbose = FALSE)
masks <- predict(borrowed, split = "validation")
dim(masks)
#> [1] 134 256 256
found <- list.files(validation_dir, pattern = "[.]png$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
images <- read_images(head(grep("/images/", found, value = TRUE), 3), size = c(256, 256))
plot_masks(images, prediction = masks[1:3, , ], colormap = binary_colormap,
           which = 1:3)



plot of chunk published-plot


The weights came down from the Hub on first use and are cached afterwards, so running this again costs nothing.
No score is reported here, on purpose. This directory and the one the weights were trained on come from the same collection and overlap, so anything measured here would flatter the model. The numbers that mean something were measured on a held-out split when the weights were published, and travel with them:
available_weights()[, c("name", "revision")]
#>               name                                 revision
#> 1       bccd-yolo3 24fbff0833455a747c7bac9c2b8dc43073ce4e82
#> 2 dsbowl-instances fd7bdc8686ef7fcaac0f21dd6d326c23b7c87471
#> 3      dsbowl-unet 5e035c6a39827c33e19507affb9415c3908ae383
#> 4       fives-unet c4492f7a23b99202d6bd55a04b2cf1248fb14fe4
#> 5        hc18-unet 9c6d859900b262cfb073b9af371ec0b29bcfe8ea
The description in that table is the part to read before trusting them - these are semantic, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them would be wrong.
One thing worth meeting here rather than later. Weights belong to an exact model, not to a task, and the rest of this vignette trains at 160 x 160 while these were trained at 256:
mismatched <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(validation_dir, validation_dir, colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("nuclei", input_shape = c(160, 160), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      weights = "dsbowl-unet", fit = FALSE))
)
platypus_fit(mismatched)
#> Error in `platypus_fit()`:
#> ! 'dsbowl-unet' was trained for a different model:
#>   - input_shape: weights say (256, 256), the model says (160, 160)
#> Loading anyway would either fail inside torch or, where the shapes happen to agree, produce a model that predicts confidently and means nothing.
Refused, with the field that differs, before anything was loaded. That check exists because the failure it prevents is silent: weights trained on a different colormap with the same number of classes load perfectly and predict nonsense.
Everything below trains a model from scratch instead, which is what you will actually do on your own data - the published weights are a demonstration and a baseline, not an answer to your problem.
crumbs: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
text:
The data
One directory per image, each holding an images and a masks subdirectory. The masks subdirectory holds one file per nucleus, which is common enough that platypus combines them for you.
data_dir <- "data_science_bowl"
train <- file.path(data_dir, "stage1_train")
valid <- file.path(data_dir, "stage1_validation")

length(list.dirs(train, recursive = FALSE))     # images
#> [1] 536
length(list.files(file.path(list.dirs(train, recursive = FALSE)[1], "masks")))  # masks in the first
#> [1] 27
crumbs: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
section: Look at it before training on it
text:
Look at it before training on it
The most useful thing to know before choosing anything else is how much of each picture is actually the thing you are looking for.
foreground <- function(sample) {
  mask <- unite_masks(lapply(
    list.files(file.path(sample, "masks"), full.names = TRUE),
    function(path) read_masks(path, binary_colormap, size = c(160, 160))[1, , ]
  ))
  mask_coverage(mask)$fraction[2]
}

samples <- sort(list.dirs(valid, recursive = FALSE))
set.seed(1)
share <- vapply(samples[sample(length(samples), 40)], foreground, numeric(1))

round(summary(share), 3)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.011   0.037   0.115   0.127   0.205   0.334
Nuclei are a minority of the pixels in every image, and how small a minority varies by a factor of thirty between images. Both facts are worth acting on now rather than discovering later.
Because the foreground is a minority, a model that predicts “background” everywhere and finds nothing at all still scores well on accuracy, and well on a Dice averaged over both classes. So the metrics below are asked for with include_background = FALSE: the number reported is then the one about the nuclei, and a model that finds none of them scores zero, as it should.
Because the share varies so much, the loss has to hold up at both ends. Plain cross-entropy will happily settle into predicting background on the sparse images; blending it with Dice, or using Focal-Tversky with alpha above a half, keeps the rare class worth getting right.
crumbs: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
text:
The specification
Two models, so there is something to compare. They share the data and differ in architecture and objective.
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    train      = train,
    validation = valid,
    test       = file.path(data_dir, "stage1_test"),
    colormap   = binary_colormap
  ),
  models = list(
    u_net(
      "unet",
      input_shape = c(160, 160),
      blocks = 4, filters = 16,
      loss    = loss_cce_dice(),
      metrics = list(metric_dice(include_background = FALSE),
                     metric_iou(include_background = FALSE)),
      augmentation = list(
        augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
        augmentation_step("VerticalFlip", p = 0.5),
        augmentation_step("RandomRotate90", p = 0.5)
      ),
      epochs = 12, batch_size = 16
    ),
    linknet(
      "linknet",
      input_shape = c(160, 160),
      blocks = 4, filters = 16,
      loss    = loss_focal_tversky(alpha = 0.7),
      metrics = list(metric_dice(include_background = FALSE),
                     metric_iou(include_background = FALSE)),
      callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping("val_dice", patience = 5)),
      epochs = 12, batch_size = 16
    )
  )
)

spec
#> platypus specification
#>   data        : /home/maju116/Desktop/PROJECTS/Personal Projects/PLATYPUS FAMILY/pyplatypus/examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_train 
#>   classes     : 2 
#>   models      : 2 
#>     unet           u_net            160x160, cce_dice, 12 epochs
#>     linknet        linknet          160x160, focal_tversky, 12 epochs
The alpha = 0.7 on LinkNet’s Focal-Tversky weights false negatives above false positives: it would rather flag something that is not a nucleus than miss one. Whether that is the right trade depends entirely on what the count is for.

Train
fit <- platypus_fit(spec)
fit
#> platypus fit
#>   models   : unet, linknet 
#>   device   : NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 (torch 2.7.1+cu126) 
#>   epochs   : linknet=12, unet=12

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
text:
Compare
evaluate(fit)
#>     model architecture loss_function parameters load_shape epochs_run
#> 1    unet        u_net      cce_dice    1942594  160 x 160         12
#> 2 linknet      linknet focal_tversky    1746754  160 x 160         12
#>   best_epoch       loss foreground      dice       iou dice_worst iou_worst
#> 1         11 0.10492591  0.1457751 0.8679105 0.7788040  0.3107798 0.1845319
#> 2         11 0.08024277  0.1343505 0.8769452 0.7917425  0.3913118 0.2433291
Read the loss column with care, and note that loss_function sits beside it. These two models were trained on different objectives, so their losses are not on a common scale - a Focal-Tversky of 0.31 is not better or worse than a CCE-Dice of 0.22, it is not the same question. The metrics are comparable, because they measure the mask rather than the objective.

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
text:
Look at what it did
predictions <- predict(fit, "unet", split = "validation")
dim(predictions)
#> [1] 134 160 160
plot_masks(
  images,
  prediction = predictions[shown, , ],
  truth      = truth,
  colormap   = binary_colormap,
  labels     = paste("image", shown)
)



plot of chunk plot-masks


The last column is the one that repays attention. Green is what was found, red what was missed, yellow what was invented - and a single overlap score cannot tell you which of the three you have.
Here almost all of the red is a thin rim around nuclei that were otherwise found. The model is locating nuclei well and drawing them slightly too small. If the question is how many nuclei are there, that hardly matters. If it is how large are they, it is exactly what matters - and the fix is a longer run or a loss that weights boundaries, not a different architecture.
Neither the Dice above nor any other single number distinguishes those two situations from a model that found three quarters of the nuclei and missed the rest. That is the reason to draw the picture.

The same thing from a file
Everything above can live in a YAML file instead, which is easier to keep beside results and to hand to someone else. The two routes produce the same object, and nothing downstream can tell them apart.

title: Finding nuclei in the 2018 Data Science Bowl
section: A note on older graphics cards
text:
A note on older graphics cards
PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta generations - a GTX 10-series card cannot run them, and no driver update changes that. Without saying anything, everything would run on the processor instead, perhaps ten times slower.
If platypus_device() reports cpu on a machine that has a GPU, restart R and ask for the older build before anything else:
library(rplatypus)
platypus_use_torch("pascal")
platypus_device()
#> torch      : 2.7.1+cu126 
#> cuda build : 12.6 
#> device     : NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
Every other vignette here ends on a score. This one ends on a length in millimetres, because that is what a sonographer writes down: a fetal head circumference, measured from an ultrasound image, read against a gestational chart. Nobody charts a Dice.
That difference is the whole of the page, and it turns out to be sharper than it sounds. The two columns - overlap and millimetres - rank the same images differently, and a model chosen on the first is not the model you wanted.
HC18 is 999 two-dimensional ultrasound images of the fetal skull with an ellipse drawn round each one by a sonographer, and a CSV giving every image’s pixel size in millimetres and the circumference that was recorded. It is CC BY 4.0. Point PLATYPUS_HC18 at the unpacked directory.
crumbs: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: Why a circumference is not a score
text:
Why a circumference is not a score
A Dice asks how many pixels two masks share. A circumference asks how long the boundary of one of them is. Those are not the same question and they fail in different directions:
A ragged boundary barely moves an integral over a region. Add and remove pixels along the edge in roughly equal measure and the area, and the ellipse fitted to it, hardly move - while the Dice falls with every one of them.
A mask that is systematically too fat or too thin moves it linearly. Grow the whole outline by a pixel and the circumference grows with it, every time, in one direction - while the Dice barely notices, because a one-pixel rim is a small share of a large blob.
So the two errors Dice is most and least able to see are the wrong way round for anybody measuring a length. That is an argument until it is measured; the last two sections measure it.
crumbs: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
The data
root <- file.path(Sys.getenv("PLATYPUS_HC18"), "training_set", "training_set")
stopifnot(dir.exists(root))

reference <- read.csv(
  file.path(Sys.getenv("PLATYPUS_HC18"), "training_set_pixel_size_and_HC.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
names(reference) <- c("filename", "pixel_mm", "hc_mm")
str(reference, give.attr = FALSE)
#> 'data.frame':    999 obs. of  3 variables:
#>  $ filename: chr  "000_HC.png" "001_HC.png" "002_HC.png" "003_HC.png" ...
#>  $ pixel_mm: num  0.0691 0.0897 0.062 0.0913 0.0612 ...
#>  $ hc_mm   : num  44.3 56.8 68.8 69 59.8 ...
Each image has an _Annotation.png beside it, and that file is a drawn curve rather than a filled region - an ellipse one or two pixels wide, with nothing inside it. A segmentation model needs the region, so the curve has to be filled before anything can be trained.
# The annotation is a CLOSED CURVE with nothing inside it, so the region has to be filled
# before anything can be trained. That is a hole fill rather than a scanline: flood the
# background inward from the frame, and what the flood cannot reach is the inside.
#
# Written as waves over indices rather than by dilating the whole image, because each pixel
# then enters the frontier once - the work is the size of the background instead of the
# background times the image's diameter. About 0.07 s an image here.
fill_holes <- function(drawn) {
  nr <- nrow(drawn)
  nc <- ncol(drawn)
  open <- !drawn
  seen <- matrix(FALSE, nr, nc)
  border <- unique(c(1:nr, nr * (nc - 1) + 1:nr,
                     seq(1, nr * nc, by = nr), seq(nr, nr * nc, by = nr)))
  frontier <- border[open[border]]
  seen[frontier] <- TRUE
  while (length(frontier)) {
    row <- ((frontier - 1L) %% nr) + 1L
    nxt <- c(frontier[row > 1L] - 1L, frontier[row < nr] + 1L,
             frontier[frontier > nr] - nr, frontier[frontier <= nr * (nc - 1L)] + nr)
    nxt <- unique(nxt[open[nxt] & !seen[nxt]])
    seen[nxt] <- TRUE
    frontier <- nxt
  }
  !seen
}

masks <- file.path(tempdir(), "hc18-masks")
dir.create(masks, showWarnings = FALSE)

prepared <- lapply(reference$filename, function(name) {
  annotation <- png::readPNG(file.path(root, sub("\\.png$", "_Annotation.png", name)))
  if (length(dim(annotation)) == 3) annotation <- annotation[, , 1]
  drawn <- annotation > 0.5
  filled <- fill_holes(drawn)
  # A curve that runs off the edge of the frame does not enclose anything: its inside is
  # connected to the outside, the flood reaches all of it, and the fill returns the curve
  # unchanged. So "did this fill" is "is the result at least twice the line I drew", which
  # needs no reference and no threshold anybody chose.
  path <- file.path(masks, name)
  if (sum(filled) >= 2 * sum(drawn)) {
    png::writePNG(matrix(as.numeric(filled), nrow(filled)), path)
  }
  data.frame(filename = name, mask = path, closed = sum(filled) >= 2 * sum(drawn))
})
prepared <- do.call(rbind, prepared)

open_curves <- prepared$filename[!prepared$closed]
open_curves
#> [1] "186_HC.png"  "346_HC.png"  "628_2HC.png" "787_HC.png"
4 of 999 annotations are open and are dropped. The sonographer’s ellipse continues outside the picture, so the recorded millimetres describe a shape the file does not contain - a real limitation of this instrument rather than a defect in the data, and the reason fitting a conic to the visible arc is how the literature handles it. Kept, they would contribute images whose mask is a line, which is the kind of thing a mean never shows you.

text:
The specification
spec <- platypus_spec(
  task = "semantic_segmentation",
  data = segmentation_data(
    train = csv,
    mode = "config_file",
    colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 255, 255)),
    split = list(
      # Three fractions, not two. The millimetres are reported on the third, so no number
      # on this page comes off the data `early_stopping` watched.
      fractions = c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2),
      group_by = "^(\\d+)_",
      seed = 1
    )
  ),
  models = list(
    u_net(
      name = "skull",
      # 800 x 540 arrives as 800 x 544, which divides by 2^4 and resamples the data almost
      # not at all. A measurement that ends in millimetres should argue with the ellipse,
      # not with the interpolation.
      input_shape = c(544, 800),
      blocks = 4,
      filters = 16,
      batch_size = 4,
      epochs = 40,
      loss = loss_cce_dice(),
      metrics = list(metric_dice(include_background = FALSE),
                     metric_iou(include_background = FALSE)),
      optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-3),
      callbacks = list(
        callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_dice", patience = 8, restore_best = TRUE)
      ),
      augmentation = list(
        # No vertical flip: an ultrasound fan has a top and a bottom, and a mirrored one is
        # a picture of nothing. The ellipse is symmetric under the horizontal one.
        augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
        augmentation_step("RandomBrightnessContrast", p = 0.3)
      )
    )
  )
)

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: From a mask to a millimetre
text:
From a mask to a millimetre
A prediction is a mask on a grid. A circumference is a length in the world, and the thing that connects the two is the pixel size, which is a property of the file rather than of the model.
# `space = "source"` rather than the model's grid. The pixel size in the CSV describes the
# image as it is on disk; a prediction resized to the model's input shape has pixels of a
# size nobody recorded, and multiplying by the file's number would be wrong by the ratio of
# the two shapes.
#
# The list comes back NAMED BY CASE, which is what makes the join below a join rather than
# a pairing by position - and the name and the mask come out of one step of the engine's
# own stream, so they cannot be misaligned. That was not true until
# `maju116/rplatypus#223`: writing this page is what found it.
predicted <- predict(fit, "skull", split = "test", space = "source")

sizes <- setNames(reference$pixel_mm, tools::file_path_sans_ext(reference$filename))
recorded <- setNames(reference$hc_mm, tools::file_path_sans_ext(reference$filename))

measured <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(predicted), function(key) {
  px <- sizes[[key]]
  # `ellipse_measure()` fits an ellipse to the largest filled object and returns its axes
  # and Ramanujan's circumference. `spacing` scales the COORDINATES rather than the answer:
  # a perimeter is not separable in its axes, so there is no number to multiply a
  # pixel-space circumference by unless the pixels are square.
  data.frame(key = key, ellipse_measure(predicted[[key]], spacing = c(px, px)))
}))
head(measured, 3)
#>      key    major    minor circumference
#> 1 080_HC 13.61917 11.01925      77.24687
#> 2 153_HC 16.80449 14.34755      97.92852
#> 3 284_HC 31.03666 24.53383     167.86182
cases_scored <- evaluate_cases(fit, "skull", split = "test")
dice <- setNames(cases_scored$dice, cases_scored$case)

against <- data.frame(
  key = measured$key,
  dice = unname(dice[measured$key]),
  mm = measured$circumference,
  recorded = unname(recorded[measured$key])
)
against$error_mm <- against$mm - against$recorded
summary(abs(against$error_mm))
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>  0.01329  0.67454  1.96079  3.50467  3.61206 53.88898

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: What the annotation costs before the model does
text:
What the annotation costs before the model does
Before blaming the model for a millimetre, measure what the pipeline costs with no model at all: put the truth masks through the same ellipse fit and compare those circumferences with the sonographer’s.
truth <- do.call(rbind, lapply(against$key, function(key) {
  mask <- png::readPNG(file.path(masks, paste0(key, ".png"))) > 0.5
  px <- sizes[[key]]
  # The engine reads a mask whose classes are values, so the filled region is class 2.
  fitted <- ellipse_measure(mask + 1L, spacing = c(px, px))$circumference
  # And the line the sonographer drew, in pixels: its area over the perimeter it encloses.
  # This is the quantity the paragraph below CLAIMS is the cause, so it is measured here
  # rather than asserted - a width of w puts the filled boundary w/2 outside the curve, and
  # a radius larger by w/2 makes a circumference larger by pi * w.
  outline <- png::readPNG(file.path(root, paste0(key, "_Annotation.png"))) > 0.5
  # In pixels on both sides of the division, so the answer is a pixel count: the perimeter
  # is measured again without `spacing` rather than divided back out of the millimetre one.
  width_px <- sum(outline) / ellipse_measure(mask + 1L)$circumference
  data.frame(key = key, mm = fitted, width_px = width_px,
             predicted_mm = pi * width_px * px)
}))

errors <- truth$mm - against$recorded
floor_bias <- mean(errors)
floor_mae <- mean(abs(errors))
c(bias_mm = floor_bias, mae_mm = floor_mae,
  line_width_px = mean(truth$width_px),
  predicted_mm = mean(truth$predicted_mm),
  correlation = cor(truth$predicted_mm, errors),
  residual_mae_mm = mean(abs(errors - truth$predicted_mm)))
#>         bias_mm          mae_mm   line_width_px    predicted_mm     correlation 
#>      1.12060105      1.12060105      2.52322765      1.10771555      0.99967824 
#> residual_mae_mm 
#>      0.01371169
The truth masks are out by +1.12 mm on average, and that number is not an error of this package. HC18’s annotation is a drawn curve of finite width - these are 2.52 pixels wide - and the mask is that curve filled, so the region’s boundary sits half a width outside the ellipse the sonographer drew. A radius larger by w/2 makes a circumference larger by pi * w, which predicts +1.11 mm against the +1.12 mm measured, correlated at 1.000 across the split with 0.01 mm left over.
That is the difference between an explanation and a guess, and it is why the prediction is reported beside the bias rather than subtracted from it: a correction folded into the measurement would hide the one number on this page that is about the dataset rather than about us. A model reproducing the truth masks perfectly would still read +1.12 mm high on this split, and that figure is not a constant of the dataset: it is pi * w converted to millimetres, so it scales with the pixel size, which HC18 records per image. The engine’s article measures the same thing on its own split and gets a smaller number for that reason, not a different answer.
So the model’s own contribution is the comparison against the truth masks rather than against the chart, and both belong on a page that reports millimetres. Reporting only the first blames the model for a drawing convention; reporting only the second hides the convention from the person reading the number.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
section: The Dice cannot see this error
text:
The Dice cannot see this error
publishable <- against[against$dice >= 0.95, ]
over <- sum(abs(publishable$error_mm) > 2)

# Both orderings run best-first - by Dice descending and by error ASCENDING - so a shared
# ordering is +1 and no ordering at all is 0. That is the direction
# `examples/measure_fetal_head_circumference.py` reports, and a pair whose two halves
# disagree about the sign of one statistic is worse than a pair that does not carry it.
spearman <- cor(against$dice, -abs(against$error_mm), method = "spearman")

c(
  dice_mean = mean(against$dice),
  median_error_mm = median(abs(against$error_mm)),
  mean_error_mm = mean(abs(against$error_mm)),
  spearman = spearman
)
#>       dice_mean median_error_mm   mean_error_mm        spearman 
#>       0.9424884       1.9607895       3.5046740       0.3454987
Of the 133 test images scoring 0.95 or better - a figure anybody would publish - 55 are still wrong by more than 2 mm (41%). The Spearman correlation between the two orderings is 0.35, where a shared ordering would be 1 and no relationship at all would be 0.
plot(
  against$dice, abs(against$error_mm), log = "y",
  xlab = "Dice", ylab = "absolute circumference error (mm), log scale",
  pch = 19, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#33442b", alpha.f = 0.5)
)
abline(h = 2, lty = 2)



plot of chunk scatter


Read the vertical spread at any fixed Dice. A column of points two orders of magnitude tall is the finding: the score does not tell you what the measurement will be.
worst <- against[order(-abs(against$error_mm)), ][1:5, ]
worst[, c("key", "dice", "mm", "recorded", "error_mm")]
#>         key      dice        mm recorded  error_mm
#> 185  009_HC 0.5361094 116.19898    62.31  53.88898
#> 64  023_2HC 0.5310252 114.16147    67.90  46.26147
#> 148  753_HC 0.7192976 262.64523   293.20 -30.55477
#> 105 133_4HC 0.7075314  72.45699    97.00 -24.54301
#> 76   802_HC 0.9117828 308.75427   330.90 -22.14573
The median absolute error is 1.96 mm and the mean is 3.50 mm. Both belong here because they disagree: the distribution has a long tail, so the mean describes the tail rather than a typical case, and the median alone would hide that some images are out by the width of a head.

title: A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see
text:
What this does not settle
One run. The same recipe, trained again, gives a different correlation. Three runs of it on the engine’s side measured 0.62, 0.44 and 0.15, and this page is a fourth at 0.35:
#>                     run spearman
#> 1    the engine example    0.620
#> 2              a second    0.435
#> 3 the published weights    0.153
#> 4         this vignette    0.345
All four are far from a shared ordering and they span a factor of four. The direction is the finding here; the magnitude is one draw, and a single number quoted from this page would overstate the case at one end.
The published hc18-unet weights are one of those runs rather than this one:
listing <- available_weights()
listing$description[listing$name == "hc18-unet"]
#> [1] "U-Net, 544x800, the fetal skull in 2D ultrasound, for measuring **head circumference in millimetres**. HC18 (CC BY 4.0), split by examination rather than by row. Median absolute error 2.44 mm against the sonographer's measurement over 199 held-out images, mean 3.84 mm, worst 48.07 mm - and 3.41 mm against the truth mask's own circumference, which is this model's contribution rather than the dataset's drawing convention. **Do not choose these weights on the Dice**: it is 0.9494, it orders the cases differently from the millimetres, and 85 of the 144 cases scoring 0.95 or better are still wrong by more than 2 mm. **CC BY 4.0, not MIT**, because the data is."
A measurement is not a measuring instrument. The worst case on this page is out by 54 mm, which is not a biometric tool with a person looking at it, let alone without.
The ellipse is the shape assumed. ellipse_measure() fits one, which is right for a fetal skull and wrong for anything that is not an ellipse. The general case - every object in an image, measured separately - is maju116/pyplatypus#272 and is not built.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
The other vignettes work on images small enough to hand a network whole. This one does not, and that is the point: a retinal fundus photograph is 2048 x 2048, the thing to find in it is about nine pixels wide, and resizing to fit the model destroys the measurement before the model ever sees it.
Three things here appear in no other vignette, and each is the reason this dataset was chosen.
It tiles. splits reads each image at full resolution and cuts it into a grid of inputs.
It is scored on a metric Dice cannot stand in for. clDice asks whether a structure is connected rather than whether its pixels coincide - and a skeleton is a property of a whole mask, so it is measured on the reassembled image rather than on the tiles.
It reports per disease rather than as one mean, which is how the interesting thing about this dataset was found - and the interesting thing turns out not to be about the disease.
crumbs: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
section: Why a vessel cannot be resized
text:
Why a vessel cannot be resized
FIVES images are 2048 x 2048, and the obvious move is to resize them to something a U-Net is comfortable with. It is the wrong move here, and the reason is a measurement rather than a preference.
A FIVES vessel is about nine pixels wide - measured as mask area over skeleton length, over six random masks, on the engine side where the skeleton lives. Resized to 256 the same vessels are about 1.2 pixels. That matters because of what happens at one pixel: shift a one-pixel structure by a single pixel and it overlaps the truth nowhere at all, so Dice, IoU and clDice alike read zero and none of them can tell a near miss from a total failure. Tiling keeps the data out of that regime, which is what splits is for.
(The nine-pixel figure corrects the one-to-five this dataset is usually described with. One to five is what remains after a resize - a property of the preprocessing, not of the retina.)
crumbs: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
The data
One 1.7 GB download from figshare 19688169, CC BY 4.0. The authors’ own split is already balanced across the four groups - 150 train and 50 test of each - so it is used rather than replaced. Point PLATYPUS_FIVES at the unpacked directory.
The dataset is laid out as Original/ and Ground truth/ with matching file names, which is not a layout platypus discovers on its own, so the pairs are written into a CSV:
root <- file.path(
  Sys.getenv("PLATYPUS_FIVES"),
  "FIVES A Fundus Image Dataset for AI-based Vessel Segmentation"
)
stopifnot(dir.exists(root))

write_split <- function(split, path) {
  # `pattern` rather than everything in the directory: the archive ships a `Thumbs.db`
  # beside the 600 training images, and a Windows thumbnail cache is not a fundus
  # photograph. Filtering by extension is also what keeps the pairing below honest.
  images <- sort(list.files(
    file.path(root, split, "Original"), pattern = "\\.png$", full.names = TRUE
  ))
  frame <- data.frame(
    # The key is what `evaluate_cases()` reports and what `group_by` reads. Without it a
    # case is called `row 55`, which names nothing on disk and cannot be grouped.
    key = tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(images)),
    images = images,
    masks = file.path(root, split, "Ground truth", basename(images))
  )
  stopifnot(all(file.exists(frame$masks)))
  write.csv(frame, path, row.names = FALSE)
  nrow(frame)
}

splits <- file.path(tempdir(), c(train = "train.csv", test = "test.csv"))
names(splits) <- c("train", "test")
c(train = write_split("train", splits[["train"]]), test = write_split("test", splits[["test"]]))
#> train  test 
#>   600   200
The disease is in the file name - _N, _A, _D, _G for normal, AMD, diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma - which is what the grouping below reads.
Two things that cost time if taken on trust rather than checked: the archive ships a Thumbs.db beside the training images, so the listing is filtered by extension; and the masks are paired by name, which stopifnot above asserts rather than assumes.
crumbs: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
The configuration
spec <- platypus_spec(
  task = "semantic_segmentation",
  data = segmentation_data(
    train = splits[["train"]],
    validation = splits[["test"]],
    colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 255, 255)),
    mode = "config_file"
  ),
  models = list(
    u_net(
      name = "vessels",
      input_shape = c(512, 512),
      # 2048 read whole and cut 4 x 4. This is the field the vignette exists for.
      splits = c(4, 4),
      blocks = 4,
      filters = 16,
      batch_size = 4,
      epochs = 15,
      loss = loss_cce_dice(),
      metrics = list(
        metric_dice(include_background = FALSE),
        metric_iou(include_background = FALSE),
        # Measured on the reassembled image by `evaluate_cases()`, not per tile.
        metric_cldice(include_background = FALSE)
      ),
      optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-3),
      augmentation = list(
        augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
        augmentation_step("VerticalFlip", p = 0.5)
      )
    )
  ),
  seed = 1
)
spec
#> platypus specification
#>   data        : /tmp/RtmprzTrKo/train.csv 
#>   classes     : 2 
#>   models      : 1 
#>     vessels        u_net            512x512, tiled 4x4, cce_dice, 15 epochs
Two things about that worth saying out loud.
metric_cldice() sits beside metric_dice() even though the run is tiled, and the engine reassembles each case before measuring it. It will not appear in the epoch log, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: an epoch averages its metrics over batches, which is exact for Dice - a ratio of sums - and meaningless for a skeleton, because a tile severs every vessel crossing its edge. So there is no val_cldice to watch, and a callback that tried would be refused when the specification is read.
Fifteen epochs rather than the forty this model wants, because a vignette that takes seven hours to rebuild is a vignette nobody rebuilds. The shape of the result is the same; the numbers are a little worse than the model can do.

#> 1 vessels        u_net      cce_dice    1942594 2048 x 2048         15
#>   best_epoch       loss foreground      dice       iou  dice_worst   iou_worst
#> 1         14 0.08282537  0.0657948 0.8644989 0.7781636 0.005716131 0.002882404
That is the whole test set as one row, and it is the least informative view of it. The distribution is the finding, and summary() gives it - including which case is the worst, because the first thing anyone does with a low score is go and look at that image:
per_case <- evaluate_cases(fit)
summary(per_case)
#>   metric   n      mean        sd    median         min       max worst_case
#> 1   dice 200 0.8644989 0.1303245 0.8975915 0.005716131 0.9581814      122_G
#> 2    iou 200 0.7781636 0.1506915 0.8142098 0.002882404 0.9197202      122_G
#> 3 cldice 200 0.8121976 0.1533799 0.8567695 0.007349078 0.9516759      122_G
Now by the disease in the file name. group_by pools a group’s cases into one score, the way a patient’s slices would be pooled:
evaluate_cases(fit, group_by = "_([NADG])$")
#> platypus scores by group (4 rows)
#>  group      dice       iou    cldice
#>      A 0.9136922 0.8410988 0.8645473
#>      D 0.8849608 0.7936589 0.8120603
#>      G 0.8849156 0.7935862 0.7343315
#>      N 0.8900695 0.8019147 0.8378514
Pooling answers “how good is it on this group”. It does not show the spread, and the spread is where this dataset is interesting, so that comes off the per-case rows:
diseases <- c(N = "normal", A = "AMD", D = "diabetic retinopathy", G = "glaucoma")
per_case$disease <- diseases[sub(".*_([NADG])$", "\\1", per_case$case)]

spread <- function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), worst = min(x))
round(t(vapply(split(per_case$dice, per_case$disease), spread, numeric(4))), 4)
#>                       n   mean     sd  worst
#> AMD                  50 0.9050 0.0600 0.7045
#> diabetic retinopathy 50 0.8666 0.0899 0.5545
#> glaucoma             50 0.8013 0.2187 0.0057
#> normal               50 0.8852 0.0573 0.6605
Compare that table with the pooled one above and the reason for having both becomes concrete. Pooled, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy are within a few thousandths of each other. Per case, glaucoma’s mean is several points lower and its spread more than twice as wide, with a worst case near zero. (No figure is quoted here on purpose: the table is directly above, and a number repeated in prose is a number that goes stale the next time this is rebuilt.) Pooling hid it because Dice is a ratio of sums: fifty images’ counts added together are dominated by the ones with the most vessel to find, and a photograph the model failed on contributes little to the numerator and little to the denominator.
Before concluding that the model is worse at the disease whose row is worst, check whether it is the group whose photographs are worse. FIVES ships a Quality Assessment.xlsx grading every image for illumination, blur and contrast; nothing in this pipeline reads it, and when it is joined to these scores the ordering above changes substantially. The engine’s measurement of that is in measurements/fives/quality.py in the project’s workbench.
That is the general lesson rather than a fact about retinas: a per-group table is worth having precisely because it invites the question why is this group different, and the first answer is rarely the right one.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
clDice beside Dice
round(c(
  correlation = cor(per_case$dice, per_case$cldice),
  mean_difference = mean(per_case$cldice - per_case$dice),
  sd_of_difference = sd(per_case$cldice - per_case$dice)
), 4)
#>      correlation  mean_difference sd_of_difference 
#>           0.9350          -0.0523           0.0560
Read those two numbers together, because they say different things. The correlation is high: the two metrics rank the cases much the same way, so clDice is not finding a different set of bad images. The mean difference is negative and not small: clDice sits about five points below Dice, which says the vessels this model draws are less connected than their pixel overlap suggests. It is getting the right pixels and breaking the lines.
That gap is a property of the model rather than of the metric, and the engine’s own run of the same configuration is the evidence: at forty epochs instead of fifteen the two agree to a correlation of 0.978 and a mean difference of +0.004. The better-trained model closes the gap. So a large negative gap here is not clDice being pessimistic - it is clDice measuring the thing that fifteen epochs had not finished learning, and Dice not noticing.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
The worst case, drawn
A table says a case scored near zero. A picture says why — and this is the panel that found the quality finding above, because the worst glaucoma photograph turns out to be nearly black.
Drawing it needs two images out of two hundred, and the whole split at 2048 x 2048 is about 6.7 GB, so predict() is asked for the two by name. It keeps one answer at a time and returns the pair in the order asked for:
chosen <- per_case$case[c(which.max(per_case$dice), which.min(per_case$dice))]
masks <- predict(fit, split = "validation", cases = chosen)

at_source <- function(what) file.path(root, "test", what, paste0(chosen, ".png"))

plot_masks(
  images = read_images(at_source("Original"), size = NULL, channels = 3),
  # One `height x width` matrix per case, stacked the way plot_masks wants them:
  # image x height x width.
  prediction = aperm(simplify2array(masks), c(3, 1, 2)),
  truth = read_masks(at_source("Ground truth"), colormap = binary_colormap, size = NULL),
  labels = sprintf("%s  dice %.3f", chosen, per_case$dice[match(chosen, per_case$case)])
)



plot of chunk worst
