section: Two of those choices, measured afterwards
text:
Two of those choices, measured afterwards
loss_cce_dice() and splits = c(4, 4) are the two decisions in the specification above that read as taste. Both have since been measured on this dataset - after this vignette was written, with the engine, and with every arm kept rather than described - and one of the answers contradicts the section this document opens with.
The tables below are transcriptions. The runs live in the project’s workbench under measurements/fives/, and each table is printed by a script that reads the stored records back: losses-read.py, boundary-read.py and tiling-read.py. Nothing in this document runs them, and no number below was produced by the knit you are reading.
The setting is not this vignette’s, which is the first thing to know before comparing anything to the numbers above. Every arm trained on 148 of the 600 training retinas - every second one within each disease group, so the four stay balanced - for up to 40 epochs with early stopping on val_dice at patience 8, and every arm was scored case by case on the same 200 test images. So no absolute Dice below is comparable to the one this document printed; what the tables are for is the differences, each paired case against case.
A difference is read against a measured floor rather than against zero. The baseline ran twice with different seeds, and the floor is the larger of that pair’s mean difference and that mean’s own standard error: 0.0009 over all 200 cases and 0.0022 over the 67 that FIVES’s own quality assessment flags - the grading the section above says nothing in this pipeline reads. The x columns are multiples of that floor, and a row at 2x says nothing.

The loss is a decision, and this configuration already had the right one
All eleven of the engine’s semantic losses, at that setting:

The menu spans 0.0760 of Dice, 87 times the floor and 25 times the 0.0030 that separated the four architectures measured on nuclei. So the loss is a decision where the architecture was a menu - which is worth knowing before spending an afternoon choosing between u_net() and linknet().
And nothing in the menu beats the default. focal at +0.0001 and cce at +0.0000 tie cce_dice, both below every floor measured anywhere here, and nine rows are worse. The family designed for thin structures under class imbalance - Tversky, Focal-Tversky, Lovasz - holds four of the five worst rows. loss_cce_dice() has been this example’s objective since it was written and nobody had measured whether that was right.
Two cautions the table carries about itself:
Nine of eleven rows have one seed. The four at the top move by less than the seed floors measured on any non-baseline loss here - 0.0120 for boundary at surface 0.3, 0.0465 for lovasz - so one seed cannot distinguish them from the baseline. Everything from boundary at surface 0.1 downwards is 10x to 87x the floor, and a second seed will not move it. lovasz is the warning worth reading twice: one of its seeds scores 0.8706, the highest single number in this table, and the other scores 0.8418.
The stopping rule is a confound, and it was priced rather than argued. Four arms stopped early enough that part of their deficit is convergence - focal_tversky at 20 epochs, lovasz’s second seed at 21, dice at 25, iou at 26 - while all three boundary arms ran into the 40-epoch cap. Re-read at 20 epochs, the budget every arm was granted, the ordering does not change.
The clDice - dice column also goes somewhere, and it was nobody’s question: it grows as the loss gets worse, from +0.0052 at the baseline through +0.0098 for iou and +0.0154 for dice to +0.0188 for focal_tversky. A worse objective loses more Dice than clDice, so what degrades first is the vessel’s bulk and its connectedness survives longer. There is exactly one exception, and it is the next table’s subject.


A surface loss is the one that breaks the lines, and it gets worse with the dose
loss_boundary() is the obvious thing to reach for on a nine-pixel structure: the boundary is the object, so an objective weighing the surface should be the one that helps. It does the opposite here, and it does so by a dose. alpha weights the region term, so the surface term’s share is 1 - alpha:

Three times the surface term costs 1.77 times the Dice and 4.18 times the gap, and the gap changes sign: at surface 0.3 clDice falls below Dice, which no baseline run does. So the argument for this loss was backwards - connectedness is what it costs first, and on the flagged photographs it costs 15 to 27 times the noise.
Two things keep that honest. The dose has its own noise and it is ten times the baseline’s, which is the last column: the two arms at surface 0.3 sit 0.0120 apart on the flagged cases where the baseline’s two sit 0.0012 apart. (That column is each pair’s own mean difference; the x column’s denominator is still the baseline’s 0.0022 from above, so the two are not the same quantity and the table would mislead if they were read as one.) That is this loss’s documented behaviour - it grows noisier the more of the objective the surface term owns - reproduced on real data, and it is also the denominator the dose claim has to clear. Judged against it the two doses are 2.1x apart, not the twentyfold the baseline’s floor would suggest. And both arms at the higher dose stopped on the epoch cap with their best at the last epoch, so part of their deficit is being undertrained rather than being worse.


Tiling against resizing, where this document’s first section is too strong
Same data, same model, same loss. One arm tiles 2048 into 4 x 4 as the configuration above does; two resize the whole retina to 512 and keep splits unset. All three are scored on the source grid, 2048 x 2048, which for the resized arms means a second scoring pass.

There are two resized arms because sixteen tiles make “the same number of epochs” the wrong comparison: 148 retinas at batch_size = 4 are 37 gradient steps an epoch resized and 592 tiled. The first resized arm is the comparison somebody would actually run - the same 40-epoch cap and the same patience. The second was granted the tiled arm’s 23,680 steps and did not spend them, stopping on patience at 41% of the budget, so that row is converged against converged. The truncation the first arm suffered is worth +0.0038, which is worth knowing before budgeting for the matched arm: a measurement that cannot afford it loses 0.004 and the ability to say so.
The overall column says the two methods are equivalent, and it is hiding the largest effect in the measurement. Resizing is better by 0.027 to 0.029 on the 67 flagged photographs and worse by 0.010 to 0.014 on the 133 clean ones, both many times their own floors - 0.0019 to 0.0025 flagged, 0.0007 to 0.0013 clean. The two are good at different pictures, and a swing of about 0.03 in each direction averages out to 0.0033.
So what survives from “Why a vessel cannot be resized” is the narrow claim: on a clean photograph resizing costs Dice, and splits is what lets an image too large to resize be trained at all. What does not survive is the stronger reading - that resizing a 2048 retina destroys the thin vessels - because on the hard pictures the vessels it was supposed to have destroyed are found more reliably from a whole blurred eye than from a sixteenth of one. A mechanism suggests itself and is recorded as a hypothesis rather than a finding: a 512 tile sees one sixteenth of a retina and has no global context to tell a vessel from an artefact, where a resized image always shows the whole eye. Separating that would need overlapping tiles or a resized arm at 1024, and neither was run.
What tiling costs is also not what the table makes it look like. Per gradient step the three arms are identical to within the noise of six readings, 0.502 to 0.554 s, so tiling is sixteen times the work rather than sixteen times the overhead, and the whole factor shows up in the epoch rather than anywhere surprising.


The rig, which is worth more than the ranking
This is the part to carry away from all three tables, and it is about measuring rather than about retinas.
evaluate_cases() builds its dataset from the model’s own specification, so it scores each model at that model’s own load_shape. Put a tiled model beside a resized one and the first is scored on 2048 while the second is scored on 512, against a truth reduced the same way. Nobody passes a flag for this and nothing warns:

as the default comparison reports it

The reported figure is 5.7 times the honest one and the rig alone is 4.7 times the effect. A table built that way would have concluded that resizing beats native-resolution tiling by a wide margin, and every number in it would have been a real Dice of a real prediction against a real mask - just not the mask the other arm was judged against.
And the bias has the opposite sign on clDice: +0.0096 to +0.0156 on Dice against -0.0156 to -0.0230 on clDice. Upsampling a 512 prediction to 2048 smooths it, and a smoothed vessel agrees better with a skeleton and worse with a boundary. So the rigged comparison flatters resizing on Dice and penalises it on clDice, and a comparison reporting only one of the two is wrong in a direction set by which one it picked.
There is an option for this since 0.8.0a32, and there was none when this was measured. The arms above were rescored onto one grid by a function written for that measurement, which lived in the workbench and not in the package - so the honest comparison was available only to somebody who had already noticed the problem, which is what maju116/rplatypus#187 was filed about. evaluate(at="source") is that function now: every prediction goes back onto the grid of the file it came from and is scored against the truth as stored, and the load_shape column reads source so a table says which grid produced it.
The grid is the files’ own rather than one you name, and that is the point rather than a limitation: a named grid resamples the truth, so the thing both models are judged against would itself be an interpolation somebody chose. Here only predictions move.
The rule the numbers above teach is unchanged and is now enforceable rather than advisory: compare two models only where their predictions and the truth are on the same grid, and say which grid that is.


What none of this says
One dataset, one architecture, one loss, at one reduction of one resolution, with 148 retinas rather than 600. The subsets already disagree by about 0.03 in either direction inside this dataset, which is the strongest available warning against reading any overall column as a rule. And the published fives-unet weights’ own score - measured on the full training set at a pinned commit - is not comparable to any row above.

title: Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace
text:
Notes
The card. This was precomputed on a GTX 1070, which is a Pascal-generation GPU and needs the last PyTorch built against CUDA 12. platypus_use_torch("pascal") asks for it, and it has to be called before anything starts the engine. Without it this machine trains on the processor and says so. platypus_device() reports what yours can see.
The cost. Fifteen epochs over 600 retinas at 2048, cut sixteen ways, takes a few hours on that card; scoring the 200 test images - including reassembling each one for clDice - takes about two minutes. Tiling is what makes the first number bearable: a tiled run reuses each decoded image for all of its tiles, which is worth roughly a factor of two.
Asking for a few cases is cheap in memory, not in time. cases = never holds more than one answer, which is what makes the figure above possible at all - but the engine’s stream is sequential, so two cases out of two hundred still run the model over two hundred. Pass a function to each = instead when you want to walk the split and keep a number rather than a mask from each image.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
One YAML file describes a whole run, and platypus_spec() reads it. This is the walk through that file; the exhaustive list of fields lives on the engine’s site, because the file is the engine’s format and keeping a second copy here would mean two of them going out of step: every configuration field.
The same file works in both packages. R reads it with platypus_spec(), Python with from_yaml(), and both hand it to the same validator. Nothing below is R-specific except the lines that run it.
Arguments and YAML produce the same object and nothing downstream can tell which was used, so a configuration file and an R script describe the same experiment - and either can be handed to a colleague.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
One file, one run
The shortest thing that trains:
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: first_try
    input_shape: [256, 256]

spec <- platypus_spec("run.yaml")
fit <- platypus_fit(spec)
evaluate(fit)

Four things are required and the rest have defaults: task, data.train_path, and a name and input_shape for each model. Everything else - the architecture, the loss, the optimiser, how many epochs - has a default that lives in the engine, so a short configuration is a complete one rather than an incomplete one. ?u_net has a Where the defaults live section saying why they are not written into the R signatures.
colormap says which colour in a mask means which class, darkest first. Masks stored as label maps rather than pictures use labels: [0, 1] instead, and giving both is an error: exactly one says how a mask is encoded.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Several models at once
models: is a list, and that is the reason this file format exists rather than only the code path. Each entry trains on the same data and lands in the same table, so comparing variants is one run rather than a loop somebody has to write.
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: shallow
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    blocks: 3
    filters: 16
  - name: deep
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    blocks: 5
    filters: 32
    architecture: u_net_plus_plus

fit <- platypus_fit(platypus_spec("run.yaml"))
evaluate(fit)            # one row per model
training_history(fit)    # one row per model per epoch

name has to be unique, because it is how a model is identified in every score table, in every record and in predict(fit, model = ...). Two models called the same thing is refused rather than resolved, by name: model names must be unique; repeated: shallow.
Two entries differing only in blocks is a legitimate configuration and a common one: this is for comparing variants, not only architectures.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Dividing one folder
With no validation_path, say how to divide train_path:
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/all
  split:
    fractions: [0.7, 0.15, 0.15]
    group_by: "^(patient\\d+)_"
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: by_patient
    input_shape: [256, 256]
Two fractions give train and validation, three add a test set. Nothing is written to disk - the samples are divided after they are discovered, so there are no new folders and no CSV. split_dataset() is still the tool when the CSVs themselves are the point.
group_by is required and may be NULL. It is a regular expression whose first group is the thing that must not appear on both sides - a patient, a scan, a slide. The mistake it prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient in both sets make validation measure memory rather than generalisation, and every number in the output still looks reasonable. An omitted key would be that choice made silently; null is the same choice made on purpose, for data where every sample is independent.
Exactly one of split and validation_path. If a run genuinely has no validation set - a final fit on everything - say validation: false, which is the third answer rather than an absence, because “I have no validation set” and “I forgot” look identical otherwise.
The same from R, where the argument answers the same question three ways:

segmentation_data("data/all", split = list(fractions = c(0.8, 0.2), group_by = NULL))
segmentation_data("data/train", validation = "data/validation")
segmentation_data("data/all", validation = FALSE)

title: Writing a configuration
section: Augmentation, callbacks, and the rest of a model
text:
Augmentation, callbacks, and the rest of a model
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: augmented
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    epochs: 40
    loss: {name: dice}
    metrics: [{name: iou}, {name: dice}]
    optimizer: {name: adam, learning_rate: 0.001}
    callbacks:
      - {name: early_stopping, monitor: val_loss, patience: 10}
      - {name: model_checkpoint, monitor: val_iou, path: runs/best.safetensors}
    augmentation:
      - {name: HorizontalFlip, params: {p: 0.5}}
      - {name: RandomBrightnessContrast, params: {p: 0.3}}
Every one of those blocks has an R constructor that builds the same thing, and the help pages for them are where the measurements are: ?losses, ?metrics, ?optimizers, ?callbacks.

u_net(
  "augmented",
  input_shape = c(256, 256),
  epochs = 40,
  loss = loss_dice(),
  metrics = list(metric_iou(), metric_dice()),
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.001),
  callbacks = list(
    callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_loss", patience = 10),
    callback_model_checkpoint(monitor = "val_iou", path = "runs/best.safetensors")
  ),
  augmentation = list(
    augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
    augmentation_step("RandomBrightnessContrast", p = 0.3)
  )
)

There is no mode on a callback that watches a number. The direction is taken from the name: anything ending in loss is better lower, anything else better higher. So monitor = "val_iou" maximises and monitor = "val_loss" minimises, and there is nothing to set inconsistently.
Augmentation applies to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. The names are albumentations’ own, and available_transforms() lists what the installed version offers; at rank = 3 the list is shorter, because support for volumes is uneven. Each step is probed at the model’s own input size while the pipeline is built, so a transform that cannot do the job says so before the first epoch rather than during it.

title: Writing a configuration
section: Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel
text:
Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel
colormap and labels both say the same thing about a voxel: it is in exactly one class. regions is the third way of naming classes and the only one that drops that assumption - classes named as unions of a label map’s values, which is how BraTS and the lesion-inside-an-organ family actually store their ground truth.
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  regions:
    - {name: whole tumour, of: [1, 2, 4]}
    - {name: tumour core, of: [1, 4]}
    - {name: enhancing, of: [4]}
models:
  - name: brats
    input_shape: [240, 240]
    loss: {name: focal}
The same from R. A region is a list(name = , of = ), and of takes the label-map values that belong to it:

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    "data/train", "data/validation",
    regions = list(
      list(name = "whole tumour", of = c(1, 2, 4)),
      list(name = "tumour core", of = c(1, 4)),
      list(name = "enhancing", of = 4)
    )
  ),
  models = list(u_net("brats", input_shape = c(240, 240), loss = loss_focal()))
)

The last region shows that a single value is ordinary rather than an edge case: BraTS’s enhancing tumour is one label.
The task is still semantic_segmentation. What changes is what a channel means.
There is no background entry, so the class count is not the one you would write as labels. Those same masks as labels = c(0, 1, 2, 4) are four classes; as the three regions above they are three channels. And a voxel whose value is 4 is in all three of them at once, which is the point rather than a tolerated side effect.
Each channel is an independent binary question - a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them - so the channels do not compete and do not sum to one. That is what makes the overlap expressible, and it is also why a prediction cannot be written back as a single picture with save_masks(): one voxel gets one colour, and a voxel here may belong to three classes.
So save_masks() refuses such a prediction rather than taking the strongest channel, and predict() refuses type = "class" for the same reason - there is no one class per voxel to return. Ask for type = "probability" and write it with save_class_masks(), which gives one binary file per region, named after the region. The channel order is the order the regions were written in, which is also the order inspect_masks() names them in and the order every per-class score is reported in.
Two regions are the minimum, because one region is ordinary binary segmentation and labels = c(0, 1) already says that - with a background channel, which regions has none of. Disjoint regions are allowed and are not a mistake: they group several values into one class and drop the background channel, which is a useful thing to ask for and is refused nowhere.
The failure this invites is quiet, so it is refused loudly. A region whose of matches nothing in the data - of = 3 against a label map holding 1, 2 and 4 - is a channel of zeros. It trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 for that region while every other number in the run looks ordinary, which is the kind of result that gets read as “that class is hard”. platypus_fit() refuses it before training, and inspect_masks() asks the same question over as much of the data as you want - naming the region rather than giving its position, because missing_classes: 1 would leave you counting entries in the file above:

inspect_masks(spec)
#>   split unmatched samples_checked total_samples present_classes      missing_classes
#> 1 train    0.0000             500          1251 whole tumour, ...    enhancing


When the overlap was drawn separately: classes_from
regions needs the overlap to be a union of one label map’s values, which is how BraTS stores it: one integer per voxel, and the scored classes are conventions over those integers. Some overlaps are not like that. A vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators’ masks of the same structure, were drawn independently, and no single integer can hold both. Those arrive as one binary file per class, and classes_from names them - one pattern per class, in class order, matched against a sample’s mask files.

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    "data/train", "data/validation",
    classes_from = c("_vessel\\.png$", "_organ\\.png$")
  ),
  models = list(u_net("crossing", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)

Everything above still holds: independent binary questions, no background entry, a prediction save_masks() refuses and save_class_masks() writes. The difference between the two namings is the file on disk and nothing else.
Every pattern must match exactly one of a sample’s mask files, and every mask file must match a pattern. Both halves are refused, because each is invisible from the other side: a pattern matching nothing is a class the model is never shown, and a file matching no pattern is a class the data has and nobody asked for. Patterns are Python regular expressions, like channels_from and group_by, so R’s own backslashes double.
The order is written rather than inferred, and here it matters more than for channels: a model trained with the vessel in the first channel and used where the first channel is the organ answers plausibly, in range, and nothing further down can notice.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Instances instead of one mask
task: instance_segmentation keeps the objects apart rather than uniting them. The data block gets shorter rather than longer: no colormap and no labels, because there are always exactly two classes - background and object - and what names the objects is the directory of per-object mask files itself.
task: instance_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  mode: nested_dirs
models:
  - name: rim
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    separation: {name: rim, width: 2}
    loss: {name: cce_dice}
    decode: [{name: nearest_seed}, {name: connected_components}]
  - name: flows
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    separation:
      name: flows
      loss: {name: mse, where: foreground}
The same two models from R. instance_data() is what says which task this is - an instance data block declares nothing a segmentation one lacks, so the constructor is the word:

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = instance_data("data/train", "data/validation"),
  models = list(
    u_net(
      "rim",
      input_shape = c(256, 256),
      separation = separation_rim(width = 2),
      loss = loss_cce_dice(),
      decode = list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components())
    ),
    u_net(
      "flows",
      input_shape = c(256, 256),
      separation = separation_flows(loss = loss_mse(where = "foreground"))
    )
  )
)
fit <- platypus_fit(spec)
evaluate(fit)

Two axes, and they are deliberately different shapes. separation is one block per model and has no default: it is what the network is trained to predict, so it sets the width of the head - three channels for rim, four for flows at two classes - and that width is derived rather than written anywhere. decode is a list, because several decodings share one forward pass: a second decoding of 134 images costs 1.41 s against an hour and a half for a second training run. evaluate() then returns a row per model and decoding.
Which mask column to read is a decision the table makes for you and it used to make it wrongly. Every row carries foreground_dice - the binary overlap of anything the model called an object against anything that is one, the same arithmetic whatever the separation is - and that is the one to read across models. The dice beside it is the training metric, a mean over the class channels the head has, so three for separation_rim() against two for separation_flows(): read down one model’s rows, never across two. On the Data Science Bowl’s validation cases the class column showed two masks 0.09 apart that are 0.0062 apart, and in the other direction.
No value appears in both lists, which is what settles which field a new idea belongs in: separation is a noun and decode is a verb. separation_rim() can be decoded by decode_nearest_seed() or decode_watershed(), separation_flows() by decode_follow_flows(), and decode_connected_components() reads no signal at all and works with every target. Leave decode out and it derives to the signal’s own decoding plus connected_components; give a list and you get the list you gave.
A model’s own loss and metrics score the mask at either separation, so they are an overlap or a cross-entropy loss here as everywhere else. separation_flows() carries its own loss for the two vector channels, which is where loss_mse(), loss_l1() and loss_smooth_l1() belong: where = "foreground" averages the error over the voxels the target is defined on, and on these images that is 13.97% of them.
What this task is worth is measured, and it is not flattering. On the Data Science Bowl the separation signal is worth +0.068 of instance average precision at best while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398, so the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6 - and a perfect semantic mask decoded by connected_components still scores only 0.7655. That is what the yardstick row is for: a run that improved the mask and did nothing for the separation improves every row at once, and without the row that ignores the signal there is nothing to notice it against.
One thing is missing from R rather than from the engine, and it is missing on purpose rather than by oversight: predict() on an instance fit refuses. The run and its scores work - evaluate() gives the row per model and decoding above - but there is no call yet that brings the objects themselves back into R as a label map, so predict() says so instead of returning a mask that is not what you asked for. platypus#103.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Detection instead of segmentation
task: object_detection changes which fields the file accepts. Boxes rather than masks, so classes and an annotation format rather than a colormap:
task: object_detection
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  annotation_format: pascal_voc
  classes: [rbc, wbc, platelets]
models:
  - name: cells
    input_shape: [416, 416]
Leave anchors out and they are fitted to your own boxes by k-means on an IoU distance, anchors_per_grid of them per grid. That is worth about 0.23 of mean overlap against COCO’s nine on blood cells - measured, 0.65 against 0.88 - so the default is the useful one and naming anchors by hand is for reproducing a published model. detection_anchors() reports them and plot_anchors() draws them against the boxes they were fitted to.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
Not training at all
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/images
  validation_path: data/images
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: published
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    weights: dsbowl-unet
    fit: false
weights takes a registry name, a local path, or hf://owner/repo/file@commit - and the hf:// form requires the commit, because weights that change under a stable name are the worst kind of irreproducibility. A registry name carries one already; available_weights() lists them.
With fit: false nothing trains and predict(fit) works immediately. The weights are checked against the model they are being loaded into before torch is touched: a shape, a channel count or a class count that does not match is a refusal naming the field, not a tensor-size error from inside a loss.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
What is checked, and when
Validation happens in this order, and the first two cost no epochs:

The file, against the schema. Unknown fields, missing required ones, a name: that no block has, a callback watching a number nothing will produce. Before any path is read - and before Python starts, for the checks R can make itself.
The data on disk, when the run begins: that the folders exist, that images and masks correspond, and that every class in colormap or labels actually appears in the masks, because a declared class appearing in none has a target channel of zeros, so the model is never shown what it is being asked to find. inspect_masks() runs that check on its own, and platypus_fit(check_masks = FALSE) skips it.
Everything else, during the run.

A refusal names the field and says what to do. The engine’s own messages are translated into R conditions rather than passed through as Python tracebacks, so tryCatch(platypus_spec("run.yaml"), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)) gives a sentence rather than a stack.

title: Writing a configuration
text:
The same run from code
The file is not a second implementation. These describe the same experiment:

spec <- platypus_spec("run.yaml")

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    "data/train",
    validation = "data/validation",
    colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 255, 255))
  ),
  models = list(u_net("first_try", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)

And as.list(spec) is the file, so a run built from arguments can be written out and kept:

yaml::write_yaml(as.list(spec), "run.yaml")

Which to use is a question about how many models and how often, not about what is possible. A file is better when there are several models, when the run is going to be repeated, or when somebody else has to see what was done; the arguments are better inside a loop over something the file cannot express, like a vector of datasets.
Note that as.list() is also how the fields are reached: the object returned by platypus_spec() carries the specification on the Python side, so spec$task is NULL while as.list(spec)$task is what you want.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
text:
Segmentation asks which pixels are tissue. Detection asks how many objects there are and where, which is a different question and needs a different answer: boxes, not masks.
BCCD is 364 photographs of blood smears with 4,888 boxes in three classes - red cells, white cells, platelets - and its own train/validation/test split. It is small, it is MIT-licensed, and its classes are wildly unbalanced, which turns out to be the most instructive thing about it.
Every number and every picture below was produced by running the code shown.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
section: Before any of that: boxes in a few lines
text:
Before any of that: boxes in a few lines
A detector trained on this data is published, so the shortest way to see whether this works is to borrow it. No training, no GPU, no waiting.
A detection dataset arrives in Pascal VOC’s layout - one flat directory of images beside one flat directory of XML - which is neither of the two layouts the package reads. Turning it into one is the only data wrangling here, and it is a dozen lines:
voc_split <- function(root, listed) {
  names <- readLines(file.path(root, "ImageSets", "Main", paste0(listed, ".txt")))
  names <- names[nzchar(names)]
  frame <- data.frame(
    key = names,
    images = file.path(root, "JPEGImages", paste0(names, ".jpg")),
    # `annotations`, not `masks`: a detection specification looks for that column, because
    # what labels an image here is an annotation file and not a picture.
    annotations = file.path(root, "Annotations", paste0(names, ".xml"))
  )
  path <- file.path(tempdir(), paste0("bccd-", listed, ".csv"))
  write.csv(frame, path, row.names = FALSE)
  path
}

splits <- vapply(c("train", "val", "test"), function(s) voc_split(data_dir, s),
                 character(1))
vapply(splits, function(p) nrow(read.csv(p)), integer(1))
#> train   val  test 
#>   205    87    72
BCCD’s own split, not one invented here - which is the only reason the numbers below can be compared with anybody else’s on this dataset.
cells <- c("RBC", "WBC", "Platelets")

published <- platypus_spec(
  data = detection_data(splits[["train"]], splits[["val"]], test = splits[["test"]],
                        classes = cells, mode = "config_file"),
  models = list(yolo3("cells", input_shape = c(416, 416),
                      weights = "bccd-yolo3", fit = FALSE))
)
borrowed <- platypus_fit(published, verbose = FALSE)
found <- predict(borrowed, split = "test")
length(found)
#> [1] 72
head(found[[1]], 4)
#>        xmin     ymin     xmax     ymax     score label name
#> 1  19.93539 300.9871 139.2865 392.0793 0.9999792     1  RBC
#> 2  27.77121 126.9517 140.5794 234.9014 0.9999719     1  RBC
#> 3 492.09385 303.5892 603.1343 396.8544 0.9999502     1  RBC
#> 4 213.10871  99.1100 404.4725 275.4815 0.9996140     2  WBC
One data frame per image, named by the sample key, in the photograph’s own pixels - so the boxes land on the picture without anything being undone first:
names(found)[1:2]
#> [1] "BloodImage_00007" "BloodImage_00011"
files <- read.csv(splits[["test"]])
images <- read_images(files$images[1:2], size = NULL)

plot_boxes(images, found[1:2], min_score = 0.5)



plot of chunk bccd-published-plot



And here, unlike the nuclei vignette, a score means something
Those weights were trained on BCCD’s 205 training images. This is its 72 test images, which the model has never seen, so measuring on them is honest:
evaluate(borrowed, split = "test")[, c("map_50", "map_50_95", "mean_matched_iou")]
#>      map_50 map_50_95 mean_matched_iou
#> 1 0.8570754 0.5003368        0.8058061
That is the figure on the model card, which anybody can check:
available_weights()[available_weights()$name == "bccd-yolo3", c("name", "revision")]
#>         name                                 revision
#> 1 bccd-yolo3 24fbff0833455a747c7bac9c2b8dc43073ce4e82
The description in that table is the part to read before trusting them. Published is the median of five seeds rather than the best - the spread is wide enough that a single number would be whichever seed was reported - and platelets are the unreliable class, which the next section shows rather than asserts.


One refusal worth meeting now
A detector’s weights decode boxes relative to the anchors they were trained with. Read with any others, the same numbers produce boxes scaled by a fixed factor: plausible boxes, plausible scores, wrong places, and nothing in any output to say so. So loading takes the anchors recorded beside the file, and a specification that also names some is two claims about one model with one of them untrue:
yolo3("cells", input_shape = c(416, 416), weights = "bccd-yolo3",
      anchors = list(list(c(0.3, 0.3)), list(c(0.2, 0.2)), list(c(0.1, 0.1))))
#> Error:
#> ! give `weights` or `anchors`, not both. A detector's weights decode boxes relative to the anchors they were trained with, so loading uses the ones recorded beside the file - which would leave these describing nothing.
Refused before anything was built. Everything below trains from scratch instead, which is what you will do on your own data.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
section: Anchors, which a detector has and a U-Net does not
text:
Anchors, which a detector has and a U-Net does not
YOLOv3 does not predict a box from nothing. It predicts a correction to one of nine anchors - fixed shapes, three per grid - and which anchors you use decides how much correcting is left to learn. Unset, they are fitted to your own boxes:
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = detection_data(splits[["train"]], splits[["val"]], test = splits[["test"]],
                        classes = cells, mode = "config_file"),
  models = list(yolo3(
    "cells",
    input_shape = c(416, 416),
    epochs = 150,
    batch_size = 8,
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-4),
    # A smear has no up or down, and a left-right flip is free: the boxes follow it
    # exactly, with no interpolation and no rounding.
    augmentation = list(augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5)),
    callbacks = list(callback_cosine_annealing())
  )),
  seed = 1
)

fit <- platypus_fit(spec, verbose = FALSE)
anchors <- detection_anchors(fit)
anchors$fitted
#> [1] TRUE
round(anchors$mean_iou, 4)
#> [1] 0.8772
anchors$per_anchor[, c("grid", "slot", "width_pixels", "height_pixels", "boxes",
                       "mean_iou")]
#>   grid slot width_pixels height_pixels boxes  mean_iou
#> 1    0    0    147.38592     137.40874   103 0.8696796
#> 2    0    1    118.59296     101.74789    71 0.8102370
#> 3    0    2     81.30258      74.30011   445 0.8863117
#> 4    1    0     68.32447      70.38699   803 0.9089707
#> 5    1    1     72.38382      58.75508   581 0.8836537
#> 6    1    2     55.40458      67.64656   349 0.8541086
#> 7    2    0     59.82368      50.76842   247 0.8363835
#> 8    2    1     30.99390      29.78902    82 0.8265114
#> 9    2    2     23.79106      23.37358   123 0.8322202
Fitted anchors cover these boxes at a mean overlap of 0.88. COCO’s own nine, borrowed, manage 0.65 on the same boxes - which is the difference between a correction and a rewrite, and it costs nothing to avoid.
A mean hides which class it is made of. A coverage of 0.65 is either “every class covered adequately” or “two covered well and the third not at all”, and those want different fixes. The picture tells them apart:
plot_anchors(fit, log = TRUE)



plot of chunk bccd-anchor-plot


Each point is one annotated box - its width against its height, both as fractions of the 416 x 416 input - and the diamonds are the anchors. Log axes, because the fitted anchors alone run from 24 to 147 pixels a side, and on linear ones the smallest class collapses into the corner.
Three clouds, because the three cell types are three sizes, and a diamond near each one. The diamonds are not spread evenly: most sit in the crowded middle where the red cells are, which is k-means doing exactly what it was asked - put the anchors where the boxes are, not where the classes are.
And one point sits far below everything else, at about two thirds of a pixel a side. That is not a drawing error and not an outlier in the statistical sense - it is a bad row. BCCD carries one annotation of zero extent in the training split and another in the validation split, and a zero-width box read under Pascal VOC’s inclusive convention comes out one pixel across. k-means drops it, because an overlap with a box that has no area is undefined, which is why the anchors above were fitted to 2,804 boxes while the picture draws 2,805. The plot keeps it deliberately: a dataset’s bad rows are worth seeing once, and this is the only place in the whole run where that one is visible at all.
It is also the clearest way to see why COCO’s nine manage only 0.65 here. Those span 10 to 373 pixels a side, because COCO holds objects of every size; these three cell types span about 6-fold. Most of that range is spent on boxes this dataset does not contain.
Worth drawing for the split they were not fitted on. Anchors covering the training boxes well and the validation boxes badly would say the two halves hold different objects, and no training curve shows that:
plot_anchors(fit, split = "validation", log = TRUE)



plot of chunk bccd-anchor-plot-valid

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
text:
What the loss is doing
tail(fit$history[, c("epoch", "train_loss", "train_coordinates", "train_objectness",
                     "val_loss")], 3)
#>     epoch train_loss train_coordinates train_objectness  val_loss
#> 148   148   5.926291          5.921908     0.0006802287  9.950191
#> 149   149   5.926131          5.921756     0.0006467079  9.976097
#> 150   150   5.926317          5.921920     0.0007015823 10.066363
The total does not reach zero and that is not a stall. Cross-entropy against a soft target bottoms out at the target’s own entropy, so the coordinate term has a floor above zero that depends on the data. Which is exactly why the four parts are reported separately: a total of 5.93 means nothing alone, while coordinates 5.92 beside objectness 7 × 10<sup>-4</sup> says the model has learned what is where and is still refining the boxes.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
section: Scoring, and the number that is missing on purpose
text:
Scoring, and the number that is missing on purpose
evaluate(fit, split = "test")
#>   model architecture parameters epochs_run    map_50 map_50_95 mean_matched_iou
#> 1 cells        yolo3   61534504        150 0.8638967 0.5083634        0.8041728
#>   n_truth n_predicted classes_without_truth
#> 1     945        2535                     0
This run’s map_50 of 0.8639 sits inside the range of the five in the table further down (0.853 to 0.887), and that is the point of the table rather than a problem with it. A seed pins which random numbers are drawn; it does not pin the order they are consumed in, and the number of loader workers - num_workers = "auto" here, four in the script that produced the published weights - changes that order. So “the same seed” means the same recipe on one machine with one worker count, and not a guarantee of the same number. Knits of this very document at the same seed have differed by more than a point of map_50, which is how the paragraph you are reading came to be written: the first version of it quoted a number, and the next knit disagreed with it.
Which is the argument for reading mean_matched_iou first, and it holds here: the overlap came out at 0.8042 against the five-run mean of 0.8040, a difference of 0.0001.
There is no overall precision and no overall recall in that table, and the absence is deliberate. Averaging them over classes needs a weighting, and every choice of weighting is a different claim: over BCCD’s 4,155 red cells, 372 white and 361 platelets, a single precision is a statement about red cells wearing the costume of a statement about the model.
Per class is the form in which they mean something:
evaluate_classes(fit, split = "test")
#>       class average_precision mean_matched_iou n_truth n_predicted precision
#> 1       RBC         0.7977684        0.8074916     805         900 0.7155556
#> 2       WBC         0.9620625        0.8503462      71          77 0.9220779
#> 3 Platelets         0.8318592        0.7196516      69         110 0.5909091
#>     recall
#> 1 0.800000
#> 2 1.000000
#> 3 0.942029
Read that table rather than the mean. White cells are nearly perfect - there is one per image and it is large. Platelets come back at a precision of 0.59 at this confidence, meaning 41% of the platelets reported are not there, and their boxes fit worst of the three at an overlap of 0.72.

mAP@0.5, mAP@[.50:.95], and which to believe
Two averages and they answer different questions. The first asks whether an object was found; the second averages over ten overlap thresholds and so also asks how well the box fits. The gap between them is localisation, and mean_matched_iou says that in one number instead of through a difference.
On this dataset, the overlap is far steadier than the average precision. Five runs of the recipe above, differing only in the seed - and measured with the engine on its own, four loader workers, rather than through this vignette:




mean
sd




mAP@0.5
0.8660
0.0159


mAP@[.50:.95]
0.5159
0.0199


mean IoU of matched boxes
0.8041
0.0026



Six times steadier. Which rank the model gives a borderline platelet moves average precision and leaves the overlap alone - so on a dataset this size, a point of mAP is not a result, and mean_matched_iou is the number to read first. That is not a general law about detection; it is what these 364 images do, and it was found by running five seeds rather than one.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
text:
Looking at it
The comparison is the point. Truth in one colour, predictions in another, on the same image:
truth <- lapply(read.csv(splits[["test"]])$annotations[1:2], function(path) {
  xml <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  nodes <- regmatches(paste(xml, collapse = ""),
                      gregexpr("<object>.*?</object>", paste(xml, collapse = "")))[[1]]
  pull <- function(node, tag) {
    as.numeric(sub(paste0(".*<", tag, ">([^<]*)</", tag, ">.*"), "\\1", node))
  }
  data.frame(
    # Pascal VOC is 1-based and inclusive of both ends, so a box written xmin=1 xmax=10 is
    # 0..10 as a continuous interval. Reading it as 0-based shifts every box by a pixel and
    # shrinks it by one - invisible by eye, and real IoU on a platelet 41 pixels across.
    xmin = vapply(nodes, pull, numeric(1), "xmin") - 1,
    ymin = vapply(nodes, pull, numeric(1), "ymin") - 1,
    xmax = vapply(nodes, pull, numeric(1), "xmax"),
    ymax = vapply(nodes, pull, numeric(1), "ymax"),
    name = sub(".*<name>([^<]*)</name>.*", "\\1", nodes)
  )
})

mine <- predict(fit, split = "test")
plot_boxes(images, mine[1:2], truth = truth, min_score = 0.5)



plot of chunk bccd-compare


A detector that found the right number of objects in the wrong places and one that found the wrong number in the right places score similarly and look nothing alike, which is why this picture is worth more than either average.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
text:
What this does not do
It is not a cell count. A precision of 0.59 on platelets means a count taken from these boxes is too high by about 69%. Counting needs either a better model for the small class or a threshold chosen for counting rather than for a figure, and either way it needs measuring against truth on your own data.
It is one small collection. 205 training images at one magnification, stained one way. BCCD is a demonstration dataset.
It is not a diagnostic tool, and a result from it is not a laboratory result.

title: Finding blood cells with YOLOv3
text:
Notes on the machine
Trained on a GTX 1070: 150 epochs, about 37 minutes. YOLOv3 is 61.5 million parameters, thirty times a U-Net at the settings in the nuclei vignette, so this is the one place in the package where the hardware matters.
A card of that generation needs the CUDA 12 build of PyTorch, which platypus_use_torch("pascal") selects - see ?platypus_device. Without it the run falls back to the processor, and the warning that says so is printed before the wait rather than after, because a run that quietly went to the CPU looks exactly like a run that is simply slow.

title: rplatypus
text:
Detection only. On a segmentation fit this refuses by name and points at evaluate_cases(). The name carries no detection_ prefix on purpose: this is an S3 generic, so a future task gains a method under the same name rather than a second spelling of one idea.



evaluate_classes(object, ...)

## S3 method for class 'platypus_fit'
evaluate_classes(object, model = NULL, split = "validation", ...)







object


A fit from platypus_fit() on a detection specification.




…


Unused.




model


Which model, when the specification trained several.




split


Which split to score.






The row that matters on unbalanced data, which is most detection data: BCCD has 4,155 red cells against 372 white and 361 platelets, so a single number is a number about red cells. evaluate() deliberately carries no overall precision or recall for the same reason - averaging them over classes needs a weighting, and every choice of weighting is a different claim.



A data frame, one row per class: average precision at IoU 0.5, the mean overlap of the boxes that matched, the number of true boxes, and precision and recall at the model’s operating_point.




library("rplatypus")

evaluate_classes(fit, "bccd")

# The row that matters on unbalanced data, which is most data: BCCD has 4155 red
# cells against 372 white and 361 platelets, so a single number is a number about
# red cells.

title: rplatypus
text:
A quick sanity check before training: a foreground of half a percent is a problem the loss has to be chosen for, and it is better to know before the run than after.



mask_coverage(mask, labels = NULL)







mask


Class indices, counted from 1.




labels


Optional names for the classes.






A data frame with one row per class.




library("rplatypus")

mask <- matrix(1L, 8, 8); mask[2:4, 2:4] <- 2L
mask_coverage(mask, labels = c("background", "nucleus"))

  class      label pixels fraction
1     1 background     55 0.859375
2     2    nucleus      9 0.140625

# A class with 0 pixels is the thing to look for: its target channel is zero
# everywhere, so there is no gradient towards it and the model is never shown
# what it is being asked to find.
crumbs: How much of each class a mask covers

title: rplatypus
text:
Weights are named rather than downloaded by hand, and a name is pinned to one commit of the repository holding it - so “dsbowl-unet” means one set of numbers today and the same set next year. This lists what is published, with the commit each name resolves to.



available_weights()




Read the descriptions rather than only the names. A model’s limitations decide whether it answers your question: the nuclei weights are semantic, so touching nuclei come back as one region and a count taken from them would be wrong.



A data frame with name, repo, filename, revision and description.



u_net() and the other architectures, whose weights argument takes a name from here, a hf://owner/repo/file.safetensors@commit reference, or a path to a local file.




library("rplatypus")

available_weights()

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("images/", "images/", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("nuclei", input_shape = c(256, 256), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
                      weights = "dsbowl-unet", fit = FALSE))
)
masks <- predict(platypus_fit(spec), split = "validation")
crumbs: The published weights, and what they are

title: rplatypus
text:
Divides one directory of samples into three sets and writes each as a CSV the specification can point at. Nothing is copied: the files stay where they are and the CSVs list them, which matters when the data is large or read-only.



split_dataset(
  root,
  out_dir,
  group_by = NULL,
  fractions = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15),
  seed = 0,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  subdirs = c("images", "masks"),
  column_sep = ";",
  strict = TRUE,
  relative = TRUE
)







root


The directory holding the samples, laid out as mode describes.




out_dir


Where to write train.csv, validation.csv and test.csv.




group_by


A pattern picking the group out of a sample’s name; see above. NULL treats every sample as its own group, which is right when one sample is one patient.




fractions


Two or three shares that add up to 1: train, validation and optionally test. Measured in samples, not in groups, so patients with very different numbers of slices do not skew them.




seed


Makes the split reproducible. The same inputs and seed give the same split on any machine and in any file order - without that, two runs are not comparable and the reason for a difference is impossible to find.




mode


“nested_dirs” for one directory per sample, “config_file” for a CSV.




subdirs


The image and mask subdirectory names, for nested_dirs.




column_sep


Separator between several paths in one CSV cell.




strict


Treat an incomplete sample as an error rather than skipping it.




relative


Write paths relative to the CSV where possible, so the dataset and its split can be moved together.






A platypus_split: the three paths, plus how many samples and groups each set received. Pass it straight to segmentation_data().



Splitting per file is the obvious thing and, for medical images, the wrong one. A scan is many slices of one patient, so dividing slices at random puts the same anatomy in training and in validation at once. The model then meets the neighbouring slice of what it is being tested on, validation measures memory rather than generalisation, and Dice comes out several points too high with nothing in the result to say so.
group_by names the unit that must not be split - usually a patient, sometimes a study, a scanner or a site. Every sample sharing a group lands in exactly one set.



group_by is passed to the engine exactly as written, and read there as a Python regular expression. In practice the dialects agree on everything you are likely to need


^, $, \d, [A-Z], +, *, () - and R’s own quoting rules still apply, so a backslash is doubled: “^(patient\\d+)_“. It is not translated on the way through, deliberately: a translation that quietly got it wrong would produce a working split with the wrong groups in it, which is the failure this argument exists to prevent.


A pattern that matches no sample is an error, never a fallback to one-group-per-sample.



evaluate_cases(), which reports a score per case rather than one per set.




library("rplatypus")

split <- split_dataset(
  "scans", "splits",
  group_by = "^(patient\\\\d+)_",
  fractions = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15)
)
split

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(split, colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("unet", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)
crumbs: Split a dataset into training, validation and test sets

title: rplatypus
text:
Call this before anything starts the engine - straight after library(rplatypus) - and before the first call that needs Python.



platypus_use_torch(build = c("pascal", "default"))







build


“pascal” for the last PyTorch built against CUDA 12, or NULL for the default.






There is one reason to: a GeForce GTX 10-series card, or anything older. PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta generations outright. No driver update brings them back. Without this, such a card is simply not used and everything runs on the processor, perhaps ten times slower, with nothing obviously wrong.
On anything from Turing - the RTX 20-series onwards - the default is correct and this is unnecessary.



The requirement string now in force, invisibly.



py_require() is session state, so this does not survive a restart - and forgetting it costs about ten times the training time without costing an error, which is the kind of bill that goes unnoticed. Set it where a session starts instead:

options(rplatypus.torch = "pascal")   # ~/.Rprofile


or PLATYPUS_TORCH=pascal in ~/.Renviron, which also reaches runs that never load an .Rprofile - Rscript, a scheduler, CI. The option wins over the variable, so a session can override what a machine was configured with. “default” asks for the ordinary build, which is how to turn the setting off for one session without editing the file it came from.
Both are read when the package is loaded, which is the last moment anything can change what the environment will be. A value neither of them recognises is reported at load and ignored: a bad line in a startup file should not make the package unloadable.



What this prints is a property of the machine it runs on, so an example output here would describe whichever machine built this page rather than yours. Run it and read your own.




library("rplatypus")

library(rplatypus)
platypus_use_torch("pascal")   # GTX 10-series and older
crumbs: Ask for a particular PyTorch build

title: rplatypus
text:
A model’s decode is a list of these, not one: several decodings share one forward pass, so a second one costs seconds where a second training run costs an hour. evaluate() then returns a row per model and decoding.



decode_connected_components(minimum_area = NULL)

decode_nearest_seed(minimum_area = NULL)

decode_watershed(minimum_area = NULL)

decode_follow_flows(steps = NULL, step_size = NULL, minimum_area = NULL)







minimum_area


Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. Unset keeps everything, and that is the engine’s default on purpose: the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method. A nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor picked here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another. It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.




steps


For decode_follow_flows(), how many Euler steps each pixel takes. Measured as not mattering: one step scores 0.9914 against 0.9923 converged, a span below the 0.0013 two runs differ by, because the field is continuous within an object and diverges at a seam - so the gap between two objects opens on the first step rather than after many. Adjustable because that argument is about this data’s object sizes.




step_size


For decode_follow_flows(), how far one step moves, in pixels, on a unit-length field. A cliff rather than a speed knob: 0.9923 at 1, 0.4715 at 2, 0.0303 at 10. A step longer than a pixel jumps over the sink it was converging on and lands in a neighbour’s basin.






Each declares which separation it can read, and asking for one that cannot read the model’s signal is refused when the specification is built rather than at the end of a run. decode_connected_components() reads none of them - it ignores the separation signal entirely - which is exactly why it belongs in every model’s list: it is the row the signal’s own row has to be read against. Left unset, a model decodes with its own signal’s decoding plus that yardstick.



A decoding block, to be passed inside a model’s decode list.



separations, instance_data()




library("rplatypus")

list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components())

[[1]]
[[1]]$name
[1] "nearest_seed"


[[2]]
[[2]]$name
[1] "connected_components"

decode_follow_flows(step_size = 0.5)

$name
[1] "follow_flows"

$step_size
[1] 0.5
crumbs: What a model is made of

title: rplatypus
text:
How the weights are updated. optimizer_adam() unless there is a reason not to: it adapts the step per parameter, so it usually trains without anything tuned except learning_rate. optimizer_sgd() with momentum is the recipe most of the classification literature’s best numbers were produced with, in exchange for depending on a tuned rate and usually a schedule - see callbacks for those.



optimizer_adam(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0,
  amsgrad = FALSE
)

optimizer_adamw(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0.01
)

optimizer_sgd(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  momentum = 0,
  nesterov = FALSE,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_rmsprop(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  alpha = 0.99,
  momentum = 0,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adagrad(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  lr_decay = 0,
  eps = 1e-10,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adadelta(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  rho = 0.9,
  eps = 1e-06,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adamax(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_nadam(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)







learning_rate


How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.




beta_1


Decay for the running average of the gradient. Lower reacts to the last few batches, higher smooths over more of them; 0.9 is the usual value and rarely worth moving.




beta_2


Decay for the running average of the squared gradient, which is what scales each parameter’s step. Below about 0.99 training gets noticeably noisier. In optimizer_adamax() it decays the largest gradient seen instead.




eps


Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. A guard, not a knob.




weight_decay


Pull the weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents. In optimizer_adamw() it is applied to the weights directly rather than through the gradient, which is the whole difference between the two.




amsgrad


Keep the largest squared-gradient average seen so far rather than the current one, so the step size never grows back. It fixes a convergence case in Adam’s proof and usually changes nothing in practice; worth trying if a run plateaus and then gets worse.




momentum


Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.




nesterov


Look ahead to where momentum is about to carry the weights before measuring the gradient. Needs momentum above 0, and giving it without momentum is refused rather than ignored.




alpha


For optimizer_rmsprop(), the decay for its running average of the squared gradient - the same work beta_2 does in the Adam family, under that family’s name.




lr_decay


For optimizer_adagrad(), shrink the rate further as training goes on, on top of the shrinking Adagrad already does by accumulating every squared gradient it has seen.




rho


For optimizer_adadelta(), how long a window of squared gradients to remember. Adadelta exists to avoid Adagrad’s ever-shrinking step and this is the parameter that does it.






No run in this project has compared them on segmentation, so this page says what each one does differently rather than which is better. available_optimizers() lists them with the arguments each accepts.
The rest are here because a configuration should be able to name what torch offers. optimizer_adamw() is Adam with weight decay applied to the weights rather than through the gradient, which is why its decay defaults to 0.01 rather than 0 - choosing it and leaving the decay at zero leaves nothing to choose. optimizer_adagrad() accumulates every squared gradient it has seen, so its step only ever shrinks and a long run can stop learning; optimizer_adadelta() is the same idea with a window instead of a sum. optimizer_adamax() tracks the largest gradient rather than the average of their squares, which is steadier where a few batches carry very large ones. optimizer_rmsprop() is Adam’s denominator without its momentum, and optimizer_nadam() is Adam with the look-ahead that SGD calls nesterov.
Every argument left unset is decided by the engine, which is where the defaults live.



An optimiser specification.



available_optimizers() for the same list with its arguments, and callbacks() for moving the rate during a run.




library("rplatypus")

optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-4)

$name
[1] "adam"

title: rplatypus
text:
How the weights are updated. optimizer_adam() unless there is a reason not to: it adapts the step per parameter, so it usually trains without anything tuned except learning_rate. optimizer_sgd() with momentum is the recipe most of the classification literature’s best numbers were produced with, in exchange for depending on a tuned rate and usually a schedule - see callbacks for those.



optimizer_adam(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0,
  amsgrad = FALSE
)

optimizer_adamw(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0.01
)

optimizer_sgd(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  momentum = 0,
  nesterov = FALSE,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_rmsprop(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  alpha = 0.99,
  momentum = 0,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adagrad(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  lr_decay = 0,
  eps = 1e-10,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adadelta(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  rho = 0.9,
  eps = 1e-06,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_adamax(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)

optimizer_nadam(
  learning_rate = 0.001,
  beta_1 = 0.9,
  beta_2 = 0.999,
  eps = 1e-08,
  weight_decay = 0
)







learning_rate


How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened by a schedule.




beta_1


Decay for the running average of the gradient. Lower reacts to the last few batches, higher smooths over more of them; 0.9 is the usual value and rarely worth moving.




beta_2


Decay for the running average of the squared gradient, which is what scales each parameter’s step. Below about 0.99 training gets noticeably noisier. In optimizer_adamax() it decays the largest gradient seen instead.




eps


Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. A guard, not a knob.




weight_decay


Pull the weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents. In optimizer_adamw() it is applied to the weights directly rather than through the gradient, which is the whole difference between the two.




amsgrad


Keep the largest squared-gradient average seen so far rather than the current one, so the step size never grows back. It fixes a convergence case in Adam’s proof and usually changes nothing in practice; worth trying if a run plateaus and then gets worse.




momentum


Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.




nesterov


Look ahead to where momentum is about to carry the weights before measuring the gradient. Needs momentum above 0, and giving it without momentum is refused rather than ignored.




alpha


For optimizer_rmsprop(), the decay for its running average of the squared gradient - the same work beta_2 does in the Adam family, under that family’s name.




lr_decay


For optimizer_adagrad(), shrink the rate further as training goes on, on top of the shrinking Adagrad already does by accumulating every squared gradient it has seen.




rho


For optimizer_adadelta(), how long a window of squared gradients to remember. Adadelta exists to avoid Adagrad’s ever-shrinking step and this is the parameter that does it.






No run in this project has compared them on segmentation, so this page says what each one does differently rather than which is better. available_optimizers() lists them with the arguments each accepts.
The rest are here because a configuration should be able to name what torch offers. optimizer_adamw() is Adam with weight decay applied to the weights rather than through the gradient, which is why its decay defaults to 0.01 rather than 0 - choosing it and leaving the decay at zero leaves nothing to choose. optimizer_adagrad() accumulates every squared gradient it has seen, so its step only ever shrinks and a long run can stop learning; optimizer_adadelta() is the same idea with a window instead of a sum. optimizer_adamax() tracks the largest gradient rather than the average of their squares, which is steadier where a few batches carry very large ones. optimizer_rmsprop() is Adam’s denominator without its momentum, and optimizer_nadam() is Adam with the look-ahead that SGD calls nesterov.
Every argument left unset is decided by the engine, which is where the defaults live.



An optimiser specification.



available_optimizers() for the same list with its arguments, and callbacks() for moving the rate during a run.

optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-4)

title: rplatypus
text:
Writes safetensors plus a .json sidecar recording what the weights are for: architecture, input shape, channels, classes, and whatever else you pass. Loading refuses a model they do not belong to, which is what the sidecar is for - weights trained on a different colormap with the same number of classes load cleanly and predict nonsense.



export_weights(object, path, model = NULL, ...)







object


A platypus_fit().




path


Where to write, with or without the .safetensors extension.




model


Which model, by the name in the specification. Defaults to the first.




…


Extra fields for the sidecar, for instance data = “BBBC038v1”, licence = “CC0 1.0”.






Anything in … joins the sidecar. The data they were trained on and its licence belong there: weights whose provenance lives in somebody’s memory cannot be used by anybody else, including you in a year.



The path written, invisibly, with the sidecar’s contents attached as the recorded attribute - so you can see what was put beside the weights without opening the file.




library("rplatypus")

export_weights(fit, "weights/my-run",
             data = "our 2026 cohort", licence = "internal use only")

binary_colormap is black background, white foreground: the ordinary two-class problem. voc_colormap is the twenty-one class palette used by Pascal VOC, kept because datasets and other people’s masks still arrive in it.



binary_colormap

binary_labels

voc_colormap

voc_labels




A list of RGB triples, or a character vector of names.



The labels are the matching class names, for figure legends and mask_coverage(). Position in the list is the class index throughout, counting from 1.



Four exported objects rather than functions. binary_colormap and voc_colormap are lists of integer vectors of length three - one RGB triple per class, 2 entries and 21 entries respectively - where position in the list is the class index, counting from 1. binary_labels and voc_labels are character vectors of the matching class names, the same length as their colormap and in the same order, so the nth label names the class the nth triple draws.

title: rplatypus
text:
One row per model per epoch, with the loss, whatever metrics were asked for, how long the epoch took and the learning rate it ran at. Two columns arrive whether or not anybody asked:



training_history(object)







object


A platypus_fit().








foreground - the share of the prediction that is not background. Not a measure of quality, because nothing is compared against the truth: it answers whether the model is still producing a segmentation at all. A model collapsing to background reports a plausible loss and, with include_background = TRUE, a Dice around 0.5.


val_<metric>_worst - the lowest any single case scored. The distribution is the finding and the mean is where a failure hides, so the number worth reading is in the table rather than only in summary() after the run.





A data frame with one row per model per epoch.




library("rplatypus")

history <- training_history(fit)
head(history)

# For a detector the loss is broken into four terms on purpose: a run whose
# coordinate loss falls while its objectness loss does not is finding the right
# places and refusing to commit, and the reverse is confident nonsense.

title: rplatypus
text:
One row per object, beside the rows instance_sizes() gives. voxels and area_mm2 answer how big; these answer how stretched - the semi-axes of the ellipse an object’s second moments imply, largest first, and for an image the eccentricity that shape analysis actually reports.



instance_shapes(labels, spacing = NULL)







labels


An instance label map from predict() - one integer per object, 0 for background, the same numbering instance_sizes() reads. Two dimensions for an image, three for a volume.




spacing


The size of one voxel in millimetres: two numbers for an image, three for a volume, in the array’s own order. Unset measures the sampling grid, and the column names say so.






The fit is not iterative, and it is the same arithmetic ellipse_measure() applies to a whole mask: for a uniform solid the variance along an axis is semi_axis^2 / (rank + 2), so the axes come out of one eigendecomposition per object. What this adds is that it is per object in one pass: the alternative a caller writes - ellipse_measure() on labels == k, once per object - rescans the whole array every time, and on a 512 x 512 map of 1939 objects that is 1989 ms against 143.
A volume gets three axes and no eccentricity, because an ellipsoid has no single one; the ratio of two columns is your division rather than a name this package invents.



A data frame with object and the semi-axes largest first - major_mm and minor_mm for an image, with middle_mm between them for a volume, named _px instead when spacing was not given. An image also gets eccentricity. One row per object present, in increasing object number; an object with fewer than rank + 1 voxels has no second moment and gets zeros, which is an ordinary outcome rather than an error.
eccentricity is unitless and it is not spacing-free. It describes whichever space it was computed in, so on anisotropic voxels the two disagree completely and in both directions: a circle of 80 pixels at spacing = c(2, 1) reads 0.0000 on the grid and 0.8660 in millimetres, while an 80 by 40 pixel ellipse at spacing = c(1, 2) reads 0.8667 on the grid and 0.0685 physically - physically almost a circle, which the grid calls strongly elongated. Pass your voxel size and read the _mm columns unless you mean the grid; the suffix on the axes is what says which of the two a row is.



instance_sizes() for how big each object is, ellipse_measure() for the same fit over a whole mask, and overlay_instances() to look at them.




library("rplatypus")

labels <- matrix(0L, nrow = 41, ncol = 81)
rows <- matrix(rep(seq_len(41), 81), nrow = 41)
columns <- matrix(rep(seq_len(81), each = 41), nrow = 41)
labels[((rows - 21) / 10)^2 + ((columns - 21) / 18)^2 <= 1] <- 1L
labels[(rows - 21)^2 + (columns - 61)^2 <= 81] <- 2L
# Wrapped because this one crosses to the engine - unlike `instance_sizes()`, which is a
# count times a product and stays in R so that a reader needs no Python to run its page.
# An eigendecomposition per object is not arithmetic a reader verifies by eye, which is
# the line `maju116/pyplatypus#270` drew between the two.
instance_shapes(labels, spacing = c(0.5, 0.5))

title: rplatypus
text:
Dice and IoU count a voxel the same wherever it sits, which is why a model can reach 0.88 on Dice while its volumes run a fifth too large: the overshoot is all at the boundary, and for a small lesion the boundary is most of the object. This adds mean(phi * p), where phi is the signed distance to the truth’s boundary - negative inside, positive outside - so a voxel predicted far outside the truth costs in proportion to how far.



loss_boundary(region = NULL, alpha = NULL)







region


The overlap term this is added to - any other loss. Unset uses the engine’s default, which is Dice. loss_focal() here is what this feature was originally asked for: focal combined with a distance metric. loss_generalized_dice() here is the combination worth knowing about, because the two features are motivated by the same picture: this loss exists for a lesion in a thousandth of a frame, and a surface term exists for an object whose boundary is most of it.




alpha


How much of the objective is the region term, 1 - alpha the surface term. Unset uses the engine’s default of 0.9.
Not 0.5, and that was measured. At 0.5 the surface term owns half the objective while the prediction is still random, which is where it is unstable: three seeds gave a volume error spread of ±28.28% against the baseline’s ±3.11%, with every number worse. Left unset here on purpose - the number is a measurement and belongs in the one place the measurement lives, so that an engine that learns better cannot be contradicted from this side.






What it buys and what it costs, measured. Three seeds, 60 epochs, lesions with ambiguous edges, against Dice alone:



loss


Dice


volume bias


volume |error|




loss_dice()


0.9525 ±0.0027


-5.18% ±3.11%


16.90% ±0.90%




loss_boundary()


0.9411 ±0.0093


-0.06% ±4.15%


22.17% ±2.88%



It trades accuracy per case for being unbiased over a series. "Is there a lesion" wants the overlap; "has it grown since March" wants a volume that is not systematically wrong, and no single number answers both - which is the same point mask_volume() makes about reporting millilitres beside an overlap score. The bias improvement is suggestive on three seeds, since the baseline’s own bias wanders ±3.11%; the costs are established.
It costs time too. The signed distance transform runs once per sample, in the loader’s workers: 5.3 ms for a 256x256 image, 23.4 ms for a 64x64x32 volume and 709.8 ms at 128^3. On large volumes give platypus_fit() workers, or the transform becomes the training.



A loss specification, to be passed to a model constructor.



losses for the losses that can be the region term - every one of them except the three that score numbers and this one, held to the engine’s own union by a test rather than counted here - and mask_volume() for reading a volume in millilitres rather than voxels.

loss_boundary()

$name

$region

$alpha
NULL

loss_boundary(region = loss_focal(gamma = 2))

$region$gamma

$region$alpha

$alpha
NULL
