text:
Four members of the U-shaped family. They take the same arguments and differ only in what happens between the contracting and expanding paths: u_net concatenates its skip connections, linknet adds them, res_u_net makes each block residual, and u_net_plus_plus fills in the nested skip pathways.

  name,
  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,
  n_class = NULL,
  blocks = NULL,
  filters = NULL,
  block_width = NULL,
  dropout = NULL,
  batch_normalization = NULL,
  separable_conv = NULL,
  spatial_dropout = NULL,
  upsample = NULL,
  deep_supervision = NULL,
  activation = NULL,
  initialiser = NULL,
  loss = NULL,
  metrics = NULL,
  optimizer = NULL,
  callbacks = NULL,
  augmentation = NULL,
  epochs = NULL,
  batch_size = NULL,
  splits = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  fit = NULL,
  encoder = NULL,
  pretrained = NULL,
  freeze_encoder = NULL,
  encoder_learning_rate = NULL,
  separation = NULL,
  decode = NULL
)

  name,
  input_shape,
  channels = NULL,

  block_width = NULL,

  separable_conv = NULL,
  spatial_dropout = NULL,

channels

n_class


Removed. The number of classes comes from the data - colormap or labels in segmentation_data() - and a model that also declared it could only ever disagree with its own data. Passing it is an error that says so.




blocks


How many times the resolution is halved. Taken from the weights file when weights is given and this is not.




filters


Filters in the first block; doubled at each level. Taken from the weights file when weights is given and this is not.




block_width


Convolutions per block. Two is the usual U-Net block; one trains faster and holds less, three rarely pays for itself. It composes with every architecture, including the residual blocks of res_u_net(), where it is the number of convolutions inside the residual rather than beside it.




dropout


Drop this fraction of activations in every block during training, 0 to switch it off. The first thing to reach for when the training loss keeps falling and the validation loss does not.

separable_conv


Depthwise-separable convolutions. Far fewer parameters, a little slower to converge.

upsample


Interpolate and convolve instead of using a transposed convolution.




deep_supervision

activation


One of “relu”, “leaky_relu”, “elu”, “selu”, “gelu”, “silu”, “tanh”.




initialiser


One of “he_normal”, “he_uniform”, “glorot_normal”, “glorot_uniform”.




loss

It is what a score table’s loss column is comparable within and not across: a Focal-Tversky of 0.05 is not better than a cross-entropy of 0.14, it is a different question, which is why the table carries the loss’s name beside the number. Unset uses the engine’s default.




metrics

A callback watching val_<metric> is refused when nothing in this list will produce it - when the configuration is read, rather than at the end of the first epoch with the epoch already paid for. Which is also why a tiled run refuses a callback watching val_cldice or val_surface_dice: those are properties of a whole mask, reported per case rather than per epoch, so the choice to tile and the choice of what to stop on are settled together.

optimizer


An optimiser, see optimizers.




callbacks


A list of callbacks, see callbacks.




augmentation


A list of augmentation_step() steps, applied to training data only.




epochs, batch_size


Training length and batch size.




splits


Cut each image into a grid of tiles instead of shrinking it: one number per spatial dimension, so c(2, 3) gives six tiles. Use it to segment a large image without throwing away resolution; predictions are reassembled to the original size.




weights


A checkpoint to start from, or to use as-is with fit = FALSE.




fit


Set FALSE to load weights and skip training.




encoder


A pretrained-architecture backbone to use as the contracting path instead of the built-in encoder, named as timm names it: “resnet34”, “efficientnet_b0”, “mobilenetv3_large_100”, “densenet121”, “vgg16” and the other convolutional families. Naming one builds that architecture; it does not load anything. 2D only - ImageNet is images, so a backbone with a 3D input_shape is refused while the specification is read. The patch-based families (convnext_, swin_) are refused too: their features start at a quarter of the input, and the half-resolution level a U-shaped decoder recovers fine detail from does not exist. blocks then says how many of the backbone’s stages to use.




pretrained


Load the backbone’s ImageNet weights. Separate from encoder on purpose, so naming an architecture never reaches the network on a machine that has none. Measured on three datasets, transfer does not beat the built-in encoder here - see encoders for the table and what it is actually good for.




freeze_encoder


Hold the transferred layers still for this many epochs, then train them. Use this rather than encoder_learning_rate alone: it was the better of the two on all three datasets measured. A number at or above epochs keeps them fixed for the whole run.




encoder_learning_rate


A separate, smaller rate for the layers that arrived pretrained. The full-resolution stage in front of them is platypus’s own and starts random, so it keeps the optimiser’s rate. Giving this instead of freeze_encoder measured worse everywhere, and on one dataset worse than no backbone at all.




separation


What the network predicts so that touching objects can be told apart - separation_rim() or separation_flows(). Giving it is what makes this an instance model: it has no counterpart on a semantic one, so a model carrying it can only mean instances, which is how a specification knows its task without anybody typing it. The data has to be instance_data() to match. The head’s width follows from the signal and the number of classes and is derived rather than stated.
It may be left out when weights names a file that records it, since pyplatypus 0.8.0a28: a published sidecar says what the channels were trained to predict, and “dsbowl-instances” is a rim of width 2 - a training decision rather than a shape, and nothing a reader can guess from a model card. So u_net(“objects”, input_shape = c(256, 256), weights = “dsbowl-instances”) beside instance_data() is an instance model, and the engine prints what it adopted.
Left out with no weights it is still semantic, and still refused beside instance_data() as two tasks in one specification - which is the pair that would otherwise be silent: the same layout and the same architecture, differing only in whether a signal is predicted at all. maju116/rplatypus#181.




decode


A list of decodings turning those channels into objects, e.g. list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components()). A list rather than one, because several decodings share a single forward pass: a second costs seconds where a second training run costs an hour, so evaluate() returns a row per model and decoding. Unset, the engine uses the signal’s own decoding plus decode_connected_components(), which ignores the signal and is therefore the row the others have to be read against. Only meaningful with separation.






input_shape is the tile the model sees: two numbers for images, three for volumes. Its length is what makes a model 2D or 3D - there is no separate switch. Every spatial dimension must divide by 2^blocks, or the decoder cannot line up with the encoder, and that is checked when the specification is built rather than part-way through training.



A model specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



Every argument below except name and input_shape is NULL unless you set it, and a NULL is left out of the request entirely - so the engine’s own default applies. The defaults are therefore written down once, in pyplatypus, rather than here as well:

spatial_dropout TRUE                upsample FALSE  deep_supervision FALSE
activation "relu"                   initialiser "he_normal"
loss cce          metrics iou       optimizer adam  callbacks none
epochs 10         batch_size 8      fit TRUE

The second reason matters more than tidiness. A value sent is indistinguishable from a value chosen, so defaults travelling from here would silence the engine’s own knowledge: weights naming a published file records its architecture, blocks and filters, and those are adopted only where the specification stayed silent. Sending blocks = 4 because that is what R happened to say would override a file that knows better.

title: rplatypus
text:
Reads a sample of one split’s masks and reports what the specification’s colours, or list of labels, actually matched. Trains nothing and loads no model.



inspect_masks(spec, split = c("train", "validation", "test"), limit = 500)







spec


A platypus_spec().




split


“train”, “validation” or “test”.




limit


How many masks to read. They are spread across the split rather than taken from its start, because datasets arrive sorted and a prefix would answer about the beginning.






platypus_fit() does a small version of this before every run and refuses when a declared class appears in none of the masks it read. This is the same question asked deliberately, over as much of the data as you want - which is what to reach for when that refusal looks wrong.



A one-row data frame: unmatched, samples_checked, total_samples, and present_classes and missing_classes as comma-separated strings so the frame stays printable - region names where the specification gave regions, and class numbers otherwise, which is what the engine’s own refusal does. The positions are attached as integer vectors in the attributes present and missing either way, so anything reading them keeps working.



missing_classes is the one to act on. A class that appears in no mask cannot be learned: its channel of the target is zero everywhere, so there is no gradient towards it and the model is never shown the thing it is being asked to find. Either the colours do not describe these masks, or they name a class the data does not contain.
With regions the classes are named rather than numbered, because a position is the one thing a reader cannot resolve: missing_classes: 1 means the second region, and counting entries in a configuration file to find out which is the step nobody takes. The positions are still there, as the missing and present attributes.
That naming matters most for the one failure regions invites: of = 3 against a label map holding 4 is a channel of zeros, so the model trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 for that region while every other number in the run looks ordinary. The engine refuses it before training and names the region; this is how to ask the same question over more of the data than the refusal reads.
unmatched is the fraction of mask pixels matching no entry, which fall back to the background class. Read it knowing that it scales with the size of the thing being segmented, so it is loud for a large structure and almost silent for a small lesion. Measured on masks that are white, with a colormap asking for a colour that is not there: a foreground covering 20% of the image gives 19.8%, and one covering 0.6% gives 0.61% - which is less than the 0.72% that JPEG compression leaves around the edge of a perfectly correct mask. That is why the refusal is built on class presence instead.




library("rplatypus")

inspect_masks(spec)
inspect_masks(spec, split = "validation", limit = 2000)
crumbs: What the colormap or labels match in your masks

text:
Builds a grid: one row per image, one column per panel. Which panels appear depends on what you pass - the image alone, the truth, the prediction, and where they disagree.



plot_masks(
  images,
  prediction = NULL,
  truth = NULL,
  colormap = binary_colormap,
  which = NULL,
  alpha = drawing_style()\$overlay_alpha,
  labels = NULL,
  slice = NULL
)







images


An image x height x width x channels array, or one height x width x channels image.




prediction


Predicted class indices, from predict.platypus_fit().




truth


True class indices, if you have them.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class.




which


Which images to show.




alpha


How strongly to tint the overlays.




labels


Row labels; defaults to the image number.




slice


For volumes, which slice to draw. A volume cannot honestly be shown as one picture, so one plane is chosen and said out loud rather than a projection being invented. Counted along the last axis, which after the canonical reorientation is the axial direction - the view a radiologist scrolls through. “middle” takes the middle slice, which is the sensible first look.






The disagreement panel is usually the one worth looking at. It separates what was found from what was missed and what was invented, and those are not interchangeable: for most clinical questions a missed lesion and a false alarm cost different things, and a single overlap score hides which one you have.



A ggplot.




library("rplatypus")

plot_masks(images, prediction = masks, truth = truth, colormap = binary_colormap)

title: rplatypus
text:
platypus_fit() leaves a record beside the weights when the specification named an output_dir: the whole specification, whatever the run worked out for itself, the epoch-by-epoch history, and the version of the engine that produced it. This reads one back.



read_record(path)







path


The run.json to read, or the directory holding it - so both read_record(“out/my_model”) and read_record(“out/my_model/run.json”) work.






Named to match read_record() in the engine, and read_images() and read_masks() here.



A platypus_record: a list with written, pyplatypus, model, specification, derived and history. Everything is plain R data, because a record describes what happened rather than being a live thing - except history, which comes back as a data frame with one row per epoch.
That frame is not quite what training_history() returns, and the difference is worth knowing before you rbind() them: a record belongs to one model, whose name is the top-level model field, so the frame has no model column. training_history() spans every model in the fit and needs one. Every other column is the same.



The specification in the record is a thing you can run again, not a description of a run. And for a detector whose anchors were fitted rather than named, derived$anchors is the only copy outside a weights sidecar - so a record is how a result stays reproducible after the session that produced it has gone.



Deliberately. Everything else in this package asks the engine; this reads a text file, and a first call to the engine provisions an environment of several gigabytes. A record you cannot read without the thing that wrote it is worth less than one you can, so this needs only jsonlite, and works on a machine that has never had Python.



training_history() for the same numbers from a fit in the current session, and export_weights(), whose sidecar answers a different question - what the weights are for, rather than what the run was.




library("rplatypus")

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("train", "valid", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("vessels", input_shape = c(256, 256))),
  output_dir = "runs"
)
fit <- platypus_fit(spec)

record <- read_record("runs/vessels")
record$pyplatypus          # the engine that produced it
head(record$history)       # one row per epoch
record$specification       # enough to run it again

title: rplatypus
text:
The objective the model is trained against. Every one of these works unchanged on volumes as well as images.



loss_iou(smooth = 1)

loss_dice(smooth = 1)

loss_generalized_dice(smooth = 1)

loss_cce(label_smoothing = 0)

loss_cce_dice(cce_weight = 0.5, smooth = 1)

loss_focal(gamma = 2, alpha = NULL)

loss_tversky(alpha = 0.5, smooth = 1)

loss_focal_tversky(alpha = 0.5, gamma = 1, smooth = 1)

loss_combo(alpha = 0.5, ce_ratio = 0.5)

loss_mse(where = NULL)

loss_l1(where = NULL)

loss_smooth_l1(beta = NULL, where = NULL)

loss_lovasz(per_image = FALSE)







smooth


Added to numerator and denominator to keep an empty class finite.




label_smoothing


For cross-entropy, train towards 1 - label_smoothing instead of towards 1, so the model is not pushed to be certain. Worth having where the labels themselves are uncertain, which on a hand-drawn boundary they are.




cce_weight


For loss_cce_dice(), how much of the total the cross-entropy half provides. At 0 or 1 it is one of the two alone, which is worth knowing before tuning it as though it were a third thing.




gamma


For focal losses, how hard to discount the pixels already classified well.




alpha


For Tversky, the weight on false negatives; raising it buys recall. Note that alpha = 0.5 is Dice exactly only when smooth = 0.




ce_ratio


For loss_combo(), how its cross-entropy half is tilted between punishing missed foreground (towards 1) and false alarms (towards 0), while alpha sets how much of the total each half provides.




where


For the three regression losses, where the target means anything and so where the error is averaged. A flow field is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards a centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background, and “everywhere” would spend most of the objective learning that zero. The foreground is 13.97% of a Data Science Bowl image, so “everywhere” gives 86% of the gradient to a constant; “foreground” is the default for that reason rather than by taste.




beta


For loss_smooth_l1(), where the quadratic part ends and the linear one begins, in the target’s own units. A flow field is scaled to roughly [-1, 1], so the default of 1 makes the whole range quadratic - which is loss_mse() with extra steps. Lower it to get any of the robustness this loss is for.




per_image


For loss_lovasz(), sort the errors of each image separately rather than over the whole batch. The harsher reading, and on mostly empty images the noisier one.






There is one documented separately because it needs a page of its own: loss_boundary() adds the signed distance to the truth’s boundary on top of any of these, which removes the systematic volume bias at some cost in per-case accuracy.
Three of these score numbers rather than classes - loss_mse(), loss_l1() and loss_smooth_l1() - and they are not alternatives to the others. A class target has nothing for them to measure and a continuous one has nothing for an overlap to measure, so they belong in exactly one place: the loss of separation_flows(), where the target is a vector field. Measured against the pinned engine rather than assumed: giving one as any segmentation model’s own loss is refused by name - semantic or instance - and giving a class loss to separation_flows() is refused by name the other way round.
One of these weights the classes rather than treating them alike - loss_generalized_dice(), by the inverse square of how much of the picture each class occupies - and the argument usually made for it is not the argument for it here. It is introduced in the literature as a fix for Dice being dominated by the background, and loss_dice() in this package is a mean over the class channels: a lesion in 1% of the frame already carries the same weight as the 99% around it. Measured on a 1% target, with one prediction that finds the lesion and leaks a false positive of equal size and one that misses it and gets the background perfect:



loss


finds it


misses it


prefers finding by




loss_dice()


0.1658


0.4731


0.3073




loss_cce()


0.1600


0.1600


nothing at all




loss_cce_dice()


0.1629


0.3166


0.1536




loss_generalized_dice()


0.3278


0.9511


0.6233



So what it adds is weight beyond an equal share - on that target the classes come out weighted 1 to 9801 - and the objective that is genuinely dominated is the per-pixel half of loss_cce_dice(): to cross-entropy a false positive and a missed lesion of the same size are the same number of wrong pixels, which is the indifference in that row. Two things follow. With every class the same size this is exactly loss_dice() pooled over the classes, so on a balanced problem it costs nothing and buys nothing. And it is not a third loss_tversky(): Tversky moves the balance between false positives and false negatives by a number you choose, loss_focal_tversky() reweights the hard pixels, and this reweights classes by how much of the image they occupy, computed from each batch rather than set by hand - so a batch holding no lesion at all is scored on flat weights, which is an argument for a larger batch_size on a sparse dataset rather than against the loss.
This page said an instance model’s own until the pin moved to 0.8.0a22, and it was true rather than wrong: the refusal lived on the instance class alone, and a semantic model accepted loss_mse() and trained with it, reporting a validation loss of 0.0014 for a mask that was half missing where loss_cce() reaches a Dice of 1.0000. The default where = “foreground” is what made it look as though it had worked - it evaluates the objective only inside the labelled objects and leaves the background unconstrained. The engine refuses it at either task now (pyplatypus#223).



A loss specification, to be passed to a model constructor.



separation_flows(), whose loss is the one place the regression losses belong




library("rplatypus")

loss_focal(gamma = 2)

$name
[1] "focal"

$gamma
[1] 2

$alpha
NULL

loss_tversky(alpha = 0.7)

$name
[1] "tversky"

$alpha
[1] 0.7

$smooth
[1] 1

loss_smooth_l1(beta = 0.1, where = "foreground")

$name
[1] "smooth_l1"

$beta
[1] 0.1

$where
[1] "foreground"

title: rplatypus
text:
Every failure that comes back from the engine is raised as a classed condition, so a script can tell one kind of problem from another instead of matching on the message. Until now that was true and undocumented, which made it true and useless.



Three or four entries, outermost first:

platypus_config_error    the specific kind
platypus_error           every failure from this package, which is the one to catch
error                    an ordinary R error
condition


So tryCatch(…, platypus_error = ) catches everything this package raises and nothing else, and a specific class narrows it. platypus_error appears once even when the engine sends no kind at all.



platypus_error, unless there is a reason not to. The specific kinds come from the engine, so the list below belongs to the version this package pins, and a later engine may add one. Catching the base class is the thing that keeps working.
Two are worth naming on purpose:


platypus_config_error


A specification that does not describe a runnable experiment. This one carries data: conditionCall() aside, the condition has a problems data frame with one row per problem - where, problem and, when it is short enough to be useful, got - and a source naming the YAML file if it came from one. The engine reports every problem it found rather than the first, so the frame is what makes "three things are wrong" readable.


platypus_training_stopped


Not a defect. A callback ended the run early, which is what it was asked to do, and anything scoring the result afterwards should treat it as a finished run rather than a failure.





One class per kind, prefixed. tests/testthat/test-conditions.R holds this list to what the engine actually defines, so a kind added upstream fails here rather than arriving undocumented.

platypus_config_error            a specification that cannot be run
platypus_engine_error            the engine could not do what the specification asked
platypus_model_error             the architecture could not be built as described
platypus_data_error              the dataset on disk is not what the specification says
platypus_image_error             an image could not be read, or is not the shape claimed
platypus_mask_error              a mask does not match its colormap
platypus_channel_error           one channel per file, and the files do not agree
platypus_volume_error            a volume, its orientation or its spacing
platypus_measure_error          a measurement whose spacing does not fit the array
platypus_dicom_error             a DICOM file or series
platypus_augmentation_error      a transform that cannot do what was asked of it
platypus_detection_error         detection metrics
platypus_detection_data_error    annotations, boxes or classes
platypus_instance_error          a separation target, or decoding one into objects
platypus_instance_data_error     the per-object mask files a case has, or has not
platypus_label_error             an image's label, or the class directories holding it
platypus_weights_error           weights that do not belong to this model
platypus_training_stopped        a callback ended the run early
platypus_unknown_case            a case or model name that is not in this run


platypus_unknown_case is the one with no class behind it in the engine: the R bridge raises it itself, because asking for a case that does not exist is a question the bridge can answer without troubling Python.



The engine exports three exception classes - PlatypusError, ConfigError, WeightsError - and raises the other fifteen internally, so a Python caller catches PlatypusError and inspects it. R derives its class from the kind the engine sends with every failure, so all of them arrive as catchable names. That is a wider surface on this side, and deliberately so: R has no exception hierarchy to lean on, and inherits() is cheaper than parsing a message.



platypus_status(), for when the problem is that the engine never started.




library("rplatypus")

# A specification with two problems, caught and read as data rather than as text.
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("train", "valid", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("m", input_shape = c(64, 64), loss = "focaal"))
)

tryCatch(
  platypus_fit(spec),
  platypus_config_error = function(e) {
    print(e$problems)        # one row per problem: where, problem, got
    invisible(NULL)
  },
  platypus_error = function(e) {
    message("something else went wrong: ", conditionMessage(e))
  }
)

title: rplatypus
text:
Shape and voxel spacing, read through the engine so the numbers are the ones training would use - including the canonical reorientation, which changes what "the first axis" means.



volume_info(paths)







paths

title: rplatypus
text:
Stochastic weight averaging. Past start, every epoch’s weights are folded into a running average and at the end that average becomes the model - the claim being that a point in the middle of a flat region generalises better than whichever corner the last epoch stopped in.



callback_swa(start = NULL, learning_rate = NULL, start_epoch = NULL)







start, start_epoch


When averaging begins - one of the two and never both. start is the fraction of the run after which it begins, 0.75 folding the last quarter, and unset uses the engine’s default of 0.75; start_epoch says the same thing as an epoch number. A fraction survives a change to epochs and an epoch count does not, which is why the fraction is the default; an epoch is the one to use when the point is a property of the optimisation rather than of the run’s length. The final epoch is always folded, so start = 1 averages one set of weights rather than none. callback_early_stopping() names the same pair with the same two words.




learning_rate


Hold the rate at this value once averaging begins. Unset leaves whatever the run was doing.
Worth setting, and the reason is the whole mechanism: averaging is only worth something while the weights are still moving, and a rate that has decayed towards zero produces a set of nearly identical snapshots whose average is the last one. For the same reason a run cannot ask for this and callback_cosine_annealing() at once - the two undo each other and the specification refuses the pair.






What it is worth is not what a table of scores shows. Three seeds, 60 epochs, lesions with ambiguous edges:



run


Dice


volume bias


volume |error|




plain


0.9639 ±0.0100


+1.71% ±12.18%


12.60% ±4.19%




callback_swa()


0.9667 ±0.0087


+2.08% ±2.15%


12.38% ±4.31%



Dice does not move and neither does the per-case error - both are inside the seed noise. What moves is reproducibility: the plain runs’ volume bias was +4.5%, +12.2% and -11.6% across three seeds, and with averaging -0.1%, +4.2% and +2.1%. A spread 5.7 times tighter, improving on all three seeds when paired, by 7.34% at 4.9 standard errors.
So read it as "the same model twice" rather than "a better model" - which is what averaging is for, and the reason it belongs beside mask_volume() in any argument about whether a measured volume can be compared across runs.
Batch-normalisation statistics are recomputed afterwards, by a pass over the training data. They have to be: an averaged weight tensor inherits the statistics of whichever epoch was last rather than averaging them, so without the pass the model is evaluated under the wrong normalisation and scores far worse than it should with nothing to say why. Models here have batch normalisation on by default, so this is nearly every run.



A callback specification, to be passed to a model constructor.



callbacks for the others, mask_volume() for reading a volume in millilitres.




library("rplatypus")

callback_swa()

$name
[1] "swa"

callback_swa(start = 0.5, learning_rate = 1e-3)

$name
[1] "swa"

$start
[1] 0.5

$learning_rate
[1] 0.001

title: rplatypus
text:
Reports whether the Python side has been started, and what it is. Calling this does not start it - use it to check before a long run, or when something is wrong.



platypus_status()




A list with the engine version, the interpreter in use and where its environment lives, or NULL fields when Python has not been started yet.



Nothing to do. Each release of this package pins one exact engine version, that pin is what gets declared when the package loads, and the environment is resolved from it on first use. Install a newer rplatypus and the next session uses the engine it asks for; the first call after the upgrade fetches the new engine - a few hundred kilobytes, with PyTorch already cached - and the environment the old version used is left alone, so going back to it costs nothing either.
That is the opposite of the arrangement most R packages wrapping Python have, where a persistent environment is installed once by hand and updating the R package does not touch it. Here there is no environment anybody maintains: there is a pin, and the environment always matches it. The cost is that the two cannot be moved separately - which is the point, since a release that could drift from its engine is the failure the pin exists to prevent.
One case is worth knowing: updating on the day the engine is published, uv may still be serving a cached index listing and report that the pinned version does not exist. It is a stale read rather than a missing release, it mends itself, and the failure message says so.
If RETICULATE_PYTHON is set, none of this applies - that Python is used whatever the pin says, and a mismatch is reported as a warning naming both versions.



What this prints is a property of the machine it runs on, so an example output here would describe whichever machine built this page rather than yours. Run it and read your own.




library("rplatypus")

platypus_status()

Reads through the engine’s own pipeline rather than a separate decoder, so what you plot is what the model was given. A picture drawn from a differently resized copy is a picture of something the model never saw, and the disagreements it appears to show may be nothing but the resizing.



read_images(paths, size = NULL, channels = 3, nearest = FALSE)







paths


Image files.




size


c(height, width) to read at, or NULL to keep each image’s own size - which only works if they all agree.




channels


3 for colour, 1 for greyscale.

Use nearest-neighbour resizing. Required for masks: interpolating one invents colours belonging to no class, which then quietly become background.

title: rplatypus
text:
The transforms the installed ‘albumentations’ offers, and - for volumes - the ones it can actually apply to them.



available_transforms(rank = 2, pattern = NULL)







rank


2 for images, 3 for volumes.




pattern


Optional regular expression to filter the names, for browsing: “Flip”, “3D$”, “Elastic|Grid”.






Worth asking rather than guessing. Support for volumes is uneven: most geometric transforms work and several intensity ones raise from inside the library, so rank = 3 returns a shorter list than rank = 2. A transform outside it is refused when the specification is built, by name, rather than failing an hour into training.
The number of names at rank = 2 is a property of the installed ‘albumentations’. The number at rank = 3 is not, and is deliberately not written down here. The engine finds that list by offering each transform a probe volume, and some of what it refuses fails for the probe’s reasons rather than the library’s: a group of transforms want three channels where the probe has one, and another group want a target - reference image, bounding box, metadata of their own - that a probe cannot supply and a specification cannot name either.
A third group used to fail on the probe’s size, which engine 0.8.0a10 fixed by retrying a refusal at a larger probe before believing it. That is also where a long-standing superstition went: the count used to vary between machines and was attributed to them, when the cause was one transform randomising its own parameters, so the same machine gave two answers. Escalating removed it. The count is still not promised, because it belongs to the installed library rather than to this package.
The check that decides your run is made when the specification is built, against your own shape and parameters.



A character vector of transform names.



augmentation_step(), which uses one.




library("rplatypus")

available_transforms()                       # everything, for images
#> 118 names, with albumentations 2.0.8

available_transforms(rank = 3)               # what volumes can take: fewer

available_transforms(rank = 3, pattern = "Flip|Crop")
#> [1] "AtLeastOneBBoxRandomCrop" "CenterCrop"   "CenterCrop3D"
#> [4] "CropAndPad"   "CropNonEmptyMaskIfExists"  "HorizontalFlip"
#> [7] "RandomCrop"   "RandomCrop3D"              "RandomCropFromBorders"
#> [10] "RandomResizedCrop"  "RandomSizedBBoxSafeCrop"  "RandomSizedCrop"
#> [13] "VerticalFlip"

# Which ones a volume cannot take, by name rather than by count.
head(setdiff(available_transforms(), available_transforms(rank = 3)), 3)
#> [1] "AdditiveNoise"      "BBoxSafeRandomCrop" "ChannelDropout"

text:
Reads the CSV that split_dataset() wrote and hands back the paths ready to use.



split_path(split, which = c("train", "validation", "test"))







split


A split_dataset().




which


“train”, “validation” or “test”.






The reason this exists rather than read.csv(): the CSVs store paths relative to themselves, so that a dataset and its split can be moved or mounted elsewhere together. validation <- split_path(split, "validation")
images <- read_images(validation$images, size = c(32, 32, 32), channels = 1)

title: rplatypus
text:
Either from arguments, or from a YAML file by passing its path as the only argument. Both produce the same object, and everything downstream treats them identically.



platypus_spec(
  data,
  models = NULL,
  task = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  deterministic = NULL,
  output_dir = NULL,
  check_paths = TRUE
)







data


A segmentation_data(), detection_data(), instance_data() or classification_data() specification, or the path to a YAML file. Which one it is decides task.




models


A list of model specifications, see models and available_models(). More than one is the ordinary case rather than the exception: they are trained in turn against the same data and the same split, which is what makes their numbers comparable, and a comparison is written by listing several entries of the same architecture with different settings. For a classifier, which has no architecture to vary, the comparison the task makes easiest is several entries differing only in encoder - ours against a pretrained backbone, on the same split.




task


Which task this specification describes, one of “semantic_segmentation”, “object_detection”, “instance_segmentation” or “classification”. Normally left unset: the data and model constructors already decide it, and segmentation_data() with u_net() can only mean one thing. Given, it is checked against them rather than trusted, so it can only agree or refuse.
The third task sharpened what this argument is for rather than making it load-bearing. An instance data block declares nothing a segmentation one lacks, so instance_data() is what says the word - but a model can still say it on its own, because separation is required on an instance model and has no counterpart on a semantic one.




seed


Makes a run repeatable as far as the arithmetic is deterministic, which goes further on some hardware than others - so it is worth knowing where it stops.
Repeatable: the split (split_dataset() gives the same partition on any machine), a detector’s fitted anchors, the order the data arrives in and its augmentation - including inside the loader’s worker processes - and, on the processor, every number to twelve decimal places.
Not repeatable: a run on a CUDA device. Measured on a GTX 1070, two runs of one configuration at one seed agreed to twelve decimals on the processor and differed in the fourth after a single epoch on the card, because cuDNN chooses algorithms neither package constrains. Nor across versions of the engine: anything that changes the order data is drawn in changes what one seed draws, and 0.8.0a3 did exactly that.
So it is the argument for comparing two of your own runs, and not for publishing a number somebody else can land on. platypus_device() reports which device yours will use.




deterministic


Ask the engine for deterministic algorithms as well, which is the only thing that makes a run on a card repeatable - seed on its own does not, as above.
The cost is real and arrives later than any other refusal here. Some convolutions become much slower, and an operation with no deterministic implementation raises when it is reached, so a run can stop ten minutes in rather than when the specification is built. Everything else this package refuses, it refuses before reading a single image; this cannot, because whether an operation has a deterministic algorithm is a fact about the installed engine and the device rather than about the specification.
Needs seed, and is refused without one: constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies leaves the run exactly as unrepeatable and only slower.




output_dir


Where to write a record of the run: the specification, the history, and anything the run worked out that the specification does not already say - a detector’s fitted anchors, which it cannot be reloaded without. NULL, the default, writes nothing.
Unset means nothing is written, not "written to a default place". A field with a default cannot be told apart from one somebody set to that default, so sending the default from here would have put files in every user’s working directory the moment the engine learned to write them - which it just did.




check_paths


Verify that the data paths exist. Turn it off to build a specification on a machine that does not hold the data.






The engine validates it, so a mistake is caught here rather than part-way through a training run - and reported against the model that has it, by the name you gave it.



A platypus_spec.




library("rplatypus")

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("train/", "valid/", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(
    u_net("unet", input_shape = c(256, 256)),
    linknet("linknet", input_shape = c(256, 256), loss = loss_focal_tversky(alpha = 0.7))
  )
)

# The same thing, from a file
spec <- platypus_spec("experiment.yaml")

title: rplatypus
text:
Things that happen between epochs. monitor is checked against the metrics the model actually asks for, so a callback watching a number that will never arrive is refused when the specification is built rather than waited on forever.



callback_early_stopping(
  monitor = "val_loss",
  patience = 10,
  min_delta = 0,
  restore_best = TRUE,
  start = NULL,
  start_epoch = NULL
)

callback_model_checkpoint(
  path,
  monitor = "val_loss",
  save_best_only = TRUE,
  when = NULL
)

callback_reduce_lr_on_plateau(
  monitor = "val_loss",
  factor = 0.1,
  patience = 5,
  min_lr = 0
)

callback_cosine_annealing(min_lr = 0, epochs = NULL)

callback_linear_annealing(min_lr = 0, epochs = NULL)

callback_step_decay(factor = 0.1, every = NULL, milestones = NULL, min_lr = 0)

callback_csv_logger(path)

callback_ema(decay = 0.999)

callback_stop_after(hours)

callback_terminate_on_collapse(
  floor = 1e-04,
  patience = 3,
  monitor = "val_foreground"
)

callback_terminate_on_nan()







monitor


What to watch: “val_loss”, “train_loss”, “val_” followed by a metric name such as “val_dice”, “val_foreground” and “train_foreground” - the share of the prediction that is not background - or “val_dice_worst” and its kind, the lowest any single case scored.
That last one is the number summary() on evaluate_cases() tells you to read, and until the engine’s 0.8.0a36 nothing could act on it: a model averaging 0.86 that scores 0.11 on some patient has a failure mode, and the mean is where it hides. Stopping, checkpointing and cutting the learning rate can all watch it now.
Validation only. The training data is shuffled between epochs, so a case has no identity in that pass and there is nothing honest to pool by - “train_dice_worst” is refused rather than quietly reported as something else.




patience


Epochs to wait before acting. For callback_terminate_on_collapse() that is epochs in a row below the floor, and it is not 1 because an early epoch legitimately predicts almost nothing.




min_delta


Improvement smaller than this does not count.




restore_best


Put the best weights back when training stops, rather than keeping the last - which are by definition the ones that were not improving. On by default. Note that callback_swa() replaces nothing if a run stops before averaging began.




start, start_epoch


When the callback may begin to act - one of the two and never both. start is a fraction of the run (0.1 leaves the first tenth alone) and start_epoch is an epoch number. Two arguments rather than one taking either, because a fraction survives a change to epochs and an epoch count does not, and in a YAML specification 1 and 1.0 are the same value once parsed - so one field would make "epoch one" and "the whole run" indistinguishable.
For callback_early_stopping() this is a warm-up: a model that needs fifteen epochs before its validation curve means anything would otherwise need patience > 15 for the whole run, paying that slack at the end as well. It delays the stopping and nothing else - an epoch inside the warm-up can still be the best one and restore_best still returns to it, because those are the best weights the run has if it ends for another reason.
For callback_swa() it is the point averaging begins, which is the same concept and therefore the same two words.




path


Where to write. For callback_model_checkpoint() that is the weights file; for callback_csv_logger() it is one row per epoch appended as the epoch ends - the same numbers training_history() returns, so a run that is interrupted still leaves its history behind. Re-read against the engine’s own text when it changed in 0.8.0a23, which is what the field-prose ledger is for: the engine’s sentence had named this package’s training_history() to a Python reader, and the fix there left R’s @param saying three words about two different files.
The checkpoint’s extension decides its format, since the engine’s 0.8.0a31: .safetensors is written as safetensors and anything else as a torch archive, which is what .pt has always meant. Before that the file was a torch archive whatever it was called, so a checkpoint named after the files this package publishes was written in one format and read as another - and reading now goes by the file’s contents rather than by its name, so a checkpoint written by an older engine still loads. A checkpoint is the run’s safety net; export_weights() is what writes a file for somebody else to load, with the sidecar that says what it is for.




save_best_only


Only write when the watched quantity improves, which is the default. FALSE writes every epoch, which is what to use when a run may be interrupted rather than when the best epoch is what you want to keep.




when


For callback_model_checkpoint(), a named list of thresholds that must all hold before anything is written: list(val_dice = 0.9, val_loss = 0.2). The direction is derived, not configured - anything ending in loss has to be below its threshold and everything else above it, the same rule monitor uses - so there is no argument to get backwards. The names are checked against what the model reports when the specification is built, not at the first epoch.
It is an extra gate beside save_best_only, not a replacement: with both, a file is written when the watched number improves and every threshold holds. A threshold is a number about your data and does not transfer between datasets, and a run whose conditions never hold writes nothing and says so when it ends.




factor, min_lr


What the rate is multiplied by, and the floor it stops at. factor is the cut on a plateau for callback_reduce_lr_on_plateau() and the drop at each step for callback_step_decay(), where it must be below 1 - a step schedule that raises the rate is a different idea and accepting it here would hide a typo. min_lr is the floor for all four.




epochs


For callback_cosine_annealing() and callback_linear_annealing(), how many epochs to spread the decay over. Unset means the model’s epochs, which is what you want: a curve that ends where the run ends.




every, milestones


For callback_step_decay(), one of the two and never both. every = 30 drops every thirty epochs; milestones = c(30, 60) drops at those epochs, 1-based and strictly increasing, which is how a published recipe states it. Two arguments rather than one that takes either, because 30 and c(30) are different schedules and a single argument holding either would be read as whichever was typed. A period survives a change to epochs; a list of milestones does not.




decay


For callback_ema(), how much of the average survives each optimiser step - not each epoch. 0.999 is the usual value and gives a half-life of about 700 steps; it is the published number because the average is fed per step, which is what the engine’s fourth callback hook was added for. Unlike callback_swa() this needs no pass over the training data at the end: the batch-normalisation statistics are averaged alongside the weights rather than recomputed.




hours


For callback_stop_after(), a wall-clock budget. An epoch cap cannot express it, because how long an epoch takes is a property of the data and the shape. Checked at the end of an epoch, so the real limit is this plus one epoch; the run’s stop reason names the clock, so a run that ran out of time does not read as one that converged.




floor


For callback_terminate_on_collapse(), the share of foreground below which a prediction counts as collapsed. A floor rather than a test for zero, because 0.01% foreground against a target that is 14% foreground has collapsed in every sense that matters. The default sits far below any real target on purpose: this guards against a failure, not against a model being merely bad, and a floor near a real foreground share would end runs that were only disappointing.






Whether the watched quantity should rise or fall is worked out from its name: anything ending in loss is minimised, everything else maximised.



A callback specification.



Every epoch reports foreground as well - for both passes, train_foreground and val_foreground - which is the share of the prediction that is not background. Nothing is compared against the truth, so it is not a measure of how good the model is; it answers whether the model is still producing a segmentation at all.
It is reported whether or not you ask for it, and that is the point. A model that collapses to predicting background everywhere is invisible in the numbers it already produced: with include_background = TRUE the Dice is a mean over class channels and the background channel is nearly perfect, so a collapsed model reports around 0.5 while its loss falls contentedly. A collapse you have to opt into noticing is one you will not notice.
callback_terminate_on_collapse() acts on it, evaluate() carries it as a column, and callback_model_checkpoint()’s when can take a condition on it.
There is a twelfth, documented separately because it needs a page of its own: callback_swa() averages the weights over the last part of the run. It watches nothing and changes how reproducible a run is rather than how well it scores.



callback_swa() and callback_ema() both replace the model’s weights when training ends, so a run takes one of them; the engine refuses both. They answer the same observation - the last epoch’s corner is not the middle of the basin - with different weightings. swa folds the tail uniformly from a declared start; ema weights recent steps more and needs no start, because an average with a decay forgets the beginning by itself.
ema is updated after every optimiser step, which is what makes its decay mean what the literature means by it: 0.999 is 0.999 per step, so over 60 epochs of 200 batches that is 12,000 updates and a half-life of roughly 700 steps. A run with few steps wants a smaller number, because an average that forgets more slowly than the run is long never leaves where it started.



Three of these compute the rate from the epoch rather than from how the run is going - callback_cosine_annealing(), callback_linear_annealing() and callback_step_decay() - and at most one of them may be used, because each recomputes the rate every epoch and two of them would simply overwrite each other.
For the same reason a schedule and callback_reduce_lr_on_plateau() cannot be combined, and the engine refuses the pair. That refusal replaced a sentence claiming the opposite: a schedule recomputes the rate from the optimiser’s initial value at the end of every epoch, so it erases whatever the plateau callback cut. Measured on six epochs of a loss that never improves, the rate with both configured follows the cosine exactly - 0.0976, 0.0905, 0.0794 from 0.1 - where the plateau alone reaches 1e-6.
A schedule beside callback_swa() is fine and the order is no longer luck: swa pins its constant rate after averaging begins, whatever position the callbacks sit in.



callback_cosine_annealing() decays the learning rate from its initial value to min_lr along a cosine. It watches nothing: it is a function of how far through the run you are rather than of how the run is going, which is the difference from callback_reduce_lr_on_plateau() - and a run may legitimately want both.
Each parameter group decays from its own initial rate, so an encoder_learning_rate set on a model is not flattened at the first epoch. That would have been invisible: the history records one learning_rate, the first group’s.
epochs unset means the model’s own epochs, which is what you want - a cosine that ends where the run ends.




library("rplatypus")

callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_dice", patience = 10)

$name
[1] "early_stopping"

$monitor
[1] "val_dice"

$patience
[1] 10

$min_delta
[1] 0

$restore_best
[1] TRUE

title: rplatypus
text:
The picture that answers "where is it looking". Background - class 1 - is left alone, so only the classes that were found are tinted.



overlay_mask(image, mask, colormap, alpha = drawing_style()\$overlay_alpha)







image


A height x width x channels array. Values in 0-1 or 0-255; greyscale is repeated across three channels.




mask


Class indices, counted from 1, matching the image’s height and width.




colormap


A list of RGB triples, one per class.




alpha


How strongly to tint, 0 to 1.






A height x width x 3 array of 0-255 integers.




library("rplatypus")

image <- array(runif(8 * 8 * 3, 0.2, 0.6), dim = c(8, 8, 3))
mask <- matrix(1L, 8, 8); mask[2:4, 2:4] <- 2L
tinted <- overlay_mask(image, mask, colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 0, 0)))
dim(tinted)

[1] 8 8 3

title: rplatypus
text:
A voxel count answers nothing on its own: the same tumour is 4000 voxels on one scanner and 12000 on another, and neither number goes in a report. Multiplied by the volume of a voxel it becomes millilitres, which is comparable between scans, between patients and against whatever the radiologist measured by hand.



mask_volume(mask, spacing, class = 2L)







mask


A mask of class indices, as predict() returns - one volume, not a stack.




spacing


Voxel size in millimetres, length 3. volume_info() reports it; so does the spacing_1/2/3 columns of its output.




class


Which class to measure, numbered from 1 as the colormap and labels are. Defaults to 2, which is the foreground in a binary segmentation.






The volume in millilitres.




library("rplatypus")

mask <- array(1L, dim = c(10, 10, 4))
mask[3:6, 3:6, 2:3] <- 2L
# 32 voxels of 2 x 2 x 5 mm: 32 * 20 mm^3 = 640 mm^3 = 0.64 ml
mask_volume(mask, spacing = c(2, 2, 5))

[1] 0.64
crumbs: How much of a volume a class occupies, in millilitres

title: rplatypus
text:
Writes each mask as a label-map NIfTI carrying the geometry of the scan it was predicted from. That is the whole reason this is not save_masks() with a different extension: a mask array without an affine cannot be laid over its scan by any viewer, any registration tool or any volume calculation - it either lands in the wrong place or is refused.



save_volumes(masks, dir, reference, names = NULL, suffix = "")







masks


Masks of class indices, as predict() returns.
A list of volumes is what predict(space = “source”) gives, and the form to prefer: each mask is already on the grid of the scan it was computed from, so the geometry matches by construction and the scans need not be the same size as each other.
An array is also accepted: one volume as depth x height x width, a stack as volume x depth x height x width, probabilities as volume x depth x height x width x class which are collapsed to the most likely class. A single volume’s probabilities have the same rank as a stack of masks and are not guessed at - collapse them yourself, or keep the volume axis.




dir


Where to write. Created if it does not exist.




reference


The scan each mask was predicted from, in the same order. Its affine is what the mask is written with, so this is required rather than optional.




names


File names, without extension. Taken from reference when unset, which works when the scans have distinct filenames. They often do not - one directory per case, the same ct.nii.gz inside each - and writing every mask to one name would silently keep only the last, so that case is an error asking for this argument. split_path(split, “validation”)$key is usually the answer.




suffix


Appended to each name, for telling two models’ output apart.






Carrying the affine means the mask has to be on the same grid as the scan, which is what predict(space = “source”) is for: it maps each prediction back out of the model’s grid onto the scan’s. Without it, a resampled or resized prediction will be refused here rather than written somewhere wrong.



The paths written, invisibly.



save_masks() for 2D masks as pictures.




library("rplatypus")

validation <- split_path(split, "validation")
masks <- predict(fit, split = "validation", space = "source")
save_volumes(masks, "predictions", reference = validation$images)

dir


Where to write. Created if it does not exist.




reference


The scan each mask was predicted from, in the same order. Its affine is what the mask is written with, so this is required rather than optional.




names


File names, without extension. Taken from reference when unset, which works when the scans have distinct filenames. They often do not - one directory per case, the same ct.nii.gz inside each - and writing every mask to one name would silently keep only the last, so that case is an error asking for this argument. split_path(split, “validation”)$key is usually the answer.




suffix


Appended to each name, for telling two models’ output apart.






Carrying the affine means the mask has to be on the same grid as the scan, which is what predict(space = “source”) is for: it maps each prediction back out of the model’s grid onto the scan’s. Without it, a resampled or resized prediction will be refused here rather than written somewhere wrong.



The paths written, invisibly.



save_masks() for 2D masks as pictures.




library("rplatypus")

validation <- split_path(split, "validation")
masks <- predict(fit, split = "validation", space = "source")
save_volumes(masks, "predictions", reference = validation$images)

title: rplatypus
text:
Six listings beside available_transforms() and available_weights(): the losses, the metrics, the architectures, the optimisers, the callbacks and the tasks. Three columns - the name you write in a specification, the arguments you may tune, and what it is for.



available_losses(task = "semantic_segmentation")

available_metrics(task = "semantic_segmentation")

available_models(task = "semantic_segmentation")

available_optimizers()

available_callbacks()

available_tasks()

available_separations()

available_decodings()







task


“semantic_segmentation”, “instance_segmentation”, “object_detection” or “classification”. Which components a specification may name depends on what it is asking for, and for losses it genuinely differs: the three regression losses are listed only at the instance task, which is the only one with a target for them, and classification lists two of the eleven - the ones that score each answer on its own rather than scoring an overlap. No count is written here on purpose - the counts are asserted in the test suite against the pinned engine, which is where a number nobody can re-measure from a help page belongs. This parameter listed two tasks until the pin moved to 0.8.0a22, three until it moved to 0.8.0a49; the third arrived in the engine’s 0.8.0a20 and the fourth in 0.8.0a49.






Worth having because the alternative is leaving R for a website. The number of named components grows with every release, and these are read from the engine’s own schema, so a loss added there appears here with nothing in this package edited. Nothing is maintained by hand; a list maintained by hand is a list that will be wrong.
description is the component’s summary line. The rest of what the engine knows about it - including the measurements, where there are any - is on the configuration reference of the engine’s own site, which is generated from the same text.



A data frame with name, arguments and description. arguments is a single string per row, comma-separated, because a column of vectors prints as something nobody can read; strsplit(x, “,”) takes it apart.
Two listings carry one column more, and it is the column they are asked for: available_decodings() has needs, the separation a decoding requires - empty where it requires none, which is connected_components and is why that one is always available - and available_separations() has head_channels, how wide a head that target makes. Taken from the engine’s own rows rather than named on this side, so a listing that grows a field arrives here without R changing.



A detection specification chooses no loss component and no metrics at all. Its objective is fixed, with box_loss on the model picking the box term, and every detection run reports the same set - map_50, map_50_95, mean_matched_iou - which comes out of the run rather than going into the specification.
So available_losses(“object_detection”) and available_metrics(“object_detection”) raise a condition whose message says that, rather than returning a table with no rows. An empty table reads as "there are none", which is a different and wrong answer.
available_models(“classification”) raises for the same kind of reason and a different fact. A classifier chooses no architecture: the network is a contracting path, pooled, with one dense layer on top, and encoder decides whose contracting path it is - ours when it is unset, any of timm’s when it names a backbone. So there is no architecture field to write and a row here would invite one. encoders is the listing that question actually has.



available_transforms() and available_weights(), the two that came first, separations and decodings for the constructors these two listings name, and platypus_spec(), where all of them are written.




library("rplatypus")

available_losses()
#>            name                    arguments
#> 1      boundary               region, alpha
#> 2           cce             label_smoothing
#> 3      cce_dice          cce_weight, smooth
#> ...

# Which metrics take an argument at all, and which do not.
available_metrics()[, c("name", "arguments")]

# The entry point, for somebody who has read nothing yet.
available_tasks()

# The two instance axes: what a model can predict, and how those channels become objects.
available_separations()[, c("name", "head_channels")]
available_decodings()[, c("name", "needs")]

# Detection says what it has instead of a loss to choose.
try(available_losses("object_detection"))
crumbs: What a model is made of
What this package can do, asked of the package

title: rplatypus
text:
One row per object. voxels is the count, which means nothing outside one scanner, and spacing turns it into a number a reader can compare - the same argument mask_volume() makes for one class, applied per object. That is the question this whole feature is for: how many nuclei, and how big is each one.



instance_sizes(labels, spacing = NULL)







labels


An instance label map from predict() - one integer per object, 0 for background. Two dimensions for an image, three for a volume.




spacing


The size of one voxel in millimetres: two numbers for an image, three for a volume. Unset means the result counts voxels and says nothing about size.






The unit is decided by the rank, and the column is named after it rather than being called size with a note somewhere: area_mm2 for an image, volume_ml for a volume. A column whose unit lives in the documentation is a column that ends up in a paper as a bare number.
Without spacing there is no such column at all, rather than a count pretending to be a measurement.



A data frame with object, voxels and, when spacing is given, area_mm2 or volume_ml. One row per object present, in increasing object number; an object number absent from the map gets no row, because a model that found objects 1, 2 and 4 found three objects.



overlay_instances() to look at them, mask_volume() for one class of a semantic mask.




library("rplatypus")

labels <- matrix(0L, nrow = 8, ncol = 8)
labels[2:4, 2:4] <- 1L
labels[6:7, 6:8] <- 2L
instance_sizes(labels)

  object voxels
1      1      9
2      2      6

# 0.5 mm pixels: object 1 is 9 pixels, so 9 * 0.25 = 2.25 mm^2.
instance_sizes(labels, spacing = c(0.5, 0.5))

  object voxels area_mm2
1      1      9     2.25
2      2      6     1.50
crumbs: How big each object is, in units somebody can use

title: rplatypus
text:
Masks stored one file per object, read as a label map that keeps each object’s identity instead of uniting them into one foreground. The question this answers is how many nuclei, and how big is each one, which a semantic mask cannot answer however good it is: two touching nuclei are one region in it.



instance_data(
  train,
  validation = NULL,
  test = NULL,
  split = NULL,
  mode = c("nested_dirs", "config_file"),
  window = NULL,
  subdirs = c("images", "masks"),
  column_sep = ";",
  shuffle = TRUE
)







train


Training data: a directory, a configuration file, or a platypus_split from split_dataset(), which carries its own validation set and division.




validation


A validation set, or FALSE for none. Exactly one of validation and split, and neither when train is already a platypus_split.




test


A test set to predict on. Scored only if it carries masks.




split


Divide train instead of naming a validation set: a list with fractions (two numbers, or three to cut a test set too) and group_by, which is required and may be NULL. Exactly one of split and validation.




mode


“nested_dirs” or “config_file”.




window


How values in real units reach the model, for DICOM and NIfTI. See segmentation_data().




subdirs


For nested_dirs, the names of the image and mask subdirectories. The second one holds one file per object rather than one mask per image, which is the layout this task is named for.




column_sep


For config_file, what separates several paths in one cell.




shuffle


Shuffle the training data between epochs.






Why this exists rather than an argument on segmentation_data(). Every field instance_data() takes, that one takes too - what makes it a different constructor is the five it refuses: colormap, labels, regions, channels_from and target_spacing do not apply to a directory of per-object masks, and the engine rejects them by name. A constructor whose contract is "these five do not apply" is a contract rather than a label, and it gets that refusal from its own argument list rather than from a table somebody has to keep in step.
The consequence worth knowing before you choose: task is still read off the constructors rather than typed. Calling this one is how a specification says it is about instances, so there is no task = “instance_segmentation” to write and nothing to keep in agreement with it. See platypus_spec().
What the model does with this is the other half, and it is one block: a model’s separation says what the network predicts - rim or flows - and decode says how those channels become objects. Neither belongs here, because they describe the run and not the data.



A data specification, to be passed to platypus_spec().



segmentation_data() for one mask per image, platypus_spec()




library("rplatypus")

instance_data("stage1_train/", "stage1_validation/")

$train_path
[1] "stage1_train/"

$validation_path
[1] "stage1_validation/"

$validation
NULL

$test_path
NULL

$split
NULL

$mode
NULL

$window
NULL

$subdirs
NULL

$column_sep
NULL

$shuffle
NULL

attr(,"class")
[1] "platypus_instance_data" "list"                  
attr(,"task")
[1] "instance_segmentation"

title: rplatypus
text:
platypus_spec() reads a YAML file and builds a specification from arguments. This is the way back, so the two are one pipeline rather than one and a half: a specification assembled in R becomes a file somebody else can run, or that a script can keep beside its results.



save_spec(spec, path, defaults = FALSE)







spec


A platypus_spec, from platypus_spec().




path


Where to write it. The parent directory must exist.




defaults


Write every field at its resolved value, including the ones you never set.






It writes what you set, not what the specification holds. A model built from two arguments holds 29 fields once the engine has filled in its defaults, and writing all of them is not merely verbose - it changes what the file does. A model given weights and no architecture takes the architecture from the weights sidecar, and that adoption happens precisely because the field was never set. Freeze the defaults into the file and the adoption can never happen again: the file looks like the original and quietly stops doing what the original did.
defaults = TRUE is the opposite want, and a legitimate one: freeze this run exactly as it resolved so it reproduces years from now. The cost is the paragraph above, by design.



The path, invisibly.



platypus_spec(), which reads one back, and read_record() for what a run did as opposed to what it was asked to do.




library("rplatypus")

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data("train/", "valid/", colormap = binary_colormap),
  models = list(u_net("unet", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)

save_spec(spec, "experiment.yaml")
identical(as.list(platypus_spec("experiment.yaml")), as.list(spec))

# Everything the engine resolved, for a run that has to reproduce in five years.
save_spec(spec, "frozen.yaml", defaults = TRUE)
crumbs: Write a specification back out as YAML

title: rplatypus
text:
The number every decision about this task’s metrics turned on, and the person who most needs it is the one who has just written a specification and not yet run anything. A prevalence a reader does not know is one they will discover from a score that looks fine.



class_balance(spec, split = "train")







spec


A platypus_spec() describing a classification task.




split


Which split to count: “train”, “validation” or “test”.






The sentence under the table is the engine’s own, printed rather than reproduced: the threshold it fires below is the engine’s number, and a copy of it here would be a second place for one fact to live.



A data frame of one row per class, in class order, with columns class, n and share, of class platypus_class_balance so that printing it adds the engine’s own remark about how lopsided the split is. The engine’s sentence is carried on the remark attribute.



classification_data(), split()




library("rplatypus")

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = classification_data("train/", "valid/", classes = c("benign", "malignant")),
  models = list(classifier("cnn", input_shape = c(128, 128)))
)
class_balance(spec)
